The Michoacán operation capped the week’s security news: Soldiers and National Guard troops arrested nine people, including two women identified as relatives of CJNG plaza boss Heraclio “Tío Lako” Guerrero Martínez, who evaded capture as the operation set off blockades that were largely cleared by Wednesday afternoon.

That flow of cooperation announcements ran alongside a separate dispute over fuel smuggling and politics. Sheinbaum said at Tuesday’s mañanera that fuel smuggling, or huachicol fiscal, is “practically over” in Mexico thanks to customs interventions and arrests — a claim she offered in the context of defending her government against opposition criticism. That criticism stems partly from the U.S. revocation of the visa of Andrés Manuel López Beltrán, son of former President López Obrador, which Sheinbaum has called a political matter, saying he “was not” ever on authorities’ radar for criminal involvement. The fuel-trafficking case itself advanced this week when Rear Admiral Fernando Farías Laguna, accused of leading a Pemex-linked smuggling ring, was extradited from Argentina and jailed at the Altiplano maximum security prison. The case has damaged the Navy’s reputation and drawn indirect allegations, which Sheinbaum has rejected, involving López Beltrán.

Strawberries, Vietnam imports and a Canada call test trade ties

Mexico is contesting a U.S. Commerce Department finding that could impose antidumping tariffs on Mexican strawberries, which supplies 98% of U.S. strawberry imports. Economy Minister Marcelo Ebrard called the U.S. criteria “arbitrarily applied” and inconsistent with USMCA provisions; a final ITC ruling isn’t expected until early 2027, and the case could affect roughly 5,000 Mexican producers and 151,000 jobs if it proceeds. Sheinbaum has warned the case could set a precedent for challenging other Mexican agricultural exports.

Separately, Mexico’s imports from Vietnam more than doubled in the first half of 2026 to $18.4 billion, a jump that has raised suspicions — flagged in a recent White House report naming Mexico a “Tier 1” transshipment risk — that Chinese goods are being routed through Vietnam to dodge Mexico’s tariffs on non-free-trade-agreement countries. Mexico has denied being a transshipment hub for Chinese goods bound for the U.S.

Against that backdrop, President Sheinbaum and Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney discussed North American trade by phone on Thursday. Carney’s office said the two underscored the importance of renewing the USMCA pact soon, and separately thanked Mexico for deploying more than 400 firefighters to help combat wildfires in British Columbia. The call came as Trump-imposed tariffs on Canadian goods, delayed this week, loomed for Saturday absent a deal. (The U.S. tariffs on Canada ultimately went into effect after trade talks collapsed late Friday night.)

Peso strength collides with a cautious Banxico

The peso dropped below 17 to the U.S. dollar this week, dropping below 16.9 on Friday, largely on dollar weakness following a U.S. Treasury bond buyback announcement. The currency has appreciated nearly 6% in 2026, a gain Banxico credits with helping cool inflation.

Even so, the central bank held its benchmark rate at 6.5% earlier this month. In meeting minutes released this week, four of five board members cited persistent services inflation as a driver of that decision. Headline inflation slowed to 3.12% in July, but Banxico now doesn’t expect it to reach its 3% target until the fourth quarter of 2027. The bank also flagged Middle East tensions as an upside risk to oil prices. Separately, INEGI’s preliminary July data showed the economy growing 2.7% annually, which Rodríguez called “another piece of good news” following 2.1% growth in the second quarter.

Other business and finance news this week:

Mañanera themes: EVs, phone lines and a presidential sick day

On Monday, Sheinbaum said she opposes a social-media ban for minors like Australia’s, calling the idea “very problematic” and noting enforcement challenges, while Education Minister Mario Delgado announced a nationwide teacher consultation on classroom device rules ahead of the Aug. 31 school year.

At Thursday’s press conference, Sheinbaum unveiled a prototype of Olinia Carga, the government’s second domestically developed electric vehicle, a light-cargo EV that can carry 650 kilograms and will sell for around 150,000 pesos starting in late 2027. The same day brought a new arrest in the 2024 kidnapping case of Sinaloa Cartel figure “El Mayo” Zambada.

On Friday, Interior Minister Rosa Icela Rodríguez, standing in for an ill Sheinbaum, told U.S. Ambassador Johnson that Mexico disagrees with Washington’s decision to deport some Mexicans to Guatemala, Honduras and Costa Rica rather than to Mexico.

Elsewhere, millions of Mexican cell phone lines were suspended after an Aug. 15 mandatory registration deadline passed, though regulators say most affected users can still recover service. Mexico also abstained from an OAS vote, which passed 29-1, to convene an emergency session on Nicaragua’s move to bar opposition candidates, with representative Alejandro Encinas citing Mexico’s non-intervention principle. Friday’s mañanera, run by Rodríguez after Sheinbaum announced she had the flu, also touched on new archaeological finds in a Chiapas cave tied to Zoque ritual traditions.

Regional news roundup:

And some good news to close out the week:

Looking ahead

Several threads left open this week are likely to develop further: Security cooperation with the U.S. continues to strengthen, while trade friction between the two countries shows no sign of easing. On a practical note, cell phone users facing the next registration deadlines — Aug. 31 for numbers ending in “1” — should act before their lines are suspended.

World.title: From the archive: How to whistle like a true Mexican
World.content:
The goal of our “From the Archive” series is to revisit popular stories that capture the unique history and culture of life in Mexico. This Sarah DeVries article — originally published in January 2025 — is a perfect example, offering humorous insight into the fine art of whistling.

I have known no jealousy like the jealousy I feel when I hear Mexicans’ elaborate category of effortless whistles.

Okay fine, they’re not effortless. They just sound that way because they learned how to do it when they were kids. You know, like speaking Spanish.

Indeed, whistling is part of the language in some meaningful ways. There are specific whistles used for getting people’s attention. There are whistles for saying “Hey buddy, what’s up?” from across the street. There are whistles for saying, “But of course, my horse” — okay, maybe not exactly that, but a kind of “You know it!” with that adorable tone. There are whistles to say, “Wowza, nice butt, strange woman I don’t know!” Some whistles say, “Okay, back up your car now, a little more, a little more, a little more, stop!” There are even whistles to tell people where they can stuff it. Careful with those.

And I am going to learn them all.

A realistic goal

Well, I’m going to try. Forget turning my health or finances around; it’s too big a task. I need something I actually stand a chance at being able to bite off. Even though the prospect of practicing them takes me back to the deep humiliation I felt trying to string a four-word sentence together in Spanish while the three-year-old next to me rattled off deep, complex sentence after deep, complete sentence, I’m committed. I did it once, and I can do it again!

I won’t necessarily use them all, or use them frequently. In fact, I’m fairly certain that men whistle much more than women around here, anyway. Like cursing, it falls into a decidedly “male” category of behavior, and is seen as somewhat crass and unladylike.

I’ve also noticed that whistling is more prevalent among lower socio-economic classes than among the more well-to-do. Part of this is simply cultural habit, growing out of the need to communicate at great distances. It’s more pleasant sounding, and clearer, than shouting. If you’re willing to do some digging, there are actually some fascinating examples of whistles-as-language. There’s a cool short video about this below.

But I don’t need to be communicating over great distances in the Oaxaca countryside. I just want to have some fun.

Indigenous Whistle Language In Mexico

Watch this video on YouTube

And I don’t want to go too fast, but I’m also an eager learner. This video is pretty cute, by the way, as an introduction to the meanings of different whistles.

Here are the specific ones that I want to learn:

Learning how to whistle in Mexico (in different styles, for different purposes)

The whistle to get someone’s attention

Say you’re walking along a busy street and you need to get someone’s attention. Maybe it’s a vendor, or maybe a taxi that didn’t notice you! This whistle is perfect for it. It’s also important for me personally, because my voice does not carry at all. My loudest is not very loud, and the strain on my voice physically hurts! This can either be a quick low-high sound, or the more universally recognized high-low-slightly higher.

The ‘you can count on me, buddy’ whistle

I mostly want to learn this one because I think it’s both hilarious and adorable. My partner does this one sometimes, and even though it’s kind of a joke, I am 100% charmed.

‘Hey, friend on the other side of the street!’

Finally, I’ve just got to learn this whistle. It’s short and sweet, and I don’t care that I’ve hardly ever heard it from a woman’s lips.

So those are the three goals. Three distinct whistles — I can kind of do a “pucker” whistle now, but not very well — should be manageable in a year, right?

In the meantime, I’m dying to know: can you whistle? Can you do any specifically Mexican whistles? I especially want to know how many women out there can — please let me know in the comments!

Sarah DeVries is a writer and translator based in Xalapa, Veracruz. She can be reached through her website, sarahedevries.substack.com.

World.title: Guadalajara residents turn to citizen science as water crisis deepens
World.content:
On a Saturday morning in Guadalajara’s historic Analco neighborhood, residents arrived at the Casa Bandera community center carrying bottles and jars filled with water from their homes.

At folding tables, researchers from ITESO, Guadalajara’s Jesuit university, showed them how to dip inexpensive reactive strips into the samples, wait for the colors to change and compare the results against a chart measuring pH, chlorine, lead, mercury and other indicators. Samples showing signs of possible bacterial contamination could undergo additional testing for E. coli.

It was the latest workshop in an expanding citizen water-monitoring network that has grown out of Guadalajara’s months-long water crisis — and out of residents’ frustration with what they see as inadequate information and action from the authorities responsible for providing safe water.

“We don’t claim to be scientific specialists or water experts,” Héctor Morales, one of the workshop presenters, told participants. “We are citizens contributing evidence from what we are observing and living through, and that is equally valid.”

“We’re not trying to compete with science,” he continued. “We’re trying to generate knowledge that comes from everyday life. That’s the approach of citizen science.”

Sunday: Mega March + Agua KK Fest

Guadalajara’s water activists will be having some fun with the theme at Sunday’s festival — without losing sight of the very serious problem behind it.

When: Sunday, Aug. 23

10 a.m.: Gather at Parque Rojo

11 a.m.: Mega March for Water departs along Av. Juárez

Noon: Agua KK Fest at Plaza Liberación

The workshops will feature home water filters, rainwater harvesting, dry toilets and water testing, plus children’s activities, music, decorated water jugs, costumes and karaoke. The cheeky Agua KK name is a play on the word caca — a pointed joke about the dirty water that residents say has been coming from their taps.

From complaints to citizen evidence

The network brings together neighborhood residents, scientists from ITESO University, the Mexican Institute for Community Development (IMDEC) and the citizen campaign #ElSiapaQueQueremos, or The SIAPA We Want — SIAPA being the city water utility.

The idea is not simply to tell residents what might be in their water. María González of IMDEC said the testing has two purposes: helping families take care of themselves, and creating a body of evidence that can be used to press authorities for action.

“This helps us protect ourselves. You are going to know what is in the water in your homes,” González told the group. But the results, she said, are also “our citizen evidence for legal action, for institutional action, for mobilization.”

Before Saturday’s workshop, the network had analyzed roughly 184 samples from 90 neighborhoods in five municipalities. Organizers said residual chlorine was found in only 12 of the 184 samples. That’s a problem, they pointed out. Chlorine is added during water treatment, and a small amount should remain as water travels through the distribution network to help protect it from bacterial contamination.

The monitoring also detected lead in 20 samples, fluoride in 52 and mercury in an unspecified number, according to Morales. Four of the 184 samples tested positive for E. coli, a form of fecal coliform bacteria.

The citizen findings are not a statistically representative survey of Guadalajara’s water supply, a limitation organizers repeatedly emphasized. The low-cost tests do not measure all of the dozens of parameters required under Mexico’s drinking-water standard.

“What does this analysis tell us?” Morales asked. “It tells us when the water is not safe. What doesn’t it tell us? It doesn’t tell us when the water is good.”

Certifying water as safe, he said, requires much more extensive laboratory testing.

Still, official testing has now documented some of the same warning signs.

In late July, Jalisco health authorities confirmed that E. coli had been detected in 18 of 297 samples analyzed between March and June in neighborhoods affected by water-quality problems. Officials also acknowledged insufficient chlorination in some areas.

The findings came after months of complaints about yellow, brown or foul-smelling water, as well as sediment and service interruptions across the Guadalajara metropolitan area. González said the #ElSiapaQueQueremos campaign has now received nearly 1,500 complaints, with water quality by far the most common problem, followed by outages and high rates.

A multibillion-peso response

The Jalisco government and SIAPA, the metropolitan water utility, have acknowledged serious problems in the aging system and announced a long-term overhaul requiring more than 20 billion pesos in investment.

Among the major projects are the replacement of the aging Chapala-Guadalajara aqueduct and the modernization and expansion of Potabilizadora No. 1 in Miravalle. Governor Pablo Lemus said this month that the federal government had agreed to support both projects.

But for the citizen coalition, repairing infrastructure is only part of the solution.

The movement is increasingly focusing on who participates in decisions about the water system, how information is shared and whether communities themselves can have a formal role in monitoring and oversight.

That shift will be on display Sunday, when the same groups organizing the monitoring workshops will hold a “Mega March for Water.” Participants will gather at Parque Rojo at 10 a.m. and march along Avenida Juárez to Plaza Liberación, where the deliberately scatological “Agua KK Fest” — a play on caca, or “poop,” in reference to residents’ complaints about dirty water — will begin at noon.

The festival will combine protest with workshops on household filters, rainwater harvesting, dry toilets, urban gardens, community water systems and water-quality monitoring. Organizers describe the event as peaceful, family-oriented and nonpartisan.

Beyond fixing SIAPA

The coalition’s demands now extend beyond cleaner water. Its latest statement calls for greater transparency, citizen participation in decisions over water quality, distribution and infrastructure, formal recognition of community monitoring and protection of the watersheds that supply the metropolitan area.

It also proposes “public-community agreements” that would bring SIAPA, universities, neighborhood organizations, workers and other sectors together to share knowledge and participate in water governance.

The organizers explicitly reject privatization as the answer to SIAPA’s failures.

“The alternative to an inefficient SIAPA is not a privatized SIAPA,” their statement says, calling instead for a public utility that is transparent, efficient and subject to democratic social oversight.

González said the campaign is also pushing for a permanent working group focused specifically on water quality, health and sanitary risks. Authorities have not yet agreed to participate.

But organizers do not intend to wait indefinitely.

The group, González said, “is going to be established with authorities or without authorities,” functioning independently if necessary to prevent health risks.

That determination reflects how far the movement has come since residents first began showing up at public meetings with bottles of discolored water.

Morales said citizen monitoring allows residents to reach places government agencies may not sample and to turn individual experiences into systematic evidence. He has watched workshop participants take what they learn back to their neighborhoods — and then into the streets.

“It’s beautiful to see people who come to the workshops later at demonstrations with signs saying, ‘There are nitrates and nitrites in our water,’” he said.

“The authorities never expected that.”

World.title: The Sahel Juntas Open a Parliament in Niamey
World.content:
By subscribing you agree to our privacy policy . We never share your email.

Western Africa · Geopolitics

Key Facts —What is happening: The first confederal session of the Alliance of Sahel States parliaments runs from 24 to 29 August 2026 in Niamey. —Where: Niger’s own Conseil consultatif de la refondation, the body that replaced the dissolved National Assembly, is hosting the delegations. No venue or sitting order has been published. —Who came: The heads of the Malian and Burkinabe legislatures arrived in Niamey on Saturday 22 August. —How members are chosen: Deputies are designated by the three national transitional legislatures, not directly elected. No seat total has been published. —What powers: Oversight of the confederation’s organs, public information and carrying citizens’ concerns upward, on the description given by Burkina Faso’s assembly president. —The paper trail: Founding instruments were drafted in Ouagadougou in September 2025 and adopted by the three heads of state in Bamako on 23 December 2025.

The AES confederal parliament holds its inaugural session in Niamey this week, giving the alliance of Mali, Burkina Faso and Niger a legislature to sit alongside its joint force. Its members are designated by three military-led governments rather than elected by any voter.

What is actually convening

The first confederal session of the Alliance of Sahel States parliaments is scheduled to run from 24 to 29 August 2026 in Niamey. The inaugural sitting takes place at the Centre de Conference Mahatma Gandhi, with the first ordinary session following two days later.

The presidents of the Malian and Burkinabe legislatures flew into Niamey on Saturday 22 August and were received by their Nigerien host. That host is Mamoudou Harouna Djingarey, president of Niger’s Conseil consultatif de la refondation.

Mali is represented by General Malick Diaw, president of the Conseil national de transition, its transitional legislature. Burkina Faso is represented by Ousmane Bougouma, president of the Assemblée législative du peuple — the body renamed from the Assemblée législative de Transition in March 2026.

The names tell you most of what you need to know about the institution. All three are the appointed legislatures of governments that took power by coup, in Mali in 2020 and 2021, Burkina Faso in 2022 and Niger in 2023.

Designated, not elected

This is the detail that defines the body. Bougouma said in June that the deputies would be designated in the coming days, using the French verb for appointment rather than election.

No seat total has been published, and no allocation between the three countries has been made public. We are not going to print a number that nobody has released.

The declared functions are modest. Bougouma described them as scrutinising the action of the confederation’s organs, informing citizens about community policies and carrying the peoples’ concerns to the confederal level.

No legislative power and no budgetary power is claimed in any account we could find. On the available evidence this is a consultative and oversight chamber rather than a lawmaking one.

Why the AES confederal parliament matters anyway

The temptation is to dismiss it as theatre, and that would be a mistake. Institutions acquire functions over time, and the three governments have been consistent about building them.

The alliance began as the Liptako-Gourma Charter of 16 September 2023, a mutual defence pact. It was upgraded to a confederation at the Niamey summit of 6 July 2024, and it has since acquired a joint force and a common security posture.

The founding instruments were adopted by the three legislative presidents at a meeting in Ouagadougou on 18 and 19 September 2025, from texts their deputies and technical advisers had prepared that August. They were adopted by the conference of heads of state in Bamako on 23 December 2025.

A confederation with a legislature is a different object from a confederation with only soldiers. It is the structure you build if you intend the arrangement to outlast the men who made it.

What it means for money

All three governments have rewritten the terms on which foreigners mine their minerals. Mali has fought Barrick over Loulo-Gounkoto, Burkina Faso has bought back mining assets from foreign firms, and Niger has taken on Orano over uranium.

A confederal chamber gives future decisions of that kind a legitimating stamp. It also gives the three a single forum in which to harmonise mining codes, which is a prospect worth watching if you hold West African mining exposure.

There is a monetary question sitting behind it too. A confederal bank has been discussed, and Mali, Burkina Faso and Niger all still use the CFA franc, whose West African variant is pegged to the euro, with a French convertibility guarantee, though the old operations account at the French Treasury was closed under reforms agreed between 2019 and 2021.

None of that is decided. But the machinery for deciding it is being assembled in public, and this week is a visible part of the assembly.

The distance from ECOWAS keeps growing

The three states formally left the Economic Community of West African States in January 2025, after a year’s notice. ECOWAS has kept the door ajar; the alliance has kept walking.

Each new confederal institution raises the cost of going back. A parliament is harder to unwind than a communique.

For businesses trading across the region the practical questions are tariffs, transit and recognition of documents, and those now depend on two rulebooks rather than one. Coastal states from Senegal to Benin sit on the other side of that line.

One caution on the reporting. The account of the arrivals comes from Niger’s state news agency, and we could not independently confirm that the session opened as scheduled on Monday.

Frequently Asked Questions

What is the AES confederal parliament? It is the legislative body of the Alliance of Sahel States, the confederation of Mali, Burkina Faso and Niger. Its inaugural session is scheduled for 24 to 29 August 2026 in Niamey. Are its members elected? No. Deputies are designated by the three national transitional legislatures rather than directly elected, and no seat total has been published. What powers does it have? On the description given by Burkina Faso’s assembly president, it oversees the confederation’s organs, informs citizens about community policies and carries public concerns to the confederal level. No legislative or budgetary power is claimed. When was it created? Founding instruments were drafted in Ouagadougou in September 2025 and adopted by the three heads of state in Bamako on 23 December 2025. How did the alliance start? As the Liptako-Gourma Charter, a mutual defence pact signed on 16 September 2023, upgraded to a confederation at the Niamey summit of 6 July 2024.

World.title: Nigeria Opens Central Bank Bills to Small Savers
World.content:
By subscribing you agree to our privacy policy . We never share your email.

Western Africa · Markets

Key Facts —The change: A Central Bank of Nigeria circular dated 12 August 2026 opened open market operations to individuals, corporates and non-bank financial institutions, routed through deposit money banks. —The yield: The first auction under the new rules cleared at 20.39% on the 103-day tenor and 20.01% on the 138-day. —The demand: The bank offered 600 billion naira (about US$445 million) on 13 August and received 4.93 trillion naira (about US$3.66 billion) of bids. It allotted 2.60 trillion. —The market: The Nigerian Exchange fell 1.35% in the week to 21 August, with the All-Share Index down to 239,351.16 from 242,619.20. —The value: Market capitalisation fell 1.33% to 154.534 trillion naira (about US$114.72 billion), a drop of about 2.09 trillion. —Still up on the year: Despite the slide the index is up 53.81% so far in 2026.

A Nigerian reform published on 12 August lets ordinary savers buy OMO bills — short-dated central bank paper issued to mop up cash in the banking system — yielding about 20%, and the Lagos stock market has fallen for nine consecutive sessions, a run that began the day before the circular appeared. The circular reverses a restriction that had kept retail money out of those auctions since 2019.

What the Nigeria OMO circular actually did

The document is titled Review of Discount Window Restrictions and Open Market Operations Participation Framework, and it is dated 12 August 2026. It was signed by Okey Umeano, acting director of the Financial Markets Department.

It authorises individuals, corporates and non-bank financial institutions to take part in both the primary and secondary markets for central bank bills. They must go through deposit money banks, which submit bids and settle on their behalf.

The central bank keeps control of volume, tenor and frequency. What it has given up is the wall that kept ordinary savers out of the highest risk-free naira yield in the country.

That wall went up in 2019, when the bank barred non-bank locals from these auctions in order to push money toward lending. Reversing it is a deliberate act of liquidity management, and it worked immediately.

The first auction was oversubscribed eight times over

On 13 August the bank offered 600 billion naira (about US$445 million), split evenly between a 103-day and a 138-day tenor. It received 4.93 trillion naira (about US$3.66 billion) in bids.

It allotted 2.60 trillion, more than four times what it had offered. The 103-day paper cleared at 20.39% and the 138-day at 20.01%.

The longer tenor tells the sharper story. Against 300 billion naira (about US$223 million) offered, investors bid 3.658 trillion, and the bank allotted 2.154 trillion at a true yield of 21.66%.

This followed a stretch of heavy liquidity. The bank absorbed more than 7 trillion naira (about US$5.20 billion) in July, mopped 4.7 trillion on 3 and 4 August, and made a single 2.48 trillion repayment on 11 August.

What it has done to equities

The Nigerian Exchange has fallen every session since the circular. In the week to 21 August the All-Share Index dropped 3,268.04 points, or 1.35%, to 239,351.16 from 242,619.20.

Market capitalisation fell 1.33% to 154.534 trillion naira (about US$114.72 billion), a loss of roughly 2.09 trillion. Measured from the day of the circular the decline is about 2.96 trillion.

The pattern is what you would expect. If a saver can get 20% from the central bank with no credit risk, the equity risk premium has to widen to compete.

The heaviest losses were in some of the most heavily capitalised stocks, which the exchange’s own commentary put down largely to profit-taking. Aradel Holdings dropped 9.99% over the week, First HoldCo 7.2%, MTN Nigeria 3.2% and Unilever Nigeria 3.6%.

Who wins and who pays

Savers win, and they have been waiting a long time. Nigerian deposit rates have lagged inflation for years, and this is the first instrument in a while that puts a real return within reach: Nigerian headline inflation was 15.43% in July, so a 20.4% yield is roughly five points of positive real return of a retail account.

Banks are more exposed than they look. Analysts expect the roughly 400 basis point gap between Treasury bills and central bank bills of comparable tenor to close, and deposit rates to be dragged up with it.

That squeezes the deposit franchise that has made Nigerian banking so profitable. Cheap current-account funding is the foundation of those margins.

For companies, the cost of raising equity has just gone up. A market where the risk-free alternative pays 20% is a harder place to price a share issue.

The caution to carry

Causation here is the interpretation of the Nigerian financial press and the analysts it quotes, not a proven fact. The same reporting also cites ordinary profit-taking.

We looked for an alternative explanation and did not find a sourced one. What the market itself is discussing is the yield.

It is also worth keeping the fall in proportion. The index is still up 53.81% for the year to date, and down 2.42% for the month.

The real question is whether this is a repricing or a rotation. A repricing settles at a new level, while a rotation keeps pulling money out for as long as the yield stays above 20%.

Frequently Asked Questions

What is the Nigeria OMO reform? A Central Bank of Nigeria circular dated 12 August 2026 that opened open market operations to individuals, corporates and non-bank financial institutions, through deposit money banks. It reverses a restriction imposed in 2019. What yield do the bills pay? The first auction under the new rules cleared at 20.39% on the 103-day tenor and 20.01% on the 138-day, on 13 August 2026. How much demand was there? The bank offered 600 billion naira (about US$445 million) and received 4.93 trillion naira (about US$3.66 billion) of bids, allotting 2.60 trillion. How far has the stock market fallen? The All-Share Index fell 1.35% in the week to 21 August to 239,351.16, and market capitalisation fell about 2.09 trillion naira (about US$1.55 billion) to 154.534 trillion. The index remains up 53.81% for the year. Is the reform definitely the cause? That is the interpretation of the Nigerian financial press and the analysts it quotes. The same reporting also cites profit-taking.

World.title: Brazil’s First Presidential Debate Held With Empty Lecterns
World.content:
Brazil · POLITICS

Key Facts — What happened Only 3 of 6 invited candidates took part in Brazil’s first 2026 presidential debate.

— How big a no-show It was the smallest opening-debate lineup since 1989, with 3 empty lecterns.

— The real story Poll leaders Lula and Flávio Bolsonaro skipped, and Romeu Zema pulled out on the day.

— The catch Attending debates is not compulsory under Brazil’s Law 9.504 of 1997, and no penalty applies.

— Where it happened TV Bandeirantes studio in São Paulo, broadcast on Band, TV Cultura, TV Gazeta and Jovem Pan.

— What comes next Free TV campaign ads start Friday 28 August 2026; first round vote is 4 October 2026.

With the two front-runners absent, the opening face-off drew the smallest lineup since 1989, just days before free TV campaign ads begin.

The National Congress in Brasília. Brazil votes in the first round on 4 October 2026.

Brazil’s first presidential debate of the 2026 campaign took place on Sunday 23 August 2026 with only three of six invited candidates on stage. The other three lecterns stood empty in the TV Bandeirantes studio in São Paulo.

A sight that underscored the absence of the two front-runners.

A Sparse Stage in São Paulo

Therefore, the first presidential debate, broadcast at 8pm local time, featured just Ronaldo Caiado, Renan Santos, and Augusto Cury. According to Poder360, three lecterns reserved for Lula, Flávio Bolsonaro and Romeu Zema remained empty throughout the event.

Folha de S. Paulo noted that this was the smallest number of participants in an opening debate since 1989.

In earlier cycles, the inaugural face-offs drew more candidates: eight in 2018, seven in 1989, 1994 and 2014, and six in 2022. The debate was organized by Band in partnership with the newspaper Estadão, as reported by G1.

However, only three of the six invited candidates took part, leaving the stage unusually empty.

First Presidential Debate Draws No-Shows

Meanwhile, Lula and Flávio Bolsonaro, the two leaders in polls, both decided not to attend. Folha de S.

Paulo reported that Lula’s justification was that he would be at a disadvantage having to answer attacks from five opponents. Flávio Bolsonaro never confirmed his attendance and issued no statement explaining his absence, according to Valor Econômico and Poder360.

Meanwhile, Romeu Zema of the Novo party pulled out on the day of the debate, blaming Lula’s absence as the reason. In addition, the broadcaster moved the debate to 23 August to try to get Lula to attend, according to Valor Econômico.

Still, both Lula and Flávio Bolsonaro stayed away, leaving the stage to the lesser-known candidates.

Zema’s Last-Minute Withdrawal

Romeu Zema’s decision came on Sunday 23 August 2026, however. O Globo reported it was due to Lula’s absence, who would have been his main opponent.

In addition, his team released a statement, quoted by O Globo. The Novo party’s position is one of opposition to the Lula government, whose record it considers a tragedy.

This left only three candidates on stage, a sharp contrast to the six that Band had originally invited. The broadcaster had even moved the debate from 16 August to 23 August, however.

This was in an attempt to secure Lula’s participation, as reported by Valor Econômico. After Zema pulled out, only three candidates remained, as reported by Folha de S.

Paulo. Meanwhile, his withdrawal highlighted the challenge of attracting top contenders to the debate.

The Empty Lecterns on Display

The visual of the three empty lecterns was striking, as described by Poder360. In fact, Renan Santos stood on the viewer’s left, followed by empty spots for Lula and Flávio, then Caiado and Cury.

This layout made the absences impossible to ignore. In fact, the sparse turnout was a talking point in the coverage, with Folha de S.

Paulo highlighting the historical low. The debate itself proceeded with just the three confirmed candidates, each representing different parties.

The empty lecterns were a visual reminder of the absent front-runners. However, the three who did show up proceeded with the debate, according to Poder360.

Who Did Show Up?

The three candidates were Ronaldo Caiado, Renan Santos, and Augusto Cury, as identified by Veja. Each brought their own background to the debate, though the coverage did not detail their arguments.

Despite the reduced lineup, the event went ahead as scheduled. The debate was broadcast on Band, TV Cultura, TV Gazeta, and Jovem Pan, according to BBC News Brasil.

The three candidates each had distinct backgrounds, as noted by Veja. However, the coverage did not detail their arguments or exchanges during the debate.

A Legal Gray Area, Not a Penalty

In Brazil, attending a televised debate is not compulsory. Article 46 of Law 9.504 of 1997 states debates follow rules set by parties and the broadcaster.

However, where there is no agreement, the broadcaster invites candidates with minimum congressional representation. Moreover, no penalty for missing a debate exists in the law or in the coverage checked on 23 and 24 August 2026.

A debate absence does not affect a candidacy registration, as confirmed by research against Law 9.504 and Superior Electoral Court Resolution 23.760. While attendance is not compulsory, the law sets no penalty for missing a debate.

As a result, the absence of the leading candidates carries no legal consequences for their campaigns.

The Road to the October Vote

Brazil’s first presidential debate came weeks before the first round on 4 October 2026, with a possible runoff on 25 October. The debate also preceded the start of free election advertising on radio and television, which begins on Friday 28 August 2026.

Thirteen presidential candidacies were registered with the Superior Electoral Court for the 2026 election, according to Agência Senado and Metrópoles. The sparse debate turnout, therefore, was not due to a lack of candidates, but rather the choices of the leading contenders.

The debate came just over a month before the first round of voting on 4 October 2026. Since free advertising starts on 28 August, the debate was one of the last major pre-campaign events.

Historical Context of Opening Debates

The first presidential debate this year had the smallest number of participants since 1989, as reported by Folha de S. Paulo.

In 2018, the opening debate featured eight candidates, the largest in the series. By contrast, 2022 had six, including Lula, Jair Bolsonaro, Ciro Gomes, Simone Tebet, Soraya Thronicke and Felipe D’Ávila.

By contrast, this year’s event saw only three candidates, a significant drop. The absence of the two poll leaders, Lula and Flávio Bolsonaro, was the main reason for the reduced turnout.

In contrast to previous years, this year’s opening debate had the fewest participants since 1989. However, the absence of the poll leaders was the main reason for the reduced turnout.

What This Means for the Campaign

The empty lecterns at the first presidential debate sent a clear signal about the strategies of the leading candidates. Lula’s stated reason for skipping was to avoid being attacked by multiple opponents, while Flávio Bolsonaro offered no explanation.

Nevertheless, the debate still provided a platform for the three candidates who attended, even if the spotlight was on those who didn’t. As the campaign moves toward the October vote, the absence of the front-runners from this debate may become a talking point.

Still, it carries no legal consequences. The empty lecterns may influence voter perceptions, but they do not affect the legal status of any candidacy.

Still, the debate provided a platform for the three who attended, even if the focus was on those who didn’t.

Frequently Asked Questions

Who participated in Brazil’s first presidential debate of 2026?

Only three of the six invited candidates took the stage: Ronaldo Caiado of the PSD. Renan Santos of Missão and Augusto Cury of Avante.

Why did Lula and Flávio Bolsonaro skip the debate?

Lula decided not to attend, according to Folha de S. Paulo, because he would be at a disadvantage having to answer attacks from five opponents.

Is it mandatory for Brazilian presidential candidates to attend debates?

No, attending a televised debate is not compulsory in Brazil. Law 9.504 of 1997 sets rules for debates but does not impose a penalty for absence.

When is the first round of the 2026 Brazilian presidential election?

The first round is scheduled for Sunday 4 October 2026, with a possible runoff on Sunday 25 October 2026. Free election advertising on radio and TV begins on Friday 28 August 2026.

Sources: Folha de S.Paulo; G1; Poder360; O Globo; Veja; BBC News Brasil; Valor Econômico; TV Bandeirantes; Superior Electoral Court.

World.title: Nigeria’s Power Grid Fell to 1,132 Megawatts
World.content:
By subscribing you agree to our privacy policy . We never share your email.

Western Africa · Energy

Key Facts —The number: National generation fell to 1,132.02 megawatts at 20:30 on Saturday 22 August 2026, having run above 4,000 megawatts earlier the same day. —The recovery: Output was back to 1,793.79 megawatts by 21:00. —Who was producing nothing: Twelve named stations showed zero output, including Egbin, Geregu, Kainji, Shiroro and Zungeru. —How many were running: Only ten generating companies were feeding the system at the low point. —The consequence: Distribution companies began load shedding, with Eko Disco — one of Nigeria’s privatised electricity distribution companies — citing low allocation from the grid. —The explanation: None. Neither the system operator nor the ministry had accounted for the failure.

A partial collapse of Nigeria’s grid on Saturday night drove national electricity generation down to 1,132.02 megawatts, roughly a quarter of what the system had been carrying earlier in the day. Twelve major power stations were producing nothing at all, and no authority has explained why.

What the partial collapse looked like on the dashboard

The figures come from the live grid performance dashboard published by the Nigerian Independent System Operator. At 20:30 on Saturday 22 August, national generation stood at 1,132.02 megawatts.

Earlier in the day the system had been carrying more than 4,000 megawatts, and reporting suggests output dipped as low as around 700 megawatts before the recovery began. By 21:00 it was back to 1,793.79 megawatts.

Only ten generating companies were feeding the grid at the low point. Jebba Hydro was the largest contributor at 483 megawatts, followed by Omotosho at 162.80 and Olorunsogo at 115.

The remainder came in small increments: Paras Energy at 80.10 megawatts, Afam III Fast Power at 76.10, Dadinkowa at 37.82, Omoku at 34.70 and Sapele Steam at 24.80.

The stations that produced nothing

Twelve plants registered zero output. They include Egbin, Nigeria’s largest thermal station, along with Geregu and Geregu NIPP (National Integrated Power Project), Kainji, Delta, Alaoji NIPP, Ihovbor NIPP, Okpai, Shiroro, Taopex, Trans Afam Power and Zungeru.

That list contains most of the country’s serious generating capacity. Kainji, Shiroro and Zungeru alone are the backbone of Nigerian hydropower.

It is worth being careful about what this means. Zero output on a system operator dashboard can reflect a plant tripping, being taken off for maintenance, or having no gas or no instruction to generate.

Without an operator statement it is impossible to say which. That absence is itself part of the story.

What happened to customers

Distribution companies began shedding load. Eko Disco told customers it was experiencing load shedding across its network because of low allocation from the grid.

For anyone living or operating in Lagos or Abuja, the practical consequence is diesel. Businesses, data centres, hospitals and residential compounds run generators against exactly this scenario.

That cost does not appear in the electricity tariff, which is why Nigerian power economics are so hard to read from the outside. The real price of electricity includes the backup you have to own.

It is a heavy tax on manufacturing, and it is the single largest reason Nigerian industrial output has struggled to scale.

A new minister and an old problem

This was the first significant grid disturbance since Joseph Olasunkanmi Tegbe became Minister of Power. He was nominated by President Bola Tinubu on 30 April 2026, confirmed by the Senate on 6 May and sworn in on 8 June.

He replaced Adebayo Adelabu, who left to pursue political office. Tegbe came to the job from a consulting career, most recently as director-general of the Nigeria–China Strategic Partnership, having been a senior partner and head of advisory at KPMG Africa.

The inheritance is not a kind one. Nigeria’s grid has failed repeatedly over the past decade, and each new minister arrives promising the structural fix that the last one also promised.

The unbundling of generation, transmission and distribution was supposed to solve this. Two decades on, transmission remains the state-owned bottleneck between privatised plants and privatised distributors.

What to watch next

The immediate thing to watch is whether an explanation appears at all. A system operator that cannot account for a 70% drop in output within days has a transparency problem on top of an engineering one.

The second is whether this was a one-off or the start of a run. Nigeria has had clusters of failures before, and a single bad Saturday is not yet a trend.

The third is gas. Most Nigerian thermal capacity depends on domestic gas supply that has historically been curtailed by pipeline vandalism and unpaid bills, though nobody has attributed Saturday’s event to that.

We are not importing a cause that no authority has given. What is established is the number, the date and the silence.

There is a wider cost that rarely gets counted. Every hour of unreliable supply pushes another factory, hospital or office block into buying its own generation, which permanently removes that customer from the grid’s revenue base.

That is how a utility death spiral works, and Nigeria is a long way into one. The people who can afford to leave the system have already left it, and the ones who remain are the least able to pay for its repair.

Frequently Asked Questions

How low did the Nigeria grid fall? National generation dropped to 1,132.02 megawatts at 20:30 on 22 August 2026, from more than 4,000 megawatts earlier that day. It recovered to 1,793.79 megawatts by 21:00. Which power stations were offline? Twelve showed zero output on the system operator’s dashboard, including Egbin, Geregu, Geregu NIPP, Kainji, Delta, Alaoji NIPP, Ihovbor NIPP, Okpai, Shiroro, Taopex, Trans Afam Power and Zungeru. What caused it? No cause has been given. Neither the Nigerian Independent System Operator nor the ministry had issued an explanation. Who is Nigeria’s power minister? Joseph Olasunkanmi Tegbe, sworn in on 8 June 2026 after Senate confirmation on 6 May. He succeeded Adebayo Adelabu. What happened to electricity customers? Distribution companies began load shedding. Eko Disco told customers this was due to low allocation from the grid.

World.title: Kenya’s Cost of Running Government Hits a Record
World.content:
By subscribing you agree to our privacy policy . We never share your email.

Eastern Africa · Public Finance

Key Facts —The number: National government spending on operations and maintenance reached KSh1.317 trillion (about US$10.2 billion) in the year to 30 June 2026, up from KSh1.118 trillion (about US$8.6 billion). —The increase: About KSh199 billion (about US$1.54 billion), or 17.82%. On Treasury records it is the largest annual rise yet. —In dollars: Roughly US$1.54 billion of extra spending, at KSh129.49 to the dollar. —What it covers: Travel, transport, fuel, supplies, repairs, hospitality, training, electricity, water and communication. —Against inflation: Average inflation over the same twelve months works out at about 4.9%, on the Kenya National Bureau of Statistics’ own monthly readings, so running costs grew almost four times faster. —What is not disclosed: Treasury data does not break down which categories drove the increase.

Kenya government running costs rose 17.82% to KSh1.317 trillion in the financial year to 30 June 2026, an increase of about KSh199 billion, or US$1.54 billion. It is the largest annual rise in Treasury records, and it happened during an austerity programme.

What the line item actually is

Operations and maintenance is the cost of the state functioning day to day. It covers travel and transport, fuel, office supplies, repairs, hospitality, training, electricity, water and communication.

It is not salaries, and it is not debt service, and it is not development spending. It is the overhead.

In the year to 30 June 2026 that overhead came to KSh1.317 trillion (about US$10.2 billion), up from KSh1.118 trillion (about US$8.6 billion) the year before. At the Central Bank of Kenya’s rate of 129.49 shillings on 20 August 2026, the increase of roughly KSh199 billion is about US$1.54 billion.

One note on the conversion. These are aggregates accumulated across a financial year, so converting them at a single August spot rate gives scale rather than precision.

Why the jump in Kenya government running costs is the story

Kenya has been running an explicit austerity programme, complete with procurement reform and public commitments to trim the cost of government. The 2026 Budget Policy Statement said as much.

The rise is also out of line with prices. Average inflation over the same twelve months works out at about 4.9%, on the Kenya National Bureau of Statistics’ own monthly readings, which makes the increase in running costs almost four times the general rise in prices.

That average is not the headline rate: annual inflation was 6.4% in June 2026, and the twelve-month mean is lower because the earlier months of the period were running near 4.5% of a twelve-month average, not a headline statistic. The Kenya National Bureau of Statistics reported year-on-year inflation of 6.4% for June 2026, and the two are measuring different things.

Either way the gap is large. Overhead grew far faster than the cost of the things the overhead buys.

Some growth is unavoidable. A state that hires more teachers and nurses needs more electricity, more fuel and more supplies to keep them working.

But the workforce did not expand by 17.82% in a year, and neither did the population being served. That is the gap the Treasury has not accounted for.

The digital procurement platform did not stop it

In July 2025 the government launched an end-to-end electronic procurement platform, intended to make public buying traceable and to squeeze out inflated pricing. It now carries more than 1,500 procuring entities and at least 33,000 suppliers.

The system was merged with the state’s existing financial management, business registration, citizen services and tax platforms. On paper it is the kind of reform that should show up in the numbers within a year.

It has not, at least not here. Those platform figures are the Treasury’s own claims and we have not independently verified them.

The most useful thing to know about that KSh199 billion (about US$1.54 billion) is what nobody will say. Treasury data does not disclose which categories drove the increase, which leaves the composition open to question.

The pattern over five years

This is not a single bad year in an otherwise flat series. Operations and maintenance has more than doubled from KSh653.7 billion (about US$5.05 billion) in 2020/21.

The annual increases have been erratic rather than steady. The rise was KSh186 billion in 2021/22 (about US$1.44 billion), then KSh26.5 billion (US$205 million), then KSh184 billion (US$1.42 billion), then KSh67.4 billion (US$521 million), and now KSh199 billion (US$1.54 billion).

The small increase in 2024/25 has an obvious explanation. That was the year the Finance Bill — Kenya’s annual tax law — was withdrawn after mass protests, and the government spent the following months trying to look frugal.

The rebound since suggests the restraint was situational. When the political pressure eased, the overhead resumed growing.

Why this reaches beyond Nairobi

Kenya is negotiating with the IMF and the World Bank while carrying public debt of KSh13.01 trillion, about US$100 billion, or 68.5% of GDP at the end of June. Every shilling of overhead is a shilling not available for debt service.

It also runs directly into the tax question. A government that cannot hold its own running costs flat has a weaker case when it asks households and businesses for more, and Kenya’s recent history shows what happens when it asks badly.

For investors holding Kenyan paper this belongs in the same file as the banking sector’s heavy exposure to government securities. Both are claims on the same revenue.

One caveat on sourcing. These are Treasury figures as reported by Business Daily, and we have not seen the underlying statement.

Frequently Asked Questions

How much did Kenya government running costs rise? Operations and maintenance spending rose about KSh199 billion, or 17.82%, to KSh1.317 trillion in the year to 30 June 2026. That is roughly US$1.54 billion of extra spending. Is that a record? On National Treasury records it is the largest annual increase in this line item. What does the spending cover? Travel, transport, fuel, supplies, repairs, hospitality, training, electricity, water and communication. It excludes salaries, debt service and development spending. How does it compare with inflation? Average inflation over the same twelve months works out at about 4.9%, on the Kenya National Bureau of Statistics’ own monthly readings, so running costs grew almost four times faster. The statistics bureau reported year-on-year inflation of 6.4% in June 2026. Which categories drove the increase? Treasury data does not disclose the breakdown.

World.title: Kenya Gives Investigators 60 Days on Fuel Case
World.content:
By subscribing you agree to our privacy policy . We never share your email.

Eastern Africa · Energy

Key Facts —The deadline: The Senate Energy Committee wants a consolidated status report from investigative agencies within 60 days of its report being adopted. —Who is under investigation: Mohamed Liban, former Principal Secretary for Petroleum; Joe Sang, former managing director of Kenya Pipeline Company; and Daniel Kiptoo, former director-general of the energy regulator. —When they were arrested: Early April 2026, over alleged manipulation of fuel stock data and procurement of an emergency cargo at inflated prices. All were released on cash bail. —The trigger: Iran’s closure of the Strait of Hormuz stranded a vessel carrying petrol at Jebel Ali. —The contracts: One Petroleum and Oryx Energies were each awarded 81.3 million litres, roughly 60,000 tonnes, on 25 March 2026. —The premium: One Petroleum quoted a premium of about US$290 a tonne, against a fixed premium of roughly US$84 under Kenya’s government-to-government arrangement — the state-to-state oil credit deal Kenya has run with Gulf suppliers since 2023.

The Kenya fuel probe into three former energy officials now has a clock on it, after the Senate Energy Committee demanded a consolidated status report from investigators within 60 days. Nobody has been charged, and the detectives have published nothing since arresting the three in April.

What the Senate asked for

The committee’s recommendation is broader than a single agency. It asks the Ministry of Energy and Petroleum, the Public Service Commission, the State Corporations Advisory Committee and the boards of the energy regulator and the pipeline company, together with all relevant investigative agencies, to report jointly.

The clock runs from the adoption of the committee’s report rather than from any calendar date. Business Daily reports the deadline lapses on 19 October 2026, which implies the committee adopted its report around 20 August. We have not seen the Senate’s own record of that adoption.

The target everyone is watching is the Directorate of Criminal Investigations. Its detectives travelled to Saudi Arabia as part of the inquiry and have published no findings.

The directorate has said publicly that the three men are not off the hook despite having resigned from government.

The three men at the centre of the Kenya fuel probe

Mohamed Liban was Principal Secretary for Petroleum and Joe Sang was managing director of Kenya Pipeline Company. Daniel Kiptoo was director-general of the Energy and Petroleum Regulatory Authority.

All three were arrested on 2 April 2026 and released on cash bail. The allegations concern manipulation of fuel stock data and the procurement of an emergency petrol cargo at inflated prices.

None has been charged. These remain allegations, and the investigating authority has produced no public evidence.

All three have since left their posts.

How a closed strait produced a scandal

The origin is geopolitical rather than domestic. Iran’s closure of the Strait of Hormuz stranded a Gulf Energies vessel carrying 85,000 tonnes of petrol at Jebel Ali.

Kenya held 124.39 million litres of petrol for its local and transit markets as of 19 March 2026, about sixteen days of cover. On that arithmetic the country faced a stock-out from 4 April.

The National Security Council Committee ordered backup imports. On 25 March, One Petroleum and Oryx Energies were each awarded contracts for 81.3 million litres, which is roughly 60,000 tonnes of petrol.

Hass Petroleum and E3 Energy also bid. The awards were made outside the normal government-to-government framework.

The price, and the cargo that failed

The pricing is where the case lives. One Petroleum quoted a premium of about US$290 a tonne, against roughly US$84 for a comparable quantity under Kenya’s arrangement with Saudi Aramco, ADNOC and Emirates National Oil Company.

The Energy Ministry alleged in April that the emergency import had not been necessary at all, because Saudi Aramco Trading Fujairah, ADNOC Global Trading and Emirates National Oil Company Singapore were all meeting their contractual obligations.

Then the cargo itself became a problem. The One Petroleum vessel was owned by BP and bound for Angola, and its petrol failed Kenyan fuel standards.

One Petroleum told the Senate in June that no penalties or formal liabilities had been imposed on it by the government, and that it had made no claim against the government.

Why this matters beyond Kenya

Uganda stores fuel in Kenya Pipeline Company reserves, so a Kenyan supply failure is a regional one. The northern corridor carries fuel for a landlocked interior.

It is also a test of the government-to-government import framework that Gulf state trading arms bid into. If emergency cargoes can be bought outside that framework at three and a half times the premium — the freight, insurance and handling surcharge added on top of the cargo’s price at the loading port — the framework is worth less than it appears.

For traders and financiers the practical question is whether the case is prosecuted or quietly filed. The Senate’s 60 days is an attempt to force that answer.

The committee has no power to prosecute. What it has is the ability to make the silence visible.

There is a reputational cost to Kenya either way. A case this public that ends without charges tells traders one thing about enforcement, and a case that ends in convictions tells them another.

Sixty days is not long in a criminal investigation that has already run five months. It is long enough to establish whether anyone intends to finish it.

Frequently Asked Questions

What is the Kenya fuel probe? An investigation into three former energy officials over alleged manipulation of fuel stock data and the procurement of an emergency petrol cargo at inflated prices in early 2026. Who is under investigation? Mohamed Liban, former Principal Secretary for Petroleum; Joe Sang, former managing director of Kenya Pipeline Company; and Daniel Kiptoo, former director-general of the energy regulator. All were arrested on 2 April 2026 and released on cash bail. What deadline has the Senate set? A consolidated status report from the ministry, oversight bodies and investigative agencies within 60 days of the committee’s report being adopted. How much fuel was involved? One Petroleum and Oryx Energies were each awarded 81.3 million litres, roughly 60,000 tonnes, on 25 March 2026. Has anyone been charged? No. The allegations remain allegations and the Directorate of Criminal Investigations has published no findings.

World.title: Pakistan Signs a Defence Deal With Somalia
World.content:
By subscribing you agree to our privacy policy . We never share your email.

Eastern Africa · Defence

Key Facts —What was signed: A memorandum of understanding on defence cooperation, signed in Islamabad on 4 August 2026. —By whom: Somali Defence Minister Ahmed Moallim Fiqi and Pakistan’s Defence Minister Khawaja Muhammad Asif. —What it covers: Counter-terrorism, military training, exchange of expertise, defence capacity building and broader security collaboration. —Who else the delegation met: Field Marshal Syed Asim Munir at army headquarters on 6 August, the air chief, and naval chief Admiral Naveed Ashraf. —What is not in it: No base, no port access and no permission to deploy combat forces has been announced. —India’s response: On 7 August the foreign ministry said it was following developments closely.

A Somalia Pakistan defence memorandum signed in Islamabad on 4 August commits the two countries to cooperate on training, counter-terrorism and maritime security. India, which has patrolled the waters off Somalia since 2008, says it is following the arrangement closely.

What the Somalia Pakistan defence memorandum agreed

The memorandum was signed in Islamabad on 4 August 2026 by Somali Defence Minister Ahmed Moallim Fiqi and his Pakistani counterpart, Khawaja Muhammad Asif. The Somali state news agency published the announcement.

Its declared scope is counter-terrorism, military training, exchange of expertise, defence capacity building and broader security collaboration. One outlet has described it as a five-year pact, which we have not been able to confirm.

What is not in it matters as much. No base has been announced, no port access has been granted, and no permission has been given for Pakistan to deploy combat forces.

This is an institutional relationship rather than a deployment. That is how most durable military partnerships begin.

The itinerary tells you the ambition

The Somali delegation included the heads of the country’s navy and air force, which is a heavier composition than a training discussion requires.

On 6 August Fiqi met Field Marshal Syed Asim Munir, Pakistan’s Chief of Army Staff and Chief of Defence Forces, a post created in Pakistan in late 2025 that puts one officer above all three services, at army headquarters in Rawalpindi. He also met Air Chief Marshal Zaheer Ahmed Baber Sidhu at air force headquarters.

The naval meeting was with Admiral Naveed Ashraf, Pakistan’s Chief of the Naval Staff. It covered Indian Ocean maritime security and the building of Somalia’s navy and coast guard.

The delegation also toured the National Defence University and Global Industrial and Defence Solutions, Pakistan’s state-owned defence manufacturer. That last stop suggests equipment is on the agenda, not only instruction.

Why New Delhi said anything at all

On Friday 7 August, India’s foreign ministry spokesperson Randhir Jaiswal was asked about the agreement at the ministry’s twice-weekly media briefing. His answer was careful.

He said India continues to follow the developments between Somalia and Pakistan closely, His answer on Somalia was a single sentence. The remarks that followed — on India’s long ties across Africa and its development cooperation with what diplomats call the Global South, meaning the developing world — came in the same reply, but answered the second half of the reporter’s question, about the India-Africa Forum Summit.

That is mild language and should not be inflated into alarm. But India was asked, and answered briefly rather than volunteering a view — but it did not decline to comment either.

The context is that the Indian Navy has run anti-piracy operations off Somalia since 2008. A Pakistani naval relationship in the same waters touches a rivalry that is usually conducted much closer to home.

The waters in question

Somalia’s coastline runs along the Gulf of Aden and up to the approaches of Bab el-Mandeb, the strait through which a substantial share of Europe-Asia trade passes. It is the most contested shipping corridor in the world right now.

Piracy off the Somali coast has returned to a ten-year high on figures from the International Maritime Bureau, with thirteen incidents in the first seven months of 2026 against five in all of 2025. That is the practical problem a coast guard is meant to address.

Somalia already hosts Turkey’s largest overseas military training base, and Turkey’s parliament extended that deployment for two years on 21 July 2026. Saudi Arabia, the United Arab Emirates and China all have interests in the same neighbourhood.

Adding Pakistan to that list does not displace anyone. It does make Mogadishu’s security relationships harder to map, which is generally the point of having several.

What it means for anyone shipping through

War-risk premiums and routing decisions in the Gulf of Aden turn on whether the Somali coast is stabilising or deteriorating. More external navies with a stake in Somali maritime capability is, on balance, a stabilising signal.

The counterweight is that competing patrons can produce competing Somali forces, which is how the country’s security sector has fragmented before. Turkey trains one set of units, others train different ones.

For a Latin American readership the useful frame is familiar. This is middle-power competition in a maritime chokepoint, conducted through training agreements rather than treaties.

The memorandum’s text has not been published, so its duration and any equipment provisions remain unverified.

For Mogadishu the logic is simpler than the geopolitics suggests. A government that cannot yet police its own coastline will take training from anyone credible who offers it.

The test will be whether Somali sailors and aircrew actually appear in Pakistani institutions over the next year. Memoranda are easy; syllabuses and seat allocations are the evidence.

Frequently Asked Questions

What is the Somalia Pakistan defence agreement? A memorandum of understanding on defence cooperation signed in Islamabad on 4 August 2026, covering counter-terrorism, military training, exchange of expertise and defence capacity building. Who signed it? Somali Defence Minister Ahmed Moallim Fiqi and Pakistan’s Defence Minister Khawaja Muhammad Asif. Does Pakistan get a base in Somalia? No base, port access or permission to deploy combat forces has been announced. What did India say? On 7 August 2026 foreign ministry spokesperson Randhir Jaiswal said India was following developments between Somalia and Pakistan closely, and pointed to India’s own ties across Africa. Why does the Indian Ocean matter here? Somalia sits on the Gulf of Aden approaches to Bab el-Mandeb, one of the world’s busiest shipping corridors, where piracy has returned to a ten-year high.

World.content:
Peru · DISASTERS

Key Facts — What happened Peru issued four separate emergency decrees on 23 August 2026, covering an earthquake, El Niño, storms and flooding.

— How big Three decrees last 60 days each; the fisheries decree runs 120 days nationwide.

— The real story Each decree is a distinct measure, not one national declaration, with different scopes and terms.

— The catch The fisheries decree is a sector emergency, so it can exceed the 60-day constitutional limit for territorial emergencies.

— What comes next No budget, financing source, or executing bodies were published for any decree.

Four separate supreme decrees, each with its own scope and term, signal a fragmented response to a week of disasters across Peru.

Peru Emergency Decrees published on Sunday 23 August 2026 address four separate crises, from an earthquake in Ayacucho to nationwide fishing troubles. The government issued four distinct supreme decrees in the official gazette El Peruano, each with its own scope and duration.

Four Decrees, Four Crises

However, Peru Emergency Decrees cover an earthquake, El Niño, southern storms and Lima flooding. Each decree is a separate measure, not one national declaration.

The first decree declares a state of emergency for 60 days in five districts of Ayacucho. The second, Supreme Decree No. 012-2026-PRODUCE, puts the fishing and aquaculture subsectors in emergency for 120 calendar days nationwide.

The four decrees were published in El Peruano on Sunday 23 August 2026. Each addresses a distinct crisis with its own scope and term.

However, each decree addresses a distinct crisis with its own scope and term. The government of Keiko Fujimori issued them on Sunday 23 August 2026.

Peru Emergency Decrees for Ayacucho

Meanwhile, the Ayacucho decree covers Chumpi, Coracora, Pullo and Upahuacho in Parinacochas province, plus Carapo in Huanca Sancos province. The reporting did not give the decree number for this declaration.

According to EFE, about 500 people were affected and three injured across these five districts. The decree allows for exception, immediate and necessary measures of response and rehabilitation.

The decree covers five districts in the Ayacucho region for 60 days. However, the decree number was not given in the reporting used.

Meanwhile, the decree covers five districts in the Ayacucho region for 60 days. However, the decree number was not given in the reporting used.

Fisheries Emergency Over El Niño

Supreme Decree No. In addition, 012-2026-PRODUCE declares a sector emergency for fishing and aquaculture nationwide. It runs for 120 calendar days due to the El Niño phenomenon of 2026-2027.

This measure is different from the territorial decrees because it is a sector emergency declared by the production ministry. Therefore, it can exceed the 60-day constitutional ceiling that applies to the other three.

El Niño is a periodic warming of the eastern Pacific that pushes anchoveta deeper. As a result, catches fall, affecting Peru’s fishmeal industry.

In addition, this decree is a sector emergency declared by the production ministry. Therefore, it can exceed the 60-day constitutional ceiling that applies to the other three.

Southern Storms and Lima Flooding

Supreme Decree No. 118-2026-PCM declares a 60-day emergency in districts of Arequipa, Moquegua and Tacna hit by the DANA storm system. The individual district names were not in the reporting.

In fact, Supreme Decree 117-2026-PCM declares a 60-day emergency in two Lima districts. Villa María del Triunfo and Villa El Salvador, after flooding.

La República reported this decree came seven days after the floods. DANA stands for depresión aislada en niveles altos, an isolated high-level depression.

It dumps heavy rain for days over one area, causing floods. Meanwhile, the DANA storm system is a cut-off low that dumps heavy rain for days.

As a result, it caused flooding in the southern regions and Lima.

What a State of Emergency Means

A Peruvian state of emergency is set out in Article 137 of the Constitution. However, it is often called by its Spanish name, estado de emergencia.

It runs for a maximum of 60 days at a time, and extending it needs a fresh supreme decree. In disaster declarations, the practical effect is administrative.

Public bodies may skip normal tendering, move money and buy relief goods quickly for a fixed window. Article 137 also permits suspending some rights, such as freedom of assembly.

However, nothing in this research says that was applied here. However, the practical effect is administrative, allowing quick spending and relief.

Still, it does not automatically suspend constitutional rights.

The Legal Instruments Explained

A decreto supremo, or supreme decree, is an executive order signed by Peru’s president and approved by the cabinet. It becomes law once published in El Peruano, the official state gazette.

PCM stands for Presidencia del Consejo de Ministros, the cabinet office of the prime minister. PRODUCE is the Ministerio de la Producción, responsible for fishing and aquaculture.

El Peruano’s Normas Legales supplement is where decrees are published. Publication there is what makes them take effect.

In addition, a decreto supremo becomes law only when published in El Peruano. Meanwhile, the Normas Legales supplement is where such decrees appear.

Background on the Ayacucho Quake

A magnitude 7.2 earthquake struck the Andean region of Ayacucho on Thursday 20 August 2026. The epicentre was 35 kilometres from the town of Coracora, according to the Instituto Geofísico del Perú.

The decrees are the government’s formal response to the quake and to the weather emergencies. The quake struck on 20 August, three days before the decrees.

However, the time of day was not reported in the research. However, the quake struck on 20 August, three days before the decrees.

Meanwhile, the time of day was not reported in the research.

Damage Reports and Toll

INDECI, Peru’s national civil defence institute, reported on 20 August damage in several districts. In Puquio, 8 homes were affected with cracks; in Pullo, 12 homes and one health post were affected.

However, Puquio is not among the five districts under the state of emergency. The three injured were reported later, on 23 August, by EFE, separate from the earlier counts.

INDECI also reported two people injured while evacuating in Coracora. Additionally, 18 populated centres were affected in Upahuacho.

Meanwhile, INDECI’s damage counts on 20 August are separate from EFE’s toll on 23 August. As a result, they should not be added together.

What Remains Unknown

The reporting gives no budget, financing source, or list of executing bodies for any of the four decrees. No sol or dollar figure appears in the research.

Still, the decrees are now in effect. Their practical impact will depend on how quickly the government can act within the fixed windows.

The reporting does not state who executes the decrees or their expiry dates. Still, the decrees are now law, and their effects will unfold.

However, the reporting gives no budget, financing source, or executing bodies. Still, the decrees are now law, and their effects will unfold.

Frequently Asked Questions

What are the Peru Emergency Decrees?

Peru Emergency Decrees are four separate supreme decrees published on 23 August 2026. They address an earthquake in Ayacucho, El Niño effects on fisheries, DANA storms in the south, and flooding in Lima.

How long does each decree last?

Three territorial decrees last 60 days each. The fisheries decree lasts 120 calendar days because it is a sector emergency declared by the production ministry.

Which areas are covered by the Ayacucho decree?

The Ayacucho decree covers five districts: Chumpi, Coracora, Pullo and Upahuacho in Parinacochas province, plus Carapo in Huanca Sancos province. Puquio is not included.

What does a state of emergency allow?

It allows public bodies to skip normal tendering and move money quickly for relief and repairs. The constitution also permits suspending some rights, but nothing in the research says that was applied.

World.title: Young mother pleads for help from Special Envoy, Women’s Department over alleged coercive and financial abuse by children’s father who made her lose her job, took away her car and washing machine
World.content:
Young mother pleads for help from Special Envoy, Women’s Department over alleged coercive and financial abuse by children’s father who made her lose her job, took away her car and washing machine

By Breaking Belize News Staff: A young mother who claims she is trapped in a cycle of coercive and financial abuse at the hands of her children’s father, a prominent attorney and businessman whose father is a sitting Minister of Government, is pleading for help from the Office of the Special Envoy, the Women’s Department and the National Women’s Commission.

The young mother, identified as Selia Stephen on Facebook, said she has faced months of alleged financial, emotional and psychological pressure since leaving the relationship and quitting her employment with the father of her children.

Stephen claims that after she found another job, he stopped arranging for the children to be picked up from school and stopped paying the babysitter, which she says caused her to lose the job. She further alleges that he took away the vehicle she used to transport the children, stopped paying for their daughter’s tutoring and even removed the washing machine after she refused to return to work for him.

“At every turn this man has found ways to create chaos to force me back into the abusive situation with him I ran from,” Stephen wrote.

She also alleges that he sometimes refuses at the last minute to take the children during scheduled visitation weekends, has withheld child support since December and is attempting to block her decision to enroll the children in public school because it is more affordable and easier for her to manage transportation.

Screenshots shared alongside the matter, purportedly showing messages from a contact saved as “Kids Dad,” contain a string of insults and remarks about money and the children. In one message, the sender calls Stephen a “dead beat mother” and says, “if you move her I will simply spend the savings on my woman n book a trip from that money u dying for.” The sender also repeatedly calls her a “dummy” and “ghetto,” and later writes that another person “might get the 1000 to prepare your child.”

Stephen further claims she has a restraining order against the children’s father for alleged harassment and for showing up at her home after she told him she did not want him to know where she lived. Despite that, she says he has questioned her sanity in court and succeeded in having the court order her to attend counselling with him.

Now saying she is at her “wits end,” Stephen is asking where women in similar situations can turn after what she describes as repeated failures by the courts and police.

“I am not asking for sympathy, I am at my wits end and seeking some kind of help to get out of this coercive and mental abuse,” she wrote, directly appealing to the Women’s Department, Special Envoy and Women’s Commission.

Stephen said she believes the alleged conduct is intended to “break me financially, emotionally and mentally.”

The allegations and the authenticity and authorship of the message screenshots have not been independently established. A response from the father of her children was not included in the material reviewed for this story.
