World.title: New system will track unsafe medicines, vaccines and fake medical products in Belize
World.content:
New system will track unsafe medicines, vaccines and fake medical products in Belize

By Breaking Belize News Staff (HP): The Ministry of Health and Wellness has moved forward with the operationalisation of a National Post-Market Surveillance System for medicines and vaccines.

The work took place during a three day workshop last week supported by the Pan American Health Organization, bringing together officials from government agencies, health facility representatives, academia, private sector specialists and patient organisations.

The aim is to strengthen Belize’s capacity to detect, assess, investigate, communicate and respond to safety and quality concerns related to medicines and vaccines.

Belize recently became a full member of the WHO Programme for International Drug Monitoring and has advanced the use of pharmacovigilance tools including VigiFlow and VigiMobile, along with national reporting forms and pathways.

With PAHO support, the country is building an integrated approach that combines monitoring of medicine and vaccine safety with the detection and management of product quality issues, suspected substandard and falsified medical products, and unregistered products.

Participants examined the proposed terms of reference for the system, including its mandate, scope, functions and coordination mechanisms.

Officials stressed that an effective system depends on clearly defined responsibilities, good quality reports, timely feedback and coordination across institutions.

World.title: Two detained after armed robbery at Independence Village shop
World.content:
Two detained after armed robbery at Independence Village shop

By Breaking Belize News Staff (HP): Two men were detained within hours of an armed robbery at a shop on Big Creek Road in Independence Village on Saturday afternoon.

Police received information of a robbery in progress around 2:30pm. On arrival, officers found a wallet on the floor of the shop containing a social security card and other items.

The shop attendant told police that two men barged into the shop. One pulled out a 9mm pistol and demanded cash while the other took the cash register pan containing an undisclosed amount of money.

Both men then left the shop in an SUV heading toward Belize City.

Coordinated information was sent to G13 personnel, who stopped and detained both suspects at the junction of George Town Village in the Stann Creek District. An undisclosed amount of money was recovered.

Police are continuing investigations. No charges have been laid as yet.

World.title: Jamaica dethroned as Haiti claim CFU U-14 boys title
World.content:
Haitian players celebrate after beating defending champions Jamaica 4-0 to take the CFU-U14 Tier 1 Challenge Series on Sunday (Photo: CFU Instagram)

KINGSTON, Jamaica — Jamaica were dethroned as kings of the Caribbean Football Union (CFU) Under-14 Boys Tier 1 Challenge Series on Sunday after they were outplayed and beaten 4-0 by Haiti in the final played at Cap Cana, Punta Cana in the Dominican Republic.

Wensley Dumorne scored twice early in the second half to take the game away from Jamaica, who trailed 1-0 at half-time and were losing for the first time in two trips to the competition.

It was the first time Jamaica had conceded a goal in the tournament after winning their previous four games by an 8-0 aggregate, including a 1-0 win over Bermuda in Friday’s semi-final.

Haiti went into the final as favourites after dismantling hosts Dominican Republic 6-1 in their semi-final.

After dominating early, Haiti were rewarded when Jodeley Sheeck Delmas opened the scoring in the 28th minute.

Dumorne doubled the lead in the 39th minute and then completed his brace in the 47th minute before Ronelson Pele Janvier added a fourth in the 59th minute.

— Paul A Reid

World.title: Stray animal highway horror
World.content:
The mangled Mitsubishi Pajero involved in the August 15 crash on the May Pen to Williamsfield leg of Highway 2000.

TOLL GATE, Clarendon — A night of T20 cricket enjoyment at Sabina Park in Kingston just over a week ago almost ended in death for three people when the sport utility vehicle in which they were travelling back to Mandeville crashed into a cow that had wandered onto the May Pen to Williamsfield leg of Highway 2000 in pitch darkness.

Hopeton McCatty, the driver and owner of the Mitsubishi Pajero; his friend Wensworth Skeffery, a former Opposition senator; and Skeffery’s 24-year-old daughter were not injured, but the cow died in the August 15 collision that revived fears of the danger posed to life by stray animals on the high-speed road.

“We took my friend’s daughter to cricket for the first time and she enjoyed it; a very good game of cricket, a fantastic crowd. We left Sabina Park and went downtown then joined the toll road at Portmore,” McCatty told the Jamaica Observer.

“We were talking about the experience of interacting with people and how to be humble. We were cruising along. We came through the tolls at Portmore, Vineyards, and May Pen. We were approaching the last one at Toll Gate driving at about 103 kilometres per hour… I had on the high beam, because the road was dark. We were in the left lane and while talking Skeffery said ‘Cow!’ ” McCatty related.

“I spotted this animal coming onto the road, so I braked and swerved to the right and we really thought we had missed it, but the cow kept coming and we hit the cow. The two airbags [deployed] and I swerved back to the left to avoid the median in the road. I wasn’t even able to see what was in front of me and I stopped,” added McCatty.

On Saturday, TransJamaican Highway (TJH) Limited Chief Executive Officer Ivan Anderson told the Sunday Observer that he had received a report on the incident and raised concern about residents living along that section of the highway repeatedly cutting through the fencing to get to their homes after disembarking buses travelling along the highway.

“The fence in this location has been cut and repaired several times since the start of the year. Since the initial cutting we doubled the fencing in this location by adding hog wire to the barbed wire; it is being cut by persons coming off buses on the highway and going into the community,” Anderson said in a WhatsApp response.

He said TJH is now in the process of identifying the owner of the cow as the animal was tagged.

On September 13 last year a woman had to be rushed to hospital after cattle strayed onto the highway shortly after midnight, causing extensive damage to two vehicles, a Toyota Axio and a Toyota Tacoma, and injuring occupants.

At that time the highway was toll-free. But when TJH commenced charging on December 27, 2025 it assured motorists of a First-World roadway supported by 24-hour patrols and consistent maintenance.

“Our commitment is to deliver a safe, reliable, and efficient driving experience across this new section in a manner that is consistent with our offerings on all legs of the TransJam Highway’s network. In order to deliver these services sustainably, we will introduce a toll rate structure at both the Toll Gate-MainLine Toll Plaza and the Toll Gate-Ramp Toll Plaza,” TJH said in an Instagram post.

However, for McCatty, the issue of stray cattle was compounded by him not seeing any patrols near midnight, and for close to an hour after the collision.

“The scary part about it is that when the car hit the cow all the lights went, because the battery got dislodged completely. We were out there on the highway in complete darkness,” he said.

“I didn’t know if a truck was going to come and run straight into us; and there has been an incident before on the highway network where people died after having an accident and then an oncoming vehicle hit them,” he added.

He said he was relieved when a tow truck, en route to Mandeville, stopped at the accident scene and subsequently removed his vehicle.

“God is good, because a wrecker was passing and stopped and had on its hazard lights; that give us some sense of calm that people wouldn’t run up into us in the darkness,” he said.

“The car bonnet seemed to have cut the cow’s neck. It took us about an hour to get off the road. During that time other vehicles stopped, but we didn’t see anybody from the toll [company] patrolling,” added McCatty.

He said he returned to Clarendon the Sunday afternoon following the accident to report it.

“We filed a report at the Four Paths Police Station on Sunday afternoon, because Sunday morning I couldn’t miss church. I had to give God thanks. We came out with no wounds. I reported the accident to the insurance company and the vehicle is basically written off,” he explained.

Vice chairman of the National Road Safety Council Dr Lucien Jones said he previously engaged the National Road Operating and Constructing Company (NROCC) — which is responsible for overseeing the design, construction, and maintenance of Jamaica’s highways — about the danger of stray animals on the high-speed road.

“Having a stray animal on a road which provides for driving at a fairly high speed to enable people to get from point A to point B in a fairly short time and therefore aid in the whole transportation sector carrying goods and people across the country, poses a severe problem,” he said.

“We have had this issue before. We have had discussions about it with operators of the highway [and] NROCC. We have had remedial things done on the highway, because the primary problem, as I understand it, has to do with people breaking or stealing the wires [fencing] on the highway and thus allowing cows to enter into a guarded space,” added Jones.

He is calling for the municipal corporations across Jamaica to reinstitute animal pounds and remove stray animals from endangering road users.

“We have had discussions about the role of the owners and now to hear that there was a crash recently involving a cow and a vehicle, thank God nobody died. It again raises the issue of how well we are guarding the space across the country on the highways. Not only the East-West or the North-South, but the one going from May Pen up into Mandeville. It raises an important issue which was addressed recently in an Observer editorial,” Dr Jones said.

He argued that the municipal authorities have “a mandate to provide for and enable the leading of stray cattle into pounds and to prevent individuals from allowing this kind of very dangerous situation to continue”.

Jones pointed to statistics indicating that 214 people have died on the nation’s roads since the start of the year, compared to 242 for the corresponding period last year.

“I would once again appeal to those who are so empowered — the municipal authorities and NROCC — to make sure, either separately or jointly, that our highways are made free of any kind of animal straying onto the road,” he said.

Dr Jones also pointed to another worrying trend of motorists driving the wrong way on highways.

On August 13 Parton Buchanan, a 56-year-old resident of Blenheim district in Hanover, died in a crash after he reportedly drove the wrong way onto the Porus off-ramp section of the highway near Williamsfield.

“In those instances where people have gone off-ramp in the wrong direction, they did so to either escape paying the toll or they are not aware of [how to use] that particular part of the highway. [It] requires an increase in public education as to how in certain areas we use the highways and to get people to be aware of the dangers,” said Jones.

McCatty is hoping that another layer of safety will be added by illuminating sections of the highway.

“When you have no light out there it is completely dark. If we can have lights where the toll booths are, why can’t we have it along the toll road? I am not saying you should have lights three feet apart, but there should be more light on the road,” he said.

World.title: Take responsibility!
World.content:
An injured Moo Moo seen at the side of a section of Walks Road in Spanish Town, St Catherine, last Monday. She was euthanised last Wednesday after Veterinary Services Division professionals determined her injuries were too severe. (Photo: Naphtali Junior)

JAMAICA needs more animal shelters, but livestock owners must stop abandoning their roaming, injured animals for the Government to fix, warned Dr Sophia Ramlal, director of the country’s veterinary services.

Her comments come in the wake of a recent case involving an injured cow, given the name Moo Moo by residents, that spent days at the side of a road in Spanish Town, St Catherine, after being struck by a vehicle, with no owner coming forward to claim her.

Dr Ramlal said while such cases are not common, they have occurred before and are a cause for concern given the dangers stray animals pose to motorists and the general public.

“The Cruelty to Animals Act would address basic welfare issues for animals, the Keeping of Animals Act as well, which speaks to how animals are supposed to be kept and basic things should be provided to them, et cetera. However, there is a need for more pounds in Jamaica. There is a need for the ability to move animals that are stray and ownerless. I want to say, it is usually an instance where we have animals that are ownerless, or owners are unwilling to come forward and claim the animals, as is the case with this cow [Moo Moo] I’m addressing. In those instances, there is a need for the ability to remove the animals from the space to determine what is to happen to them,” said Ramlal.

She noted that a handful of organisations are already performing work that extends beyond what their limited infrastructure can reasonably support.

“The Jamaica Society for the Prevention of Cruelty to Animals (JSPCA) does really fantastic work, but they are probably, along with a couple of other entities, they are tasked with doing almost national duties without necessarily the infrastructure, so we need to be looking at more shelters, shelters even that work during disasters,” she told the Jamaica Observer.

Ramlal said the Government is actively working to tackle rising public safety risks, crop destruction, and traffic hazards caused by stray livestock and roaming animals. Most recently, the Clarendon Municipal Corporation developed a new 20-acre holding facility and retrofitted transport trucks to manage roaming cattle and stray animals.

While State intervention is paramount, Dr Ramlal made it clear that this should not be left up to the Government to assume responsibility for animals whose owners can be identified or are unwilling to come forward.

“In this recent case, yes, the Government had stepped in to mobilise the agency as a State to both treat with euthanasia as well as the disposal of the carcass. There is also the process, though, in law, that if injuries occur and the owners are found, that through the court system, a judge may determine what costs are applicable and so on and so forth. In this case [involving Moo Moo], the State had to step in to mobilise and treat with the euthanasia and the disposal of the carcass.

“It is the owner’s cost to cover. It ought to be. The journey, the treatment of the animal, the euthanasia of the animal, if the animals were moved to a pound, all of those things, it is set out in law where those costs would have to be borne by the owner,“ Ramlal told the

Sunday Observer. “But given the circumstances of this cow and given the time frame and the confirmation from the police that nobody had come forward to claim ownership of the animal, then the necessaries had to be done in really the interest of the cow to relieve pain and suffering and to treat with this matter.”

She stressed that greater partnership is needed between the Government, communities and animal owners to keep animals safe, urging the public to report instances of neglected animals as quickly as possible.

“More shelters are needed, but we also need persons who own animals to be responsible owners. They need to be kept confined, they need to be fed, they need to be watered, they need to have proper shelter, and they need to be able to live normal, happy, healthy lives,” said Ramlal.

“We are looking to update our legislation to talk about not just basic cruelty, but also how it is that all of these five freedoms can be embodied in our legislation. We talk about how animals should be kept, how they should be treated if you’re using animals for work or sport, those kinds of things are in train, as we really also want to look at strengthening the legislation,” she added.

Ramlal said the latest incident proves that more and more Jamaicans are looking out for animals and this is a welcome move.

“I think Jamaicans love animals. I think it is growing amongst us that. Look, animals are a part of our ecosystem. More and more Jamaicans are embracing what we like to call in the veterinary medical fraternity and the medical fraternity, the concept of one health. More and more, we Jamaicans see animals not just as pets, but as companions, as service animals. Jamaicans’ view on animals and their contribution to society is on a positive trajectory, and I think what we saw unfolding with this cow tells you that Jamaicans from all walks of life can appreciate that animals are living beings and that they need support and that they’re willing to jump in and roll up their sleeves and help,” said Ramlal, reminding citizens to report any incident of animal abuse or neglect.

World.title: Eager for more
World.content:
Bloom: On Earth As It Is In Heaven (2026) by Avree Walker is delivered by the NDTC during Sunday evening’s sold-out performance at Iberostar Resort in Montego Bay.

MONTEGO BAY, St James — A standing ovation and packed auditorium at Iberostar Rose Hall Resort, Sunday evening, was a signal to principals of the National Dance Theatre Company (NDTC) that Montego Bay is eager to play a larger role in its annual season of dance.

Enthralled by an evening of intense and beautifully choreographed pieces, the appreciative audience applauded heartily after each performance and were left appearing eager for more.

There were audible oohs and ahhs of amazement as members of the troupe twisted, twirled, leapt, and executed a range of intricate moves across the stage.

The show was also remarkable in that it was the first time ever in its 64-year history that the NDTC was closing its season in the second city.

As Montego Bay’s Mayor Richard Vernon explained, the show had a dual purpose: To assist local dance troupe First Dance Studios as it recovers from the impact of last October’s Hurricane Melissa and to fulfil NDTC’s Artistic Director Marlon D Simms’ long-held dream of bringing the event to St James.

“We’re happy to welcome the NDTC [to] the city of Montego Bay and I trust that this will not be, in the future, for the sake of Melissa, but for the sake of culture…” Vernon told the gathering Sunday night. “[T]his is real, sustainable and something we can look forward to.”

Also present was hotelier and Montego Bay Arts Council Chairman Josef Forstmayr, who said more of these events are needed in the western city.

“We have to work hard; Montego Bay is better than its reputation. We are not just about sun, sea, and sand. This is a place now that has a very solid demand for cultural entertainment more than reggae, and we need to make sure that we get our fair share,” he said. “As we can see tonight, we have the potential to make it a worthwhile and financially successful enterprise, and we all need to work together to get a proper theatre, to get a proper venue where we can host events of that nature; we deserve it.”

Forstmayr did not hold back in his assessment of the event.

“You can see the turnout; it’s a fantastic turnout. There is an energy here. It makes you proud and then to see world-famous choreography, Many Rivers to Cross by [Rex] Nettleford, I mean, performed exquisitely by the elite dancers, it’s a once-in-a-lifetime experience — it’s spectacular, it’s just amazing, I’m over the moon,” he said.

The production was a feast for the senses, with its striking backdrops, vibrant colours, and eye-catching costumes complementing choreography that was precisely synchronised.

“It was exciting, we were all transfixed by what was happening on-stage…[I]t was a well-executed event, and I am very happy that I came this evening and we are looking forward to more for Montego Bay,” vice-president of the Montego Bay Chamber of Commerce and Industry Nadine Spence shared.

Local architect Isiaa Madden was also among those captivated by the performance.

“I think it’s fantastic! I think this is a great addition for Montego Bay, and I hope they’ll be back soon so that I can use my Sunday evenings to come to something like this, because it was great,” she said.

The NDTC’s artistic director also hinted that the performance could mark the beginning of something bigger for the company and the city.

“Perhaps tonight is more than a historic first; perhaps it’s the beginning of a new tradition,” Simms said to roaring applause.

He went on to thank the city of Montego Bay for welcoming the company so warmly, for standing with First Dance Studios, and for showing so resoundingly that the arts have a vibrant home in western Jamaica.

The mayor touched on a long-standing challenge: The lack of a dedicated space for performances of this kind.

Fairfield Theatre now lies in ruins, leaving the city with few suitable venues.

“We have heard the call, as well, for a theatre in Montego Bay. I do not want us to take that lightly; we need it. We have many young talents and youngsters doing their bit right across Montego Bay,” Vernon said. “They need a place to express themselves on a Sunday evening like this so that the entire Montego Bay can come out and enjoy themselves.”

In a follow-up with the Jamaica Observer, Vernon explained how he believes such a facility could become a reality.

“We have property that we can use and we can look at it from two perspectives. One, we would make it be a Government approach and, two, it could be a joined-up approach with Government and private sector, and I am hoping for any of the approaches,” he said.

“At the moment we have property space to envision and to implement something like this; we just need the partnership to make it happen. We are not going to leave it at that, we are going to have the conversations with the relevant persons and see how best we can bring that into our space, because there is a need for it, not a want,” he charged.

World.title: Six years of sleepless nights
World.content:
Shakira Warmington and her son Ayoze WarmingtonPhotos: Naphtali junior

FOR Shakira Warmington, raising a child with rare genetic condition congenital hyperinsulinism has been an uphill battle peppered with sleepless nights, financial strain, fights for a place in the country’s school system, and at times, questions of whether she has the strength to keep going.

Her son, Ayoze Warmington, is just six years old with a condition that sees his pancreas making too much insulin, causing severe and dangerous drops in his blood sugar. His condition, she said, is so rare that he is the only child in Jamaica diagnosed with the disorder, which was confirmed by his medical doctor.

Shakira said her son became sick at six months old, experiencing seizures and what she described as minor strokes. However, she said it was not until he was one year old that doctors were able to identify the condition.

Since then, Ayoze’s parents have had to reshape their lives around his health.

“Having a child with a rare illness in Jamaica is very challenging for us. His care, medication, schooling — just being able to ensure that he has a normal life — it impacts my work, and we are not necessarily in a position where I can stay at home. Both of us [her and Ayoze’s father] do our nine-to-fives and we both still have to do jobs on the side in order to maintain his health,” said Shakira, who is a teacher.

She said maintaining Ayoze’s health comes at a steep cost, with the family spending approximately $100,000 or more monthly on his care, depending on his health status, while also taking care of their daughter and covering all other household expenses. Shakira said the situation had been a lot worse, as previously they had to pay $40,000 every two weeks to access the medication Ayoze needs. However, thankfully, through the Ministry of Health’s Compassionate Care Fund that cost is now fully covered for six months, providing much-needed relief.

But perhaps the most taxing associated challenge is the fact that Ayoze requires 24-hour care.

His mother told thevJamaica Observer that she uses a glucose monitor at least three times a day when he is healthy, and up to 10 times daily when he is ill. She said some days she has to stick him every hour, resulting in a lack of sleep that causes her hands to tremble due to exhaustion.

“Because he gets ill so often I have to be the one to take care of him, ensure that he’s fed correctly and he’s fed on time, because of the weight issues. He throws up a lot and so eating has to be calculated, otherwise he throws it all up — and that, too, affects the weight. He will lose five pounds in a week just like that. He will be healthy this week; next week, he’s not eating. And when he doesn’t eat, the sugar goes down, and the sugar levels have gone into the negatives sometimes,” she told thevSunday Observer.

“I am mother, counsellor, and nurse. Over the six-year period it has impacted my nerves. I shake because you have to watch him while he sleeps. He has to be fed in his sleep because, naturally, the sugars in our bodies go low while we sleep, and his are already going low so it means while he sleeps it is a high possibility that he dies in his sleep, so he has to be fed,” she said, her hands shaking as she spoke.

“We have to feed him using a syringe while he sleeps because he doesn’t want food, he wants sleep; but whether he wants it or not, he has to get it because you have to keep pumping his body with the food. There was a time when he was being fed every hour, and I’m the one feeding him every hour, so it means I’m not sleeping. I have to feed him throughout the night; I still have to wake up to go to work, function throughout the work[day], get things going, doing it all over again — and that is if he’s healthy enough,” she added.

She said the suggestion was made for her to purchase a Dexcom machine to monitor his glucose levels, but that is an extra cost they cannot afford, so she became the machine.

Beyond the home, Shakira said challenges also exist with regard to Ayoze’s access to education. She said after he completed basic school she struggled to find a primary school that would take him. She said Ayoze was rejected by 15 schools, which said they did not have the resources to facilitate him.

Thankfully, he has now been enrolled in a private school to start in September — another expense for the family. A shadow has also been approved by the Ministry of Education for her son but because the stipend for shadows is low, they had to promise the shadow more money to make the job more attractive.

Shakira also believes her son needs to be assessed for learning and psychological challenges, but after applying for the assessment to be done she said they were number 200 in line. The mother has also tried to get him registered with the Jamaica Council for Persons with Disabilities, so as to access benefits on offer, but experienced challenges.

“I can tell you that dealing with special needs in Jamaica, it edges you into insanity. I’ve gone through many stages of depression because it’s like every day I’m questioning, ‘How will I?’ There’s just always a list, and much of life is taken up by him. I don’t have a social life. I feel so alone. It really is just my family here — me, him, my daughter, his daddy, and our family.

“I’ve gone through stages of feeling as though maybe I didn’t do something as a mother, or my body didn’t do something. It takes that effect on you mentally as a parent and makes you say, ‘Oh, maybe I wasn’t enough,’ or ‘I didn’t produce enough of something, and that’s why he became ill,’ ” said Shakira.

“I have had to deal with that, telling myself that it’s not my fault, or it’s nobody’s fault why my own child is ill. It feels like we are well-rooted, good, upstanding citizens doing what we should do in our community, and when we seek to get help for our sick child, it’s hard,” a visibly exhausted Shakira told the Sunday Observer.

She said the option was presented for Ayoze to undergo surgery to remove his pancreas, but that is a cost she and his father cannot afford. She noted that the surgery is not a cure, because he would become diabetic, and she is not sure the family will be able to manage that.

Defeated, Shakira asked for help to provide her son with the best level of comfort and care. She said he currently sleeps on a mattress on the floor because she fears he will fall to the ground and hurt himself while having a seizure. She asked for assistance to get him a customised bed, install a railing in the bathroom for him to use, and financial assistance to help the family maintain his care

“I want a big bed that is comfy,” said young Ayoze.

He said he loves when his mother takes care of him but he does not like being sick because it makes him feel sad.

“I want to get better because if I get better I will be happy,” he told the Sunday Observer.

Highlighting the challenges parents often experience trying to advocate for their children, Shakira said more needs to be done to assist families with children who have special needs.

“Find out more from parents. Gather us parents who have varying challenges and various children with types of special needs and find out what our daily life looks like and how, as a government, you can put in place policies that help to keep those of us with children or family members with disabilities to have some sustainable ways to gain assistance or gain support for our children,” she appealed.

“Where a nine-to-five job is concerned, there have to be some policies and policy changes that will impact us as parents dealing with children with special needs. You have your workplace policy, but if I have a situation that impacts how I can produce or how I can function, is it that the only option for me should be that I don’t work? If I don’t work, how will I feed my family? We need to see what can be done to allow us to be able to work but also take care of and manage our children with special needs without taking on the high possibility that we either drop down at work or drop down at home,” added Shakira.

World.title: Settling the score
World.content:
Race winner Oblique Seville celebrates as he crosses the finishing line in the men’s 100m during the IAAF Diamond League athletics meeting at London stadium, in England, on July 19, 2025.

JAMAICA’S Oblique Seville and Nigeria’s Kayinsola Ajayi are set to clash in the men’s 100m on the second day of the Wanda Diamond League meeting, the Kamila Skolimowska Memorial in Silesia, Poland.

The race will give Seville another opportunity to end Ajayi’s dominance over him this season, with the Nigerian having beaten the Jamaican at the Prefontaine Classic and the London Diamond League meeting. Ajayi will be competing for the first time since finishing third in the men’s 100m at the Commonwealth Games.

The Silesia meeting is the penultimate regular-season Diamond League meeting before Thursday’s meeting in Zurich, which will be the last event before the Diamond League final in September.

Sixteen Jamaicans are set to compete on the second day following Commonwealth Games champion Romaine Beckford’s second-place finish in the men’s high jump on the opening day.

The men’s 100m will be contested over two rounds, a semi-final and final. Cameroon’s Emmanuel Eseme, who won the Commonwealth Games gold medal, is also down to compete along with a second Jamaican, Ackeem Blake, and Americans Ronnie Baker, Kenneth Bednarek, Trayvon Bromell and Christian Coleman.

The Clayton twins, Tina and Tia, as well as Brianna Lyston, are set to compete in the women’s 100m during which they will face Olympic Games champion Julien Alfred along with Americans Sha’Carri Richardson and Melissa Jefferson-Wooden.

National champion Stacey Ann Williams and Nickisha Pryce will contest the women’s 400m where they will face world leader Marileidy Paulino of the Dominican Republic, Aaliyah Butler of the United States, Norway’s record holder Henriette Jaeger, Lieke Klaver of the Netherlands, and former world champion Salwa Eid Naser of Bahrain.

A trio of Jamaicans — Danielle Williams, Ackera Nugent and Megan Simmonds — will line up in the 100m hurdles. They will face former world record holder Kendra Harrison, Alaysha Johnson, and Rayniah Jones of the United States, as well as Poland’s Pia Skrzyszowska.

Orlando Bennett, who has already qualified for the Diamond League final and was fourth in Lausanne, Switzerland, on Friday, will contest the men’s 110m hurdles. He will face a number of athletes who also competed in Lausanne.

World leader Ja’Kobe Tharpe, who finished at the back of the field in Lausanne after hitting a hurdle, will hope to make amends while Jamal Britt, who won in Lausanne, will be looking to finish first again.

Rajindra Campbell will compete in the men’s shot put, which is not part of the Diamond League schedule, against a quality field that includes world leader Leonardo Fabbri of Italy and Americans Joe Kovacs, Jordan Geist and Roger Steen.

Lamara Distin is down for the women’s high jump where she will face Ukraine’s Yaroslava Mahuchikh; Australians Nicola Olyslagers and Eleanor Patterson; and Serbia’s Angelina Topic, all of whom have cleared 2.00m this season.

National champion Ralford Mullings and Olympic Games gold medallist Roje Stona are listed for the men’s discus throw during which world leader and Commonwealth Games champion Matthew Denny of Australia will lead the field.

Steven Richter of Germany, Mykolas Alekna of Lithuania, and Kristjan Ceh of Slovenia are also listed.

Commonwealth Games silver medallist Ackelia Smith is set for the women’s triple jump where she faces world leader Thea LaFond of Dominica; Cubans Davisleydi Velazco, Leyanis Perez-Hernandez and Liadagamis Povea; as well as Saly Sarr of Senegal.

On opening day Beckford cleared 2.29m in the men’s high jump to finish second behind Italy’s Gianmarco Tamberi, who won with 2.31m. American JuVaughn Harrison was third with 2.26m.

Beckford, who is third in the Diamond League standings and is expected to qualify for the lucrative final in September, used all three attempts to clear 2.26m and 2.29m before failing at 2.31m.

Nia Robinson, who failed to record a legal mark at the Commonwealth Games, was ninth in the women’s long jump with 6.29m (0.1m/s) after two fouls.

American Alyssa Jones won with a dramatic final-round jump of 6.98m (1.5m/s) to overtake Portugal’s Agate de Sousa, who had also jumped 6.98m (1.0m/s) in the second round. Jones won on a better second jump.

Monae Nichols of the United States was third with 6.95m (0.1m/s).

In a non-Diamond League event, Danniel Thomas-Dodd was eighth with 18.16m as American Chase Jackson won with a season’s best 20.92m. Jackson also broke her own meeting record of 20.38m, set four years ago.

Jessica Schilder of the Netherlands was second with 20.20m and Commonwealth Games champion Sarah Mitton of Canada was third with 19.34m.

World.title: The Tilemakers
World.content:
Featured tile patterns from Indigo House: Horizon (centre), and (from left) Ipanema, Sunrise, Solid, Solstice, and Leaf of Life.

The buzz…

Indigo House was founded by two friends with a shared love of design. Amber Godfrey works in architecture while Michelle Arroyave brings expertise both in project management and interiors. Godfrey was first exposed to cement tiles while working in an architecture and interiors practice in London, and Arroyave has roots in Colombia — a country with a rich cement tile tradition. Both were drawn to the character and charm that cement tiles bring to a space.

Widely used throughout Europe, Central America and parts of the Caribbean, they are rarely seen in contemporary Jamaican buildings. Together, united by a love of materials and a shared curiosity to explore texture, pattern and colour, Godfrey and Arroyave set out to design and source cement tiles that reflect the vibrancy of Jamaica and the Caribbean. Their tiles go beyond the functional, treating every surface as an opportunity for beauty and craft.

The product… Cement tiles were first manufactured in the mid-1800s, and the fabrication process has changed very little since. Each tile is handmade by skilled artisans using Portland cement, marble powder, fine sand and natural pigments — a craft with origins in Catalonia, Spain.



The process begins with a mould, which forms the framework for the tile. Pigments are carefully poured into the mould to create the pattern, before the tile is placed under a hydraulic press and compacted under high pressure. It is then cured and finished by hand.

The result is a surface that brings warmth, character and artistry to both residential and commercial spaces. Subtle variations in colour and texture are part of the charm — a celebration of the individuality inherent in anything made by hand. Cement tiles are perfect for those who value authenticity, craftsmanship and the stories told by the materials they choose.

“At Indigo House, we believe in making things with intention — tiles that are considered in their design, handcrafted, and built to last. We believe in spaces with character, joy and craft. Known for their bold patterns and enduring quality, our tiles are fully customisable. Choose from our existing catalogue of designs and select your own colours, request modifications to an existing pattern, or design something entirely from scratch — our team can even colour match to a reference image or sample. Every tile is made to order, crafted specifically for you” Amber Godfrey, co-principal, Indigo House.

Photos courtesy of The Indigo House

World.title: The shipping industry profits from conflict and looks East
World.content:
The responses reveal a level of confidence that exceeded expectations. An overwhelming 94​​​ percent​​​​​​​ express optimism about their company’s prospects.

​​The industry also treats this as a lasting reset rather than a temporary challenge. 76​ percent​​​ expect the effects of the Hormuz crisis on global shipping to outlast six months, and opinion splits almost in half on whether this is the sector’s most serious crisis of the past 50 years, ​which covers​​​ the oil shocks, the tanker war, the global financial crisis and C​ovid​​​-19. One phrase from our interviews captures the mindset behind optimism: ​“​​​​Shipping keeps working even when the world stops.​​”​​​​

We therefore asked the uncomfortable question directly. Does global shipping today want peace​​ or does it benefit from turmoil? The peace camp wins, but only just: 54​ percent​​​ to 46​ percent​​​. Even among those who say the crisis hurts their own company, a third concede that the industry gains. Such cando​​r is rare in any sector, and it tempers any expectation that shipping will lobby hard for de-escalation. Markets gaining on volatility do not vote against it.

Confidence, however, does not mean that the influence equilibrium stays the same. Asked which power will affect developments in global shipping the most in the years ahead, 76​ percent​​​ of our respondents point to the East, meaning China and India, while 17​ percent​​​ choose the West. China is rated the leading shipbuilding nation by 69​ percent​​​, the operator of the most competitive fleet by 62​ percent​​​ and a near-universal 96​ percent​​​ ​​call its role important for ​​strengthening ​​global shipping. Trust, though, has not moved East with the tonnage. Only 17​ percent​​​ rate Chinese ship management highly, while traditional maritime powers such as Greece, Norway​​ and Germany continue to be recognized as the industry’s superior managers.

The same shift appears when executives rate the world’s leaders. Xi Jinping​, the president of China,​ stands alone at the top with a net favourability (percent of positive minus percent of negative views) of ​​+44, ahead of Narendra Modi​, the prime minister of India,​ at +24, while the bottom of the ranking is crowded with political leaders at the cent​er​​​ of today’s wars and confrontations. For an industry that plans in decades, predictability seems to weigh more than political alignment, and maritime leaders reward the global actors who ensure a more predictable environment.

Nearly half of the industry’s leadership regards turmoil as good for business​​.​

The study’s technology section shows where the next edge will be decided. Shipping’s digital core has advanced from its experimentation phase. Remote monitoring and voyage optimi​z​​​ation are standard equipment, used by over seven in ten companies, while a second wave, predictive maintenance and ​Internet of Things ​​​sensors, is scaling, and a third, ​artificial intelligence (​AI​)​ analytics and digital twins, is only emerging. Each wave reaches roughly half the companies of the one before it. Tradition survives alongside the sensors, since 70​ percent​​​ still track fleet performance with the noon report (a holdover from the age of sail). ​AI​​​ is the divide to watch​:​​​ 65​ percent​​​ of companies already use or pilot AI, yet only 7​ percent​​​ use it extensively​​ and adoption splits along tonnage lines. Among fleets above one million deadweight ​​tonnes, 79​ percent​​​ work with AI, against 50​ percent​​​ in the mid-sized tier. Scale buys data, teams and budgets, the returns compound, and command of AI and cybersecurity will help set the new shipping hierarchy. As one shipowner told us, “Better positioning produces better data, which produces better positioning.”

No such technology will replace shipping crews. The shortage of skilled personnel remains the third most serious problem in the ranking, at 37​ percent​​​, and companies respond with high safety standards, competitive pay, internet access on board and training. Two findings point to a deeper change​:​​​ 72​ percent​​​ of companies intend to employ more women at sea​​ and 74​ percent​​​ now call ESG​ (environment, social, governance)​ performance important to their overall business strategy.

World.title: Britain told EU citizens to trust its settled status system. Then it mixed up identical twins.
World.content:
The eVisa database keeps a record of a person’s full name, date of birth, nationality, and a facial photograph. But these traits are by definition often a very close match for identical twins, including Webb, whose name is similar to that of her sister.

Many such cases

Monique Hawkins, acting CEO of the3million, which campaigns for the rights of EU citizens living in the U.K., said problems with the eVisa system sometimes left people unable to prove their identity when they needed it most.

“We have seen many cases where someone else’s immigration status is entangled with another person’s eVisa account. We had hoped, after repeatedly raising this issue, that the Home Office had taken more steps to prevent it happening. It just shows how, despite claims that the eVisa system is highly resilient, it can fail people at the critical moments they need it to work,” she said.

Hawkins said it was “crucial that people have a genuinely stable means by which to prove their status” and described the digital-only system as “rushed,” adding: “We regularly see people not only denied boarding, but also compensation, as carriers and the Home Office play a blame game shifting responsibility between each other.”

While a Home Office spokesperson did not dispute Webb’s account, they defended the eVisa system, arguing it had worked for many people.

“Over 10 million people have already successfully used eVisas to prove their immigration status,” the spokesperson said. “As we expand our digital system, we are committed to data accuracy and ensuring that the safeguards in place to support eVisa users are accessible to anyone reliant on the digital system. In the rare cases where errors are identified, the majority of cases are resolved within 24 hours.”

World.title: Ukraine widens its targets — and its tolerance for causing civilian casualties
World.content:
The numbers help illustrate the change. In 2025, Ukrainian attacks inside Russia killed 253 civilians, according to the United Nations, which says it was not able to independently verify the numbers. This year, in the month of July alone, Russian authorities reported that 79 civilians were killed and 601 injured, a marked increase in the casualty rate.

Zelenskyy has said that Wildberries is a legitimate target because it has been “used by the aggressor to ensure the supply of sanctioned components for the production of drones and navigation equipment.” Russian soldiers supplement their equipment by purchasing items from Wildberries.

Maryana Bezuhla, a Ukrainian lawmaker and one of the most outspoken critics of Zelenskyy and Ukraine’s military leadership, is unapologetic about the increased risk to civilians. “Russia’s logistics system is used to wage the war of aggression against Ukraine,” she told POLITICO. “Russia has been targeting Ukrainian civilians all the years of the war.”

Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov has denied accusations from Ukraine that Wildberries handles military supplies but conceded to journalists that “the situation is indeed difficult” for the company.

Dmitry Peskov attends a meeting at the Kremlin in Moscow on June 3, 2026. | Pool photo by Ramil Sitdikov via AFP/Getty Images

There is no indication that Ukraine is deliberately targeting civilians — even as Russia continues to hit apartment buildings, hospitals, schools and other civilian infrastructure with ballistic missiles and drones. And yet, there is no indication that the rising civilian toll in Russia is causing Kyiv to reconsider its approach.

“It is a very important thing to stress from the outset, that any civilian casualties resulting from Ukrainian attacks are collateral damage,” said Jaroslava Barbieri, Ukraine expert at Britain’s Chatham House. “No Ukrainian strikes have deliberately targeted civilian districts.”

World.title: Germany’s establishment has a plan to contain the far right. Sort of.
World.content:
As premier, one of Siegmund’s earliest duties would be to take over the annually rotating chair position of the regular conferences of Germany’s 16 state premiers. The role usually comes with a visit to Berlin and a joint appearance with the chancellor before the press.

Calling this uncharted territory would be an understatement. “The AfD is questioning the fundamental decisions made by the Federal Republic of Germany since 1949,” Merz once said.

The chancellor is not alone in his concern. All other major parties, and large parts of the German media, see the AfD as a threat to the country’s liberal postwar order. Yet, if the party takes power in a state for the first time, the political establishment will no longer be able to keep it at arm’s length. While normal relations may be out of the question, at least for the foreseeable future, Germany’s federal system requires a minimum of cooperation and mutual support.

So how would the German establishment deal with a state governed by the AfD?

POLITICO put this question to officials in the federal government and several state governments. The reluctance to answer was striking, especially among Merz’s center-right Christian Democratic Union and their Bavarian sister party, the Christian Social Union. Senior party figures and state ministers either refused to comment or would not be quoted by name.

The hesitation is understandable. The CDU and the CSU once owned the political space to the right of center. Today, the AfD is eating into it. State ministers from both the Social Democrats and the Greens were more prepared to discuss strategy on the record.

World.title: The UK assisted dying bill is coming back. Its Labour champion is looking to Australia for inspiration.
World.content:
Though Edwards argues her own legislation is “preferable and has stronger safeguards” than the Australian model — unbearable suffering is not a criterion for eligibility in her bill — she found it helpful to see how assisted dying has worked in practice the last time British MPs tackled this issue.

It’s an experience from which many in Labour still bear the scars — and on which new Prime Minister Andy Burnham already appears to have drawn a line in the sand.

Stepping forward

MPs passed fellow Labour backbencher Kim Leadbeater’s Terminally Ill Adults (End of Life) Bill last year by 314 votes to 291. But it failed to become law after delays in the U.K.’s House of Lords.

Now Edwards is reintroducing the bill — and is adamant that the groundbreaking social change can succeed this time around.

It means that next month, the House of Commons will once again be thrust into a divisive vote on a matter of conscience, deciding whether to legalize assisted dying in England and Wales for terminally ill adults judged as having fewer than six months left to live.

“When Kim’s bill came up, I did have conversations with my dad about how things have gone in Australia,” Edwards says. The situation reassured her compared to “more extreme examples” like Canada, where a terminal condition is not required for patients to be eligible, but instead an irreversible, “advanced state of decline” and “unbearable physical or mental suffering.”

World.title: From iPods to wired headphones: Why more Gen Zers are picking retro tech
World.content:
Social media and the digital sphere has taken over much of our lives in the last few years. This has especially impacted younger generations such as Gen Z and Gen Alpha, who have practically grown up in the digital era.

 

Endless screen time, constant notifications and rising fear of missing out (FOMO) have led to more chronically online users and more mental health issues such as depression, anxiety and low self-worth.

A rising number of ads and tracking features, along with more data privacy and security concerns have also contributed to growing unease around popular social media platforms like Instagram, TikTok and Facebook now.

This has led to an increasing number of Gen Zers choosing to adopt more retro tech like flip phones, iPods and vintage cameras as a way to digitally detox and take a break from social media.

Why retro tech is becoming so popular with younger people

More Gen Zers are interested in early and mid-2000s tech, as a way of escaping the constant stream of notifications, pressure and anxiety that often accompanies most social media platforms.

Some also see tech like “dumb phones” as a way to reduce hours of daily smartphone scrolling and the resulting algorithmic noise, offering a slower, more peaceful experience.

These simpler, single-purpose gadgets also provide fewer distractions, as they lack ads, tracking and constant notifications, allowing people to focus fully on more important goals or just be present for friends and family. In some cases, it also means simply being less reachable.

In many cases, retro and physical tech provides tangible ownership, rather than endless streaming subscriptions, which could change rules or hike prices unexpectedly. This provides a tactile, intentional experience and real ownership of media, without the risk of losing albums due to sudden digital licensing dropouts.

For some Gen Zers, retro tech, such as vintage cameras and grainy photos can signify more authenticity than hyper-curated and filtered digital feeds. Similarly, some retro gadgets are increasingly sought after due to their unique designs and colours, in contrast to increasingly modern, minimalist tech.

In some cases, vintage tech is also a fun style or personal statement for Gen Zers interested in mid-2000s culture.

Which retro tech is Gen Z loving right now?

Although there are several retro gadgets making a comeback right now due to rising Gen Z interest, there are a few which have become particularly popular.

Early-2000s digital cameras and camcorders

These early digital cameras are once again seeing a rise, despite still being grainy, oversaturated and imperfectly designed. They represent a perfect escape from over-processed smartphone photography and capture raw aesthetics.

Gen Zers are loving the vintage colour grading and harsh flash glare offered by Y2K cameras, along with the element of surprise that comes from not seeing a flawless live preview. Handheld tape camcorders are also massive hits for filming nights out and festivals with a distinct nostalgic texture.

Some popular models include the Canon PowerShot series, with older models like the PowerShot ELPH and G-series seeing a marked boost due to viral social media trends and celebrity visibility.

The slim and colourful pocket friendly Sony Cyber-shot from the mid-2000s is also still valued for their distinct, retro built-in flash look, along with the Nikon Coolpix for its chromatic grain and early-era colour science.

Dumbphones and flip phones

Basic single-purpose phones are also making a huge comeback right now, mainly as a secondary device for weekends and social outings. Users often swap their SIM cards into vintage flip phones to intentionally disconnect.

These devices effectively limit access to notifications and apps that can distract from the social plans at hand, while still keeping essentials like calling and text messaging working.

This also helps cut down on screen time and doomscrolling, potentially boosting mental health.

While some believe that this is mainly a temporary trend-driven fad, others think that more people could choose to keep smartphones for their daily life and on the weekdays, while switching to dumb phones for fun plans.

Brands like Nokia/HMD are becoming particularly popular again, especially models like the Nokia 2660 Flip, prized for its outstanding battery, low cost and pocket-friendly size.

Handheld and classic consoles

Devices like the Nintendo Game Boy and PlayStation Portable (PSP) are other retro gadgets seeing a rise at the moment. These offer distraction-free gaming without the constant update loops and microtransactions often seen in modern gaming consoles now.

This provides an offline, low stress environment to people who still genuinely enjoy gaming with complete, functional games. It also removes the pressure of online leaderboards, daily quests and competitive multiplayer games.

Unlike modern digital libraries tied to expiring subscriptions, a dedicated handheld or physical cartridge also feels much more permanent and authentic, while costing far less.

In many cases, collecting older systems like the Game Boy, PS2 or SNES has become a trendy, culturally-driven hobby too, valued for long-lasting physical durability too.

Wired headphones and earphones

Wired headphones and earphones are seeing a boost too, mainly due to a mix of Y2K retro fashion trends, with the dangling wires being seen as a style statement. This has been driven by celebrity and pop star influence as well.

They are also considered to be more practical, as they don’t need to be charged and offer uninterrupted, lag-free audio for watching videos, gaming or listening to music. They are also much more affordable than high-end wireless alternatives, with the wire making them harder to drop and lose as well.

In some cases, it supports mindful tech habits, turning listening to music into a deliberate action rather than an invisible, all-day background noise.

Vinyl records and CDs

Vinyl records, CDs and retro-style cassette players also provide a fun, tactile ritual to music listening, which streaming platforms like Spotify lack. Touching album art, opening CD cases and sliding tapes into a deck can make music feel much more real and special.

Instead of skipping tracks every 10 seconds, putting on a whole album forces people to listen from start to finish, offering a deep listening experience.

Like dumb phones and handheld consoles, these offer real ownership forever too, something that is increasingly rare nowadays, while giving users a break from screen fatigue and digital noise.

Older, uniquely designed tech also provides a personal touch to spaces like bedrooms, allowing people to show off their distinct styles and taste.

World.title: Why is UK football club hiring booming, with data analyst roles surging?
World.content:
Football is increasingly becoming an industry for international investors while technology has already become a significant part of the sport. Global hiring platform Indeed announced that football club recruitment in the UK has tripled since 2018.

 

Data and analytics roles now account for a record 3.2% of professional football club hiring. Their share has more than doubled over this period as clubs invest in professionals who help shape recruitment, performance and tactical decisions.

The data focuses on the UK, but European football is highly interconnected. Data and analytics are also playing a significant role in the top European leagues such as Spain, Germany, Italy and France.

For example, LALIGA in Spain became the epicentre for big data in football in 2024. “Data is revolutionising the football industry, with clubs using it for both match preparation and post-match analysis,” a LALIGA release stated.

“Furthermore, in the context of economic control rules, this data helps clubs to identify key players within the competition, allowing them operate more intelligently in the transfer market.”

Indeed data shows that professional football clubs accounted for 714 job postings per million UK jobs in 2025. This was 247 in 2018. That means the figure almost tripled between 2018 and 2025.

Their share is expected to grow in 2026. Indeed estimates that it will reach 722 job postings per million UK jobs.

"Football clubs are no longer simply sporting institutions. They are complex media, data and commercial operations, and their hiring reflects that. Alongside coaches, clubs are recruiting chefs, stewards, marketers, community officers and, increasingly, data analysts,” Jack Kennedy, senior economist at Indeed, said.

Bigger slice of a smaller pie

Football club hiring is on the rise, but football remains a small part of the overall job market according to Indeed. Only 0.07% of UK job postings relate to this sector.

The share of retail is 4% and around 2.3% in software development. Football’s share is closer to that of a specialist field such as aviation.

“Football-club hiring held broadly steady, so clubs now make up a bigger slice of a smaller pie,” Kennedy said.

What roles do football clubs hire for?

Sports and coaching remain the largest category of club hiring. They accounted for 11.0% of UK professional football club job postings by occupation between July 2025 and June 2026 according to Indeed.

These roles include coaching, football coaches, sports coaching, football managers and personal trainers.

Food preparation and service also had a double-digit share at 10.8%. Management roles also have a significant share at 9.7%.

Administrative assistance accounts for 6.0% of football job postings, followed by therapy at 3.8% and sales at 3.7%. Arts and entertainment and marketing also have more than 3% share.

The share of data and analytics roles is growing

Data and analytics roles ranked ninth in football club job postings with 3.2% share. Despite its relatively small share, it has become a central role for professional football over the past decade.

The share of data and analytics roles in club hiring has more than doubled, from 1.5% in 2018 to 3.2% in the year to June 2026.

Most popular titles in data and analytics roles are performance analyst, analyst, data scientist, data analyst and data science intern.

“What began with basic performance tracking now supports player recruitment, tactical preparation, injury prevention and commercial strategy,” Kennedy said.

“The challenge is not acquiring data but knowing what to do with it, and the clubs that can translate analytical insight into better decisions, on the training ground, in the transfer market, and in the dugout, are increasingly the ones pulling ahead.”

40 times the size of the playing squad

The number of staff in football clubs largely vary.

Some of the biggest clubs now employ as many as 1,000 staff according to Indeed. This is around 40 times the size of a Premier League playing squad.

World.title: Ukraine launches drone strikes on Russian e-commerce giant Ozon
World.content:
Russian e-commerce giant Ozon said four of its logistics hubs in southern Russia were targeted by Ukrainian drones on Monday, as Kyiv expanded a campaign aimed at disrupting Moscow's commercial supply networks.

 

Drone debris also struck apartment buildings and set warehouses on fire.

A fire broke out at an Ozon centre in Makhachkala, the capital of Russia's Dagestan region, after a drone attack at around 05:00 local time, the company said.

Several people were wounded but their lives were not in danger, according to Ozon, which said the facility had suspended operations.

A large fire was also reported at an Ozon logistics centre in Enem, in the Krasnodar region, although staff were evacuated and no casualties were reported.

Warehouses in Adygeysk and Nevinnomyssk were also evacuated because of the threat of drone attacks but escaped damage.

Two children were killed and nine people injured, including seven children, when drone debris hit a private childcare centre in Krasnodar during the overnight attacks, regional governor Veniamin Kondratyev said.

The latest incidents bring the total to six Ozon facilities targeted since Saturday, when Ukraine announced it was turning its attention to Russia's second-largest online marketplace after weeks of strikes against rival Wildberries.

"After Ukrainian units hit the 15 largest logistics hubs of Wildberries, it is now Ozon's turn," Ukraine's defence ministry said.

Kyiv says warehouses operated by the retailers store dual-use goods and form part of supply networks supporting Russia's military.

Ozon facilities in the Samara and Orenburg regions were targeted over the weekend (see cover image), forcing hundreds of employees to evacuate and disrupting operations.

The latest attacks also hit investors, with Ozon shares falling as much as 12% on the Moscow Exchange on Monday.

Russia has condemned Ukraine's attacks on what it describes as civilian infrastructure.

The strikes come two days after Russia launched a major daytime drone attack on the city of Kryvyi Rih, the hometown of Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy.

World.title: Thai PM meets security chiefs after coordinated attacks in three southern provinces
World.content:
Thailand’s Prime Minister Anutin Charnvirakul, already facing a flood crisis in the country’s north, held an urgent meeting on Sunday with high-level security officials in response to coordinated violence overnight in three southern provinces where a small-scale Muslim insurgency is active.

 

The meeting, held shortly before Anutin flew north to inspect the badly flooded province of Nan, followed 51 incidents on Saturday night in the southernmost provinces of Narathiwat, Pattani and Yala.

The attackers did not engage with military or police forces. Only three civilians were known to have been wounded and they were reported to be recovering on Sunday.

The violence primarily involved small bombs, arson and other forms of property damage. The highest-profile target was a 7-Eleven convenience store in Pattani.

A video circulating on social media appeared to show armed men stalking outside the store while customers and workers fled before it was set on fire.

A bomb that damaged rail tracks in Narathiwat forced the suspension of local and long-haul services. It was not clear when they would be restored due to the uncertain security situation.

Thailand's Prime Minister Anutin Charnvirakul, left, speaks with a delegation member in Canberra, 19 August, 2026 AP Photo

As has often been the case with such incidents, no group was immediately publicly blamed or claimed responsibility for the actions.

However, such attacks are generally believed to be carried out by the Barisan Revolusi Nasional Melayu Patani (BRN). It is the major insurgent group in the south with the organisational means and support to stage such an action.

It is also the group with which the Thai government has been holding intermittent peace talks.

The three southernmost provinces are the only ones with Muslim majorities in predominantly Buddhist Thailand and the BRN has said that it is seeking self-rule for them.

Muslim residents have long complained of being treated like second-class citizens in Thailand, and separatist movements have been periodically active for decades.

Insurgent violence escalated sharply in 2004 and was met with heavy-handed crackdowns, further fuelling discontent.

According to Deep South Watch, a think tank based at the Prince of Songkla University’s campus in Pattani, 7,837 people have died in the violence in the past 22 years.

The last major flare-up came in July, when about 10 attackers opened fire and threw pipe bombs at soldiers at a security checkpoint in Narathiwat. Five paramilitary soldiers were killed and six civilians were wounded, including a 10-year-old boy.

A 7-Eleven convenience store damaged by arson in Pattani province, 23 August, 2026 The Government's Internal Security Operations Command via AP/The Government's Internal Security Operations Command

Don Pathan, an independent security analyst, says the BRN carries out attacks largely for leverage as it negotiates with the Thai government.

“From the ground, BRN combatants are turned off by the boasting of military officials and wanted to use the spike in violence to demonstrate their capabilities," said Pathan.

"Many of the targets in these latest incidents were civilians, but BRN combatants were not after body counts. They want to send a stern message to the Thais of what they are capable of doing.”

World.title: Owner of Swiss bar in deadly New year blaze held for domestic abuse, media say
World.content:
The owner of the Swiss bar ravaged by a deadly New Year fire is in pre-trial detention, accused of domestic abuse against his wife and co-owner of the establishment, media reported on Sunday.

 

French couple Jacques and Jessica Moretti have been the focus of intense scrutiny since the fire ripped though their bar Le Constellation, in the Crans-Montana ski resort in the early hours of 1 January.

The blaze killed 41 people, most of them teenagers, injuring 115 other people.

The Morettis are among 16 people facing criminal investigation in the case. They face charges including manslaughter by negligence and arson by negligence over the fire.

Jacques Moretti has now been arrested and detained following alleged violence against his wife earlier this month, local Geneva broadcaster Léman Bleu reported.

People light candles and place floral tributes outside the sealed off Le Constellation bar in Crans-Montana, 3 January, 2026 AP Photo

The incident reportedly happened on the night of 11 August at the couple's home in Switzerland's southwestern Wallis canton and was so serious that Jessica Moretti had to be hospitalised.

Neither the public prosecutor's office nor the couple's lawyers responded immediately to requests for comment.

However, the Moretti's lawyers released a statement on Sunday evening referring to the report, stressing that the alleged events were being investigated in a separate case pertaining "exclusively to their private life."

"They should not be confused with the Constellation tragedy," the lawyers said in the statement.

They added though that the reported events "nevertheless fall within a context that cannot be ignored: that of a particularly intense ordeal that the Morettis have been trying to face together since 1 January."

World.title: Turkey, Saudi Arabia and Pakistan strengthen ties as Israel tensions rise
World.content:
Tensions between Turkey and Israel have intensified after an Israeli airstrike targeted a Syrian military airbase near the Turkish border. The strike came days after Turkey’s new military pact with Saudi Arabia and Pakistan.

Advertising

Ankara swiftly condemned Tuesday's Israeli airstrike on Syria’s Abu Duhur military airbase, 70 kilometres from its border, calling it illegal and a breach of Syrian sovereignty.

Ankara is a key ally of Syria's new authorities. Israel justified its actions, accusing Turkey of seeking to expand its military footprint in Syria, which it sees as a serious threat.

“Israel is uneasy about the Turkish presence in Syria, and Turkish ambitions to play a major role in Syria’s future are unsettling from an Israeli perspective,” explains Turkey expert Gallia Lindenstrauss of Israel's Institute for National Security Studies.

“There's concern that Turkey will establish its own bases in Syria,” she added.

Israeli-Turkish tensions have risen over Israel’s war in Gaza and Lebanon, and Ankara’s support of Hamas, evolving into a broader regional rivalry.

“In general, there's uneasiness [in Israel] about Turkey's assertiveness, both in Syria and in the Mediterranean and other parts of the Middle East and the greater regional arena," said Lindenstrauss.

Landmark agreement

Earlier this month, Turkey, Saudi Arabia and Pakistan made headlines by signing a landmark military accord in the Saudi city of Mecca. Known as the Mecca Accord, this alliance pledges mutual defence if any member is attacked, akin to NATO’s Article 5.

Turkish international relations expert Soli Ozel claims the impetus for the agreement is uncertainty around Washington’s willingness or ability to protect its regional allies amid ongoing tensions involving Iran.

“Undoubtedly, the United States is proving to be an increasingly unreliable partner. Countries worldwide, especially in the larger Middle East region, are looking for other ways to provide security for themselves,” said Ozel.

Iran says ‘Muslim Nato’ pact reflects retreat from US security umbrella

The Mecca Accord members view each other as bringing complementary strengths to deal with shared concerns.

"Pakistan brings military capabilities and is a nuclear power. The Saudis have the money. Turkey has a budding defence industry and a large army. It claims not to be against any country, but I think those three parties agree that Iran is a destabilising actor, as is Israel,” explained Ozel.

The Mecca Accord is set to boost defence and intelligence ties, with Saudi Arabia expected to bolster Turkey’s expanding defence sector.

But many analysts see Iran and Israel as the accord’s principal focus.

“The deal is meant to signal both to Iran and Israel that they will be isolated in the region if they continue with assertive, belligerent policies,” said Asli Aydintasbas of the United States-based Brookings Institution.

Turkey steps up as Europe's indispensable and uncomfortable defence partner

'Two axes in the Middle East'

Despite Iran’s recent attacks on Saudi Arabia, Aydintasbas argues that while the Mecca Accord has a mutual defence clause – meaning an attack on one member is an attack on all – Turkey and Pakistan will not be drawn into a conflict with Iran.

“We know that they have no desire to get involved. But it does mean there will be greater military cooperation,” said Aydintasbas.

Countering Houthi rebel attacks in the Red Sea on Saudi tankers could be the first real test of the alliance.

But Aydintasbas cautions that the Mecca Accord will not replace the US as the “ultimate security provider” for the region. Instead, it's more about burden sharing, a move that fits well with Washington’s wider agenda.

Washington has given its blessing to the accord, and expansion talks are already under way.

European Union slams 'inflammatory' Houthi Red Sea tanker attack

Turkish Foreign Minister Hakan Fidan hinted that Egypt could be the next member, with Turkish media reporting that Egypt’s foreign minister will join his Saudi, Turkish and Pakistani counterparts for a meeting in Istanbul later this month.

“Developments in Egypt are of major concern to Israel,” said Lindenstrauss. But she believes the Mecca Accord is an opportunity for Israel, given there are mutual concerns among its allies over the Accord.

“Israel already has very close relations with Greece, Cyprus, the United Arab Emirates and India,” she noted. "And I do envision a deepening of this relationship. And so we have the formation of two loose axes in the Greater Middle East."

World.title: New Zealand proposes social media ban for under-16s
World.content:
The government is set to follow Australia's lead and introduce a bill banning children from social media. But the plan already faces opposition from within the ruling coalition.

New Zealand's government is set to introduce legislation Monday banning children under the age of 16 from social media, following the lead of several countries across the world, including neighbor Australia.

What does New Zealand's social media ban entail?

The Online Safety Bill would require platforms like Instagram, TikTok, Snapchat and Facebook to verify users are 16 or older using tools such as facial age estimation and digital ID, with fines of up to 10% of global revenue for non-compliance.

​​Platforms would also have to assess the risks they pose to young users and report on efforts to reduce them.

Prime Minister Christopher Luxon said the harm to children is too great to ignore.

"We simply cannot accept the harm being done to a generation of New Zealand children," he said, citing effects on mental health, sleep and education. The government's data shows one in three children aged 13 to 17 now spend at least five hours a day on social media.

Social media bans: What it means for you To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Education Minister Erica Stanford said the bill places the legal burden on platforms, not families: "No penalties are proposed for children, their parents or caregivers."

When will the bill be introduced?

Even though New Zealand spent more than a year examining the potential ban, the bill's future is uncertain, as coalition partners NZ First and ACT have both voiced opposition, questioning the law's effectiveness.

Australia's similar ban took effect last year, barring under-16s from platforms including Facebook, Instagram and TikTok as part of an effort to shield children from bullying and "predatory algorithms." But a June peer-reviewed study by Australian researchers found little evidence it reduced teen social media use.

World.title: US: Wildfire forces mass evacuations near Reno, Nevada
World.content:
A wind-driven wildfire has forced roughly 42,000 people to evacuate and destroyed homes as fire crews continue to battle extreme conditions.

A fast-moving, wind-driven wildfire forced tens of thousands of people to evacuate their homes near Reno in the US state of Nevada over the weekend.

An unknown number of homes have been destroyed and at least six people have been injured.

Officials have expanded the "GO NOW" zone to include almost 90,000 residents as conditions make the fire unpredicatable.

What do we know about the Hawk Fire in Nevada?

The fire started Saturday morning off Hawk Meadow Trail and spread rapidly through the Peavine Peak area northwest of the city, growing to between roughly 13,000 and 15,000 acres by Sunday.

About 42,000 residents were ordered to evacuate, with another 45,000 told to be ready to leave, officials said. The evacuation zone stretched to the edge of the University of Nevada in northwest Reno, a city of more than 280,000 people near the California border.

At least six people were injured — three first responders and three civilians — local authorities said. Officials said the fire was human-caused but have not released further details.

"The Hawk Fire is a very dynamic incident for us as it's being driven by the winds. The wind-driven fires move very rapidly into our residential areas," fire chief Richard Edwards told AFP.

Officials say the Hawk Fire was human-caused Image: Trevor Bexon/Getty Images/AFP

Nevada Governor Joe Lombardo declared a state of emergency in Washoe County and mobilized the National Guard, deploying two helicopters and 60 troops to assist firefighting and security efforts. "This is an active and rapidly evolving situation, and I urge everyone in the affected areas to remain vigilant and follow the direction of local officials," he said, according to Reuters.

Human cost of the wildfire

The fire has already destroyed homes. Cari Kieffer told AP her family fled with only minutes to spare, grabbing clothes, a Bible, her wedding photos and her mother's ashes, but leaving behind birth certificates and childhood photos.

"I kept looking outside and the flames just kept getting closer and closer every time I looked," she said. "I was like, we gotta go like now."

"We lost all our stuff. Everything we own is gone."

Can Germany teach Europe how to prevent wildfires? To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Nearly 10,000 customers remained without power in Washoe County on Sunday, down from about 60,000 the day before, AP reported. Parts of US Route 395 were closed, two hospitals evacuated patients, and officials monitored whether the county jail would need to be evacuated. The Reno-Tahoe airport remained outside the evacuation zone, with flights operating normally.

The blaze adds to a wave of fire activity across the drought-stricken Western United States this year. Fifteen new fires broke out across Nevada on Saturday alone.
