World.title: New official tasked with promoting Poland criticised over error-strewn, potentially AI-generated report
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support. A government official appointed last month to promote Poland abroad has been hit by a wave of criticism after it emerged that she authored a report containing errors and which shows signs of being generated by artificial intelligence. The document mislocated major Polish cities and included bizarre language mixing Polish and English. It was marked as being part of a project financed by the sport and tourism ministry, though the ministry itself has denied that claim. The opposition has called on prosecutors to investigate potential misuse of public funds. ⁉️ Czy “Markę Polska” ma nam wygenerować sztuczna inteligencja? ⁉️ Czy Ministerstwo Sportu i Turystyki zapłaciło 200 000 złotych w ramach zadania publicznego za raport wygenerowany przez AI? ⁉️ Czy mogę prosić Panią Minister prof. @b_mroz_gorgon o odniesienie się do tych pytań… pic.twitter.com/lM2AY88oAh — Sebastian Meitz (@MeitzPL) August 20, 2026 The official in question, Barbara Mróz-Gorgoń, is a professor at Wrocław University of Economics who was appointed three weeks ago as the government’s plenipotentiary for the promotion of Poland’s brand, a newly created position. She was presented at a press conference by Prime Minister Donald Tusk. However, this week, journalists and commentators began highlighting cases of bizarre errors from a report, titled A Self-Portrait of the Poles (Polaków Portret Własny), published last year with Mróz-Gorgoń named as the author, in her position as president of a think tank called Marka Polska (Brand Poland). The report contained some glaring errors, such as describing the city of Katowice as being in “north central” Poland (whereas in fact it is in the south) and Wrocław as being in the “northwest” (when it is actually in the southwest). Geografia – czyli gdzie leżą Katowice A propos miast jest też ciekawy chochlik lub też, jakby to powiedział ktoś złośliwy, klasyczna halucynacja AI. Przy opisie badań FGI miasta opisane są w następujący sposób (zdjęcie poniżej): 👉 Olsztyn – północny wschód 👉 Szczecin -… pic.twitter.com/SF6XBRfhWS — Sebastian Meitz (@MeitzPL) August 20, 2026 Other parts contain strange analysis, such as noting that “after World War Two, Germany did not build its brand on the Holocaust”. The text also features unusual language, including random use of words in English, some of which have been turned into Polish ones. It is also regularly features words written in capital letters. One sentence, for example, refers to “INSTABILNOŚĆ” and “REZILIENCE”, presumably meaning “instability” and “resilience”, but neither of which is a Polish word. Another section claims that 95% of Poles born after 1990 are “polilingwalni” (an invented Polonised version of “polylingual”) who speak “angielski fluent”, a strange linguistic mix that means they speak English fluently. As well as the unusual language, the very claim that 95% of young Poles speak fluent English, as well as that many additionally speak Mandarin, has been questioned by many commentators. The report also contains bizarre errors in footnotes, which are numbered randomly (on one page, three consecutive footnotes are numbered “41, 517, 6”) and some of which are completely empty. A number of expert commentators have suggested that the text contains clear indications that it was generated by AI, a claim supported by evidence from programmes that check texts for AI-generated content. AI czy nie AI, oto jest pytanie Czytając ten raport kilkukrotnie, trudno mi było pozbyć się wrażenia, że nikt poważny, a szczególnie naukowiec z tytułem doktora habilitowanego, nie wygenerowałby dużych części raportu, za który zapłacili podatnicy, w jakimś LLM. No bo przecież… pic.twitter.com/jyTexgmeXS — Sebastian Meitz (@MeitzPL) August 20, 2026 As well as bearing Mróz-Gorgoń’s name as author, the report also features on its front cover the logo of the sport and tourism ministry. The first page then includes a note saying that the project was carried out under an initiative co-financed by the ministry. After the issue began to draw attention and criticism on Thursday, the ministry issued a statement saying that the report was not ordered by them, was not part of any agreement to which the ministry was a party, and that no request to use the ministry’s logo was submitted. However, a social media post last November by deputy sport and tourism minister Piotr Borys shows him attending an event to present the report. He thanked Mróz-Gorgoń for coordinating the project and inviting him to the presentation. 📚W Akademii Leona Koźmińskiego odbyła się prezentacja raportu „Polaków Portret Własny”, przygotowanego Think Tank Marka Polska. To wyjątkowe wydarzenie poświęcone premierze badań dotyczących DNA Marki Polska. 🧬To pierwsze tak kompleksowe badanie, które pokazuje, kim jesteśmy… pic.twitter.com/jb7KdCJTPM — Piotr Borys (@piotr_borys) November 26, 2025 On Thursday evening, Mróz-Gorgoń herself addressed the controversy in an interview with Polsat News. She said that the report was actually a “work in progress” that “should never have appeared in the public space”. However, she still defended the work, saying that “the research was conducted reliably” and “the conclusions stand up to scrutiny”. But she also admitted that the writing of the report had been “aided by artificial intelligence”. In separate remarks to the Polish Press Agency (PAP), she said that “we used AI tools solely for transcription, summarising and text editing; they did not design research content or draw conclusions…We worked according to social science methodology, diligently and without cutting corners”. Meanwhile, on the Marka Polska think tank’s website, where the report had been published, it was initially changed on Thursday to being marked as a “draft version” before later being deleted entirely. Od raportu i deklaracji, że “praca badawcza [została] przeprowadzona zgodnie z zasadami nauk społecznych, rzetelnie i merytorycznie, w oparciu o opisaną metodologię”, przez “work in progress”, aż do “Oops! That page can’t be found”. Myślę, że to słowo “Oops!” jest najlepszym… pic.twitter.com/OaSTxkwKwa — Sebastian Meitz (@MeitzPL) August 20, 2026 On Thursday evening, the main opposition party, Law and Justice (PiS), announced that it was submitting requests to both prosecutors and the Central Anti-Corruption Bureau (ABW) to investigate the use of around 200,000 zloty (€46,380) in state funds for the project that the report was allegedly part of. PiS has also called on Mróz-Gorgoń to resign or to be fired. On Friday, a deputy digital affairs minister, Dariusz Standerski, told the Wirtualna Polska news website that “all the circumstances surrounding the creation of this report will be clarified”. The controversy around Mróz-Gorgoń comes just days after the sport and tourism ministry was involved in the launch of a new advertising campaign designed to encourage tourism to Poland, but which many commentators have argued was poorly conceived and executed. Poland has launched a new advertising campaign to attract tourists from Europe and the US. The first video, under the slogan "Poland. More than you expected", features footballer Robert Lewandowski, Hollywood star Jesse Eisenberg and supermodel Anja Rubik https://t.co/3jtqyUWQyy — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) August 19, 2026 Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! A speed of 253 km/h (157 mph) has been reached by a Pendolino train during tests carried out as part of preparations to speed up rail connections between Poland’s major cities from next year. The plans will see the journey time between Warsaw and Kraków cut to well under two hours. “Polish rail is accelerating – and 250 km/h is just the beginning,” declared the infrastructure minister Dariusz Klimczak, alluding to plans for Poland to later begin running trains at speeds of up to 320 km/h. Osiągnęliśmy 250 km/h na Centralnej Magistrali Kolejowej❗🚅 Dzisiejsze nocne testy systemu GSM-R na linii nr 4 zakończyły się pełnym sukcesem. Oznacza to, że pociągi pojadą tą trasą z rozkładową prędkością 250 km/h już w przyszłym roku❗ Pozwoli to znacznie skrócić czas… pic.twitter.com/ndXvePZP4t — PLK SA (@PKP_PLK_SA) August 18, 2026 The tests on the GSM-R data transmission system, a communication standard designed to be used at very high speeds, were carried out on Monday night. Trains will be able to run on Poland’s Central Main Line (CMK), which connects Warsaw with Kraków and Katowice, at a scheduled speed of 250 km/h from December 2027. That will cut the expected journey time between Warsaw and Kraków, the country’s two largest cities, by around half an hour to 1 hour and 52 minutes, reports rail news service Portal Kolejowy. It will also be possible to travel from the capital to Wrocław, Poland’s third-largest city, in around three hours. The fastest current connection is 3 hours and 30 minutes. Reaching the target speed of 250 km/h was a “very important moment for Polish rail”, said Maciej Kaczorek, a board member of PKP Polskie Linie Kolejowe, the state railway infrastructure manager, quoted by news website Money.pl. Poland has been operating Pendolinos, built by France’s Alstom, since 2014. The trains are designed to run at speeds of up to 250 km/h, but currently operate at a maximum of 200 km/h in Poland and run on routes connecting Warsaw, Kraków, Wrocław and the Tricity area. However, this week’s tests are not a record rail speed in Poland. In 2013, a Pendolino reached 293 km/h during a test on the CMK a year before the high-speed trains commenced passenger services in the country. A Polish Pendolino high-speed train has begun running in the Czech Republic for the first time. The Prague-Bohumín service will run until June as part of a certification process that Polish operator PKP Intercity hopes will lead to a Warsaw-Prague route https://t.co/hmUNd7ft0E — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) March 10, 2026 Speaking to Rynek Kolejowy, deputy infrastructure minister Piotr Malepszak said that it had “taken too long” for the network to be adapted to allow regular speeds of 250 km/h. The current government, which took power in December 2023, has much broader plans for expanding high-speed rail travel in Poland, including building 2,700 km of tracks capable of carrying trains at 320 km/h. In December 2025, state rail operator PKP Intercity launched a tender for 20 such trains. They would cut the journey time between Warsaw and Gdańsk, on Poland’s Baltic coast, to around 100 minutes – from 2 hours 25 minutes currently – by 2040, Malepszak told the Polish Press Agency in June. Passenger numbers on Poland’s rail network have been booming in recent years. In the first half of 2026, a record 44.7 million passengers travelled with PKP Intercity, more than 10% up on the previous year’s record and some 45% higher than three years earlier. Poland has launched a tender to buy 20 trains that can reach speeds of 320 km/h (199 mph), making them the fastest ever to travel on Polish tracks. Currently, Poland's fastest trains, Pendolinos, can reach maximum speeds of 200 km/h https://t.co/XcGdJJggkx — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) December 31, 2025 Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. World.title: Polish government proposes middle-class tax cuts funded by increased rates for wealthiest
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support. Poland’s government has unveiled plans to reduce income tax rates for an estimated 3.5 million people earning around or slightly above average salaries. The costs of the cuts would be covered by increasing the tax rate for large companies and individuals with the highest earnings. The changes, which Prime Minister Donald Tusk says are intended to “provide relief and assistance to the growing middle class”, would come into effect from next year – when the government is facing re-election. However, the proposals still require approval from parliament, where Tusk’s ruling coalition, which ranges from left to centre right, has a majority, and President Karol Nawrocki, who is aligned with the right-wing opposition and has vetoed a record number of bills. 📊 Nowa skala PIT będzie lepiej dopasowana do rosnących wynagrodzeń. Do 130 tys. zł pozostaje stawka 12%, między 130 a 150 tys. zł pojawi się 24%, a 32% zacznie obowiązywać dopiero powyżej 150 tys. zł. 💰 #WięcejWPortfelu pic.twitter.com/1S2MpSkVoC — Kancelaria Premiera (@PremierRP) August 19, 2026 The main elements of the proposed changes, which were outlined by Tusk and finance minister Andrzej Domański on Wednesday, are an increase in the earnings threshold at which the lowest rate of income tax is paid and the introduction of a new rate between the lowest and highest earnings brackets. Currently, there are two income tax brackets: the first taxes earnings of up to 120,000 zloty (around €27,800) at a rate of 12%; the second taxes earnings above that level at a rate of 32%. There is also a tax-free allowance for earnings of up to 30,000 zloty. Meanwhile, anyone who earns more than 1 million zloty a year pays an additional “solidarity levy” (effectively a third tax bracket) of 4% on income above that amount. Under the new proposals, the threshold for the first 12% tax bracket would be raised to 130,000 zloty. For earnings between 130,000 and 150,000 zloty, a new tax bracket of 24% would be introduced. Then earnings above 150,000 would be taxed at 32%. Tusk noted that, since his government took office, wages in Poland have increased by around 30%, bringing increasing numbers of people into the higher tax bracket. According to figures from Statistics Poland (GUS), a state agency, in June this year, average monthly earnings at companies employing more than nine people were 9,401.58 zloty, the equivalent of almost 113,000 zloty a year. “We’re not talking about millionaires here; we’re talking about a growing middle class…on whose shoulders the financing of state security, defence spending, etc. rests to a large extent,” said Domański. “We want to change this…so that those who work hard to earn their average wage can clearly feel the relief,” added Tusk. “And we want this to be financed by the wealthiest companies and the wealthiest individuals, who have the lowest tax burden.” The number of ultra-wealthy individuals in Poland has more than doubled since 2021, a faster rate of growth than anywhere else in the world, according to a new study https://t.co/MNKgmjzn2U — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) May 11, 2026 Therefore, in order to finance the middle-class tax cuts, Tusk and Domański announced that the government would seek to increase corporate income tax from 19% to 22% for firms and tax capital groups that generate annual revenues above €50 million. Meanwhile, the solidarity levy for individuals earning over 1 million zloty a year would be increased by one percentage point, to 5%. “I am absolutely convinced that this will make our tax system more equitable,” declared Tusk. However, he also conceded that raising the income-tax-free amount from 30,000 to 60,000 zloty – as his Civic Platform (KO) party promised to do within its first 100 days in office – would not be possible for budgetary reasons, in particular the need to finance high defence spending. Poland has introduced a new type of account that will allow individuals to invest up to 100,000 zloty (€23,200) tax free. The government says the scheme is designed to encourage Poles to build savings and channel money into the domestic financial market https://t.co/1xDHHJGYKX — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) August 14, 2026 The prime minister said that the planned tax changes would be discussed further this week at a cabinet meeting devoted to next year’s state budget, which is currently being prepared. The relevant legislation will subsequently be submitted to parliament, with the aim of bringing it into force in 2027. However, Tusk acknowledged that there is a strong possibility of a veto by Nawrocki, who has blocked dozens of government bills, including fiscal measures. In December, Nawrocki vetoed an increase in the tax on alcoholic and sweet drinks. Last month, he effectively blocked a windfall tax on fuel companies’ excess profits by sending it to the constitutional court for review. However, he did approve a law increasing the corporate income tax rate for banks. President @NawrockiKn has obstructed a planned windfall tax on fuel companies by sending it to the constitutional court, where it could stay for years The tax aimed to offset fuel price protection costs after the Iran war surgehttps://t.co/UojVuYhvdV — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) July 27, 2026 Next year’s budget will be closely watched given that Poland’s fiscal situation has become increasingly problematic in recent years. In 2024, the European Union placed Poland under its excessive deficit procedure, requiring Warsaw to commit to measures to bring down the deficit. However, last year the deficit actually rose, from 6.4% of GDP in 2024 to 7.3% in 2025, which was the second-highest level among all EU member states. This year, Poland’s public debt passed the EU’s limit of 60% of GDP for the first time on record. The situation has led two of the big three rating agencies, Fitch and Moody’s, to shift Poland’s credit outlook to negative. This year, Fitch warned that the political gridlock between Nawrocki and the government was making tackling the deficit and debt more difficult. Given that Poland will hold parliamentary elections in autumn 2027, it is unlikely that either the government or Nawrocki – who will be supporting the right-wing opposition – will be keen on any fiscal measures that either raise taxes or reduce spending in areas such as social policy and defence. Poland’s public debt has passed 60% of GDP for the first time, thereby exceeding the limit enshrined in EU law. World.title: Poland launches tourism campaign featuring Lewandowski, Eisenberg and Rubik
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support. Poland has launched a new advertising campaign to promote itself internationally and attract more tourists from “key European markets” and the United States. The new initiative, which has the slogan “Poland. More than you expected”, features global Polish icons such as football star Robert Lewandowski, supermodel Anja Rubik, and Hollywood filmmaker Jesse Eisenberg, who received Polish citizenship last year. A series of videos, the first of which was released Tuesday, will aim to present Poland as “modern, safe, diverse and authentic”, as well as “defying stereotypes”, says sports and tourism minister Jakub Rutnicki. Commissioned by his ministry and launched by the Polish Tourism Organisation (POT), the campaign will be conducted in Germany, Spain, Italy, the United Kingdom and the United States. The first video promotes Warsaw, Poland’s capital, and features Lewandowski, Rubik and Eisenberg appearing near the city’s landmarks. Polish actor Nikodem Rozbicki, meanwhile, plays the role of renowned 19th-century Polish composer Fryderyk Chopin. In the 30-second spot, Chopin’s character declares that Warsaw is “where my heart is” – a reference to the fact that Chopin’s heart, preserved in cognac, was brought back to the city from Paris by his sister shortly after his death in 1849 and is now immured in a pillar in the city’s Holy Cross Church. Lewandowski, who recently joined US football team Chicago Fire, tells viewers that Poland offers “more than you expected”, a reference to the campaign’s main slogan, which suggests to viewers that Poland may surprise them positively. “Research shows that people who have visited Poland rate it much more favourably than their previous perceptions or media reports suggested,” notes POT in its press release. Magdalena Krucz, the head of POT, adds that she believes the campaign “will be as surprising to audiences as Poland itself is to tourists who come to us for the first time”. However, the slogan is not new: it has been used by POT to promote Poland since 2021. The new campaign will also feature Nobel Peace Prize winner and former president Lech Wałęsa, who led the Solidarity movement that brought down Poland’s former communist regime. POT notes that he remains “one of the most recognisable symbols in the world of the fight for freedom and democracy”. The music is arranged by Radzimir Dębski, better known as Jimek, a Polish composer and conductor who has regularly performed with US rap legend Snoop Dogg. Polish-American NBA star @JeremySochan has joined a campaign to promote Poland as a tourist destination. His appearance has been received positively, but Sochan responded directly to one commentator who said a black person shouldn't be advertising Poland https://t.co/KXDok7IAXP — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) November 15, 2024 Poland has experienced a tourism boom in recent years. Last year, the country recorded the European Union’s second-fastest growth in the number of nights spent in tourist accommodation, behind only Malta. The biggest tourist draw is the historic city of Kraków, which was last year named the best city break destination in Europe by members of British consumer association and magazine Which? for the fifth time. This year, Time Out magazine rated Kraków the 16th best city in the world. However, the country has a wide range of tourist-friendly destinations, including long, sandy beaches on the northern Baltic coast, mountains in the south, the lake district of Masuria, as well as many historic cities and modern museums and galleries. Poland saw the EU's second-fastest growth in tourism in 2025, behind only the Mediterranean island state of Malta https://t.co/WVkRbHtU7o — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) January 19, 2026 The city of Lublin in eastern Poland, which will be a European City of Culture in 2029, last year welcomed a record 2.2 million visitors, including over half a million from abroad. The city is known for its rich Jewish history, and featured prominently in the 2024 Oscar-nominated film A Real Pain, directed by and starring Eisenberg, whose ancestors were Jews from Lublin and the nearby town of Krasnystaw. Last year, the sport and tourism ministry announced that it wants tourism to contribute 9% of GDP within a decade, from about 5% now. The strategy includes creating a “Polish brand” through which internationally recognised athletes, artists, historical figures and products are showcased more prominently. Last month, the government appointed a marketing and branding expert to develop a unified strategy for promoting the country abroad, saying the move will help boost tourism, support Polish products and attract foreign investment. The city of Lublin in eastern Poland welcomed a record 2.2 million visitors in 2025. World.title: Warsaw Uprising veteran and activist Wanda Traczyk-Stawska dies aged 99
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support. Wanda Traczyk-Stawska, a veteran of the Warsaw Uprising against Nazi-German occupation during World War Two, has died aged 99. Traczyk-Stawska, who survived imprisonment in German camps after the uprising, in her later years became a vocal advocate for the rights of women and disabled people. “Warsaw has lost someone extraordinary,” wrote Warsaw’s mayor, Rafał Trzaskowski, announcing her death on Wednesday. “A heroine, a soldier…but above all a teacher who, throughout her life, taught us what matters most: courage, dignity, and responsibility for our fellow human beings.” Odeszła Pani Wanda. Trudno w to uwierzyć. Warszawa straciła kogoś wyjątkowego – Bohaterkę, żołnierkę Powstania Warszawskiego, Honorową Obywatelkę miasta. Ale przede wszystkim nauczycielkę, która przez całe życie uczyła nas tego, co najważniejsze: odwagi, godności i… pic.twitter.com/uSNcsZ7c1P — Rafał Trzaskowski (@trzaskowski_) August 19, 2026 Traczyk-Stawska, born in Warsaw in 1927, was only 12 years old when Nazi Germany invaded Poland. She initially became involved in the Grey Ranks (Szare Szeregi), an underground resistance movement associated with the Polish scouting movement, participating in sabotage operations. She later joined the Home Army (AK), Poland’s main resistance force, and, at the age of 17, served as a riflewoman and liaison during the Warsaw Uprising, taking the nom de guerre “Pączek” (meaning “Bud”). Traczyk-Stawska was seriously injured while fighting in the uprising. After the revolt was defeated, she was taken prisoner and subsequently held in various prisoner-of-war camps in Germany until the end of the war. After returning to Poland, Traczyk-Stawska earned a degree in psychology and began working as a teacher of disabled children in Warsaw. At the same time, she became an active figure in commemorating the uprising and its participants. In her final years, Traczyk-Stawska also became politically active. In 2018, she visited parliament to support a protest by disabled people and their carers, who were seeking more state support. Two years later, at the age of 93, she and another female uprising veteran, Hanna Stadnik, joined the mass Women’s Strike protests that broke out in response to the introduction of a near-total ban on abortion under the national-conservative Law and Justice (PiS) government. “We women will not relent this time,” she told broadcaster TVN at the time. “In the uprising, we fought for our freedom, because there is no dignity without freedom. If we are currently treated like incubators, we have the right to fight for our dignity…We will fight – unarmed, but to the last woman – not to be treated like objects.” Traczyk-Stawska was also among a group of female Uprising veterans who that year criticised PiS leader Jarosław Kaczyński for wearing, during a speech condemning the Women’s Strike protests, a badge featuring the anchor symbol that was used by the Home Army during the war. She was also an advocate for women’s rights more broadly. In 2023, in a speech at the 79th anniversary of the uprising, Traczyk-Stawska noted that, “at the beginning, the generals shouted: ‘Why do we need so many women?'” But, by the time the uprising ended, “we had been given the same rights as boys. And we won’t get rid of these rights. Because everyone, whether a man or a woman, is a citizen of this country and has equality written into the constitution”. Her speech then became overtly political, saying that “this [PiS] government needs to be completely changed, as it doesn’t remember that women have their own position enshrined in the constitution. That we are equal to men.” In both the 2020 and 2025 presidential elections, Traczyk-Stawska expressed support for the candidacy of Trzaskowski, who is a deputy leader of the centrist Civic Coalition (KO) party that is PiS’s main opponent. However, in both elections, Trzaskowski lost to PiS-backed candidates. Odeszła Wanda Traczyk-Stawska ps. „Pączek” – Bohaterka, Patriotka, wzór odwagi i niezłomności. Pokazywała, że prawdziwy patriotyzm to budowanie wspólnoty, empatia i otwartość na świat. Cześć Jej pamięci! 🕯️🤍 Najgłębsze wyrazy współczucia dla Bliskich. pic.twitter.com/nY0ijDSBlJ — Monika Sikora ⚡️ (@Moni_Sikora) August 19, 2026 Following news of Traczyk-Stawska’s death, many prominent figures paid tribute to her, in particular from the current KO-led ruling coalition. “Farewell, heroine,” wrote KO leader and Prime Minister Donald Tusk, sharing a photo of himself with Traczyk-Stawska and quoting one of her statements: “Do not stand, do not watch when evil happens, but react immediately, for that is your duty.” While she had fought against German occupation, Traczyk-Stawska later called for reconciliation. In her 2023 speech, she called Germany “our best neighbour” and said that the two countries must now “stand together”, including supporting Ukraine against Russian aggression. Today, Germany’s ambassador to Poland, Miguel Berger, expressed his “great sadness” at Traczyk-Stawska’s death, calling her an “advocate of dialogue in the process of Polish-German reconciliation and a passionate champion of peace, freedom, and human dignity”. „Nie stój, nie patrz, gdy się zło dzieje, tylko reaguj natychmiast, bo to jest twój obowiązek." – Wanda Traczyk-Stawska Żegnaj, Bohaterko. pic.twitter.com/MhfqlszVcI — Donald Tusk (@donaldtusk) August 19, 2026 Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. World.title: A Multi-Brand K-Beauty Pop-Up Is Coming to Prague This September
World.content:
A Korean beauty pop-up will bring eight K-beauty brands and K-pop entertainment to Prague’s Vltava River this September.

The HARUNARU K-Beauty Pop-up will take place aboard KVASOUL, a self-brewing boat restaurant, from September 4 to 8.



An industry preview for beauty professionals and influencers will be held on September 3.

Visitors will be able to discover, test and buy products from eight Korean brands, including GASH, ranked No. 1 at Olive Young, South Korea’s leading beauty retailer, and ilso, known for its pore-care products.

The event will also feature K-pop performances, a Random Dance Challenge, an idol-style makeup show and a dedicated selection of K-pop albums and merchandise.

The pop-up is aimed at introducing emerging Korean beauty brands to consumers and industry professionals in the Czech Republic and across Central and Eastern Europe.

Entry is free, although visitors are encouraged to register online in advance.

The event is organized by Bramasole Prague s.r.o., which operates several Korean restaurant brands in Prague.

World.title: Dancing House Marks 30 Years With a Free Weekend of Dance in Prague
World.content:
Prague’s Dancing House will celebrate its 30th anniversary with a free two-day program of dance classes, performances and workshops on August 29 and 30.

Jiráskovo náměstí, next to the landmark on the Vltava embankment, will host a temporary stage and dance floor throughout the weekend.



The program will run from 11 a.m. to 7 p.m. on both Saturday and Sunday.

Visitors can join professional instructors for classes in bachata, street dance and Latin American dance. There will also be sessions for children, dance demonstrations and opportunities to meet and talk with instructors.

The event is open to all levels, with participants able to watch performances or take part in the classes.

Weekend program

The schedule is the same on both days until the evening finale.

11:00 a.m. – Opening

11:05 a.m. – Children’s dance class

11:50 a.m. – Talk with the instructor

12:00 p.m. – Bachata demonstration

12:05 p.m. – Bachata class

12:50 p.m. – Talk with bachata instructors

1:00 p.m. – Street dance demonstration

1:05 p.m. – Street dance class

1:50 p.m. – Talk with the street dance instructor

2:00 p.m. – Latin American dance demonstration

2:05 p.m. – Latin American dance class

2:50 p.m. – Talk with instructors

3:00 p.m. – Hat Jazz performance

3:05 p.m. – Children’s dance class

3:50 p.m. – Talk with the instructor

4:00 p.m. – Bachata demonstration

4:05 p.m. – Bachata class

4:50 p.m. – Talk with bachata instructors

5:00 p.m. – Street dance demonstration

5:05 p.m. – Street dance class

5:50 p.m. – Talk with the street dance instructor

6:00 p.m. – Latin American dance demonstration

6:05 p.m. – Latin American dance class

6:50 p.m. – Talk with instructors

7:00 p.m. – Acrobatic performance

7:05 p.m. – Hula Hoops performance

The closing acrobatic performance will differ each day. Saturday will feature a handstand performance, while Sunday will bring Duo ReAct.

Admission is free. Organizers will also provide light refreshments.

Completed in 1996, the Dancing House is one of Prague’s best-known examples of modern architecture. It stands at the corner of Rašínovo nábřeží and Jiráskovo náměstí, overlooking the Vltava.

The building was designed by Croatian-Czech architect Vlado Milunić in collaboration with Canadian-American architect Frank Gehry. Its curved forms and leaning towers give the impression of a dancing couple, which inspired its Czech name, Tančící dům.

The building is also known by the nickname “Ginger and Fred,” referring to American dancers Ginger Rogers and Fred Astaire.

World.title: Bolt Launches App-Free Ride Kiosks in the Czech Republic
World.content:
Bolt has introduced self-service kiosks in the Czech Republic that allow customers to order a ride without a smartphone, mobile data or the Bolt app.

The first kiosk is now operating at Westfield Chodov in Prague. A second will open at Westfield Černý Most on September 1. The company says it plans to consider other high-traffic locations in the future.



The kiosks use TapBox technology and provide access to the same Bolt driver network, pricing and safety standards available through the app.

Customers can place an order directly at the screen, making the service available to people who do not use smartphones or cannot access their phones at the time.

Both shopping centres have also introduced dedicated parking spaces for Bolt drivers collecting passengers. Customers are directed to these designated areas rather than having to meet drivers at potentially unsafe stopping points such as bus stops.

How Bolt kiosks work

Ordering a ride takes several steps. Customers enter their destination, select a ride category and provide their phone number. The available categories are Standard, Comfort, Premium and XL.

Payment is made by card. Once the booking is completed, the kiosk prints a confirmation and sends an SMS containing the vehicle details, estimated arrival time and instructions for finding the driver.

The kiosks operate around the clock and support Czech, English, German, French and Ukrainian.

Each ride booked through a kiosk carries an additional CZK 25 fee.

Bolt says the system could also benefit drivers by connecting them with customers who might otherwise be unable to use the app. The company expects the kiosks to reduce waiting times between rides at busy shopping centres and create additional opportunities for drivers.

The Czech launch follows the introduction of similar kiosks in Slovakia earlier this summer, including at airports.

World.title: Prague Adds 18 Kilometers of Cycle Routes but Cycling Numbers Barely Rise
World.content:
Prague is continuing to expand its cycling infrastructure, but the number of recorded bicycle journeys across the city has remained largely unchanged.

Automatic counters installed on major cycling routes recorded about 5.6 million passages in 2025, roughly 1 percent fewer than the previous year.

After adjusting for counter failures and temporary route closures, however, the Technical Road Administration (TSK) calculated a 0.4 percent increase in cycling traffic.



Prague Adds 18 Kilometers of Routes Away From Traffic

The city added 18 kilometers of two-way cycle paths and other cycling routes separated from motor traffic during the year. The total length of marked cycling routes increased by one kilometer to approximately 550 kilometers.

Routes separated from car traffic now account for 263 kilometers of the network, an increase of seven kilometers compared with the previous year.

TSK operates automatic counters at 31 locations on Prague’s main cycling routes. The devices use induction loops or radar to record cyclists and can determine their direction of travel.

The largest increase in two-way cycling routes came over the past year. Their combined length grew from 63 to 81 kilometers. These routes allow cyclists to travel in both directions on streets that are otherwise one-way for motor vehicles.

New two-way routes were added mainly in Prague 7 around Letná, in Prague 5 in Barrandov, and in Prague 6 around Na Petynce, Rozdělovská and Podbaba.

Modřany Remains Prague’s Busiest Cycling Route

The highest number of cyclists was recorded in Modřany, at the intersection of Vltavanů and U Kino streets. The counter registered 578,016 passages during the year.

Another 540,656 cycling journeys were recorded on Povltavská Street south of Troja Castle.

The largest year-on-year increase was recorded on the Barrandov Bridge, where cycling traffic rose following the completion of its more than two-year reconstruction.

World.title: “Upcycling” Prague: Old Offices and Industrial Sites Find New Life as Apartments
World.content:
Former offices, commercial properties and industrial sites in Prague are being converted into apartments rather than demolished, giving developers another option in a city struggling to build enough new homes.

The approach is sometimes described as “upcycling” — adapting ageing buildings for a new purpose while making use of structures and land that are already developed.

One recent example is in Pankrác, near Vyšehrad, where an office building has been converted into the Mo-cha HOME residential complex.



Developed by Cimex, the project opened this spring with 91 fully equipped apartments, most of them in the Czech 2+kk layout, consisting of a living room with a kitchenette and one separate bedroom.

Existing buildings offer valuable locations

Owners of older properties increasingly have to decide whether to renovate them, change their use or demolish them. Many were built for different needs and standards than those expected from buildings today.

Their locations, however, can be a major advantage. Older properties are often close to public transport, shops and other services, making them attractive for residential conversion.

Transforming an existing building can also be faster to prepare than developing a completely new project on a brownfield, although each property must be assessed individually.

The approach can preserve existing structures, reduce demolition and make better use of land that is already developed.

More former offices are becoming homes

Pankrác is not the only part of Prague where old buildings are being converted into housing.

In Holešovice, the former Tesla complex, once used for light-bulb production, has been transformed into a residential project with 149 apartments. The building had stood unused for years, but its main structure remained in relatively good condition.

In Prague 7, another former administrative building near Urania has also been adapted for residential use.

In Prague 3, PSN is preparing the reconstruction of a former telecommunications exchange on Fibichova Street. Built in 1926 and designed by architect Bohumír Kozák, the building is expected to become a rental housing project with 116 units.

One of the largest transformations is planned in Žižkov, where the functionalist former General Pension Institute will be converted into an apartment building with smaller units. The project received a building permit last year.

Not every older building is suitable for conversion. Technical condition, layout, location, project costs and future use all determine whether redevelopment makes economic and practical sense.

World.title: More Czech Companies Test Four-Day Work Weeks Despite Political Resistance
World.content:
A growing number of companies in the Czech Republic are experimenting with a four-day working week, with some reporting higher productivity and greater employee satisfaction.

But politicians remain reluctant to make the arrangement a standard option across the country.

Under the model, employees work four days instead of five while keeping their full salaries. Companies that have introduced the system say workers can maintain their output while having more time to rest.



At Trinity Group, the arrangement has been in place for five years. Jan Hanulík, the company’s product and marketing director, said productivity had risen despite employees working one day less each week.

“Although we have one working day less, productivity has increased,” Hanulík said, adding that the company’s results have roughly doubled since the system was introduced.

A survey cited in the report found that around 70 percent of employees in the Czech Republic would welcome a four-day working week.

Politicians remain cautious

The idea has already been adopted in different forms elsewhere in Europe. In Belgium, for example, employees can request to work their weekly hours over four days rather than five. The system therefore does not necessarily mean fewer working hours.

Czech politicians, however, argue that a single system would not work across all sectors.

Labor and Social Affairs Minister Aleš Juchelka of ANO said a legally mandated four-day week could create problems in areas already facing staff shortages, including social services and health care.

SPD lawmaker Lucie Šafránková also said the working week should reflect the conditions of individual professions and employers rather than follow one nationwide rule.

Czech companies are already experimenting

Several companies have introduced or tested four-day schedules, including SAB Finance, Phonexia, Sherpas, Digiskills and Café Eternity.

Not every experiment has lasted. The Cognito agency eventually returned to a traditional five-day working week after testing the shorter schedule.

World.title: Foreign Workers Now Make Up 22% of Czech Employees
World.content:
Foreign workers accounted for around 22% of all employees in the Czech Republic at the end of 2025, according to data from the Czech National Bank (ČNB).

Their number has nearly tripled over the past decade, rising from about 323,000 in 2015 to 935,000 last year.

The increase has significantly changed the makeup of the Czech labor market. Foreign workers represented roughly 8% of all employees in 2015. By the end of 2025, their share had reached 22%.

Ukrainians made up the largest group of foreign employees, with approximately 358,000 working in Czechia at the end of last year. Slovaks were the second-largest group, numbering almost 230,000.



The Czech labor market has also seen increasing numbers of workers from other countries outside the European Union, including the Philippines and India.

Foreign workers are particularly important in several sectors, including manufacturing, construction, retail, transport and hospitality.

Their presence is most pronounced in accommodation, food services and hospitality. Foreign nationals accounted for more than half of all employees in the sector at the end of 2025.

The figures should, however, be interpreted with some caution when comparing individual industries. The CNB notes that employment agencies can distort the sectoral breakdown.

Workers employed through agencies are recorded in official statistics under administrative and support services, even when their actual jobs are in manufacturing, construction, logistics or other industries.

World.title: Tesco Teams Up With Wolt. Can Express Delivery Save Its Czech Business?
World.content:
Tesco will launch a new express delivery service in Prague in September, working with Wolt to deliver orders within 40 minutes.

The service, called Tesco Hned, will initially be available from selected Tesco stores in the Czech capital.

The launch comes as speculation continues over a possible sale of Tesco’s Central European operations and the British retailer’s future in the Czech Republic.



Tesco Hned is designed for customers who need groceries and other everyday products quickly rather than as part of a larger planned shop. Orders will include food, drinks, cosmetics, household products, pet supplies and other goods.

The company says its standard online shopping service will continue to focus on larger orders, while the new option is aimed at customers who need a few items immediately.

Tesco has already tested the service at six Prague stores. It plans to extend Tesco Hned to another 22 locations in the coming weeks.

Delivery will be provided through Wolt, giving customers access to Tesco products through the courier company’s platform.

Tesco faces questions over its future

The new service comes at a difficult time for Tesco in Central Europe.

According to the Financial Times, Tesco’s British owners are considering selling their operations in the region, including the Czech Republic. The Schwarz Group, which owns Lidl and Kaufland, and Polish retailer Biedronka have reportedly been mentioned among potential buyers.

Tesco has not announced plans to leave the Czech market, and the launch of Tesco Hned suggests the company continues to invest in its services.

World.title: Billions at stake in NATO’s new pledge: how much of the defence spend stays in Hungary?
World.content:
NATO’s new 5% defence commitment could become one of Europe’s most important fiscal and economic-policy questions over the next decade. For Hungary, the sums involved could run into several billion euros a year, but the economic impact will depend heavily on how much of that additional spending is retained in the domestic economy. Halftermayer & Partners’ latest defence-industrial and macroeconomic study is authored by Dr. Ferenc Antal, a defence industry and critical infrastructure expert. The analysis finds that the same headline level of defence expenditure can produce very different growth outcomes depending on whether it is spent on imported equipment or on production, services and technology that create domestic value added.

Author: Dr Ferenc Antal

At the 2025 Hague Summit, NATO Allies agreed a new Defence Investment Pledge. By 2035, Allies aim to devote at least 3.5% of GDP to core defence requirements and up to a further 1.5% to broader defence- and security-related expenditure (NATO, 2025; NATO, 2026).

This represents a significant step up from the previous 2% benchmark and moves the debate well beyond defence policy alone. Higher military and security spending can affect budget deficits, public debt, industrial output, imports, investment and employment at the same time. The economic-policy question is therefore not only whether European countries can meet the commitment, but also how the money is spent and what economic structure develops around it.

Not every euro of defence spending has the same GDP effect

One of the central findings of the study is that policymakers need to distinguish between the location of procurement and the domestic value added actually created. A company operating in Hungary may still rely heavily on imported inputs, while a foreign-owned plant producing in Hungary can generate substantial local value added through wages, taxes, engineering work and supplier contracts.

From an economic perspective, the relevant question is therefore not simply the nationality of the contractor, but how much of total public expenditure ultimately becomes domestic production and income. If a major military platform is imported as a finished product, its direct domestic GDP contribution is limited because higher public demand is accompanied by higher imports. Domestic manufacturing, maintenance, infrastructure, engineering services, R&D and supplier activity, by contrast, generate activity inside the economy.

European value capture is not the same as Hungarian domestic value added. EU defence-industrial policy increasingly seeks to retain a larger share of defence expenditure within the European Defence Technological and Industrial Base (EDTIB). This can strengthen Europe’s collective industrial capacity, but procurement from another EU Member State may still generate only limited direct value added in Hungary (European Commission, 2024, 2025; Council of the European Union, 2025).

There is no single ‘defence multiplier’

International research does not support the simple proposition that every increase in defence spending raises GDP by the same amount. Studies by the IMF, OECD, Bank of Finland and others produce a wide range of estimates. The outcome depends on what governments buy, the foreign value-added content of procurement, how expenditure is financed and whether sufficient productive capacity is available (Bank of Finland, 2025; Furceri et al., 2026; OECD, 2026).

Investment- and technology-intensive spending can generate stronger economic feedback than consumption-like expenditure. However, if domestic industry cannot absorb rapidly rising demand, part of the additional spending may show up in higher prices, longer delivery times or further imports rather than higher real output. This is particularly relevant for Europe as countries simultaneously seek to increase defence demand and expand manufacturing capacity.

If you missed it: Deterrence needs a balance sheet: The rise of Europe’s defence finance ecosystem

For Hungary, the scale could be EUR 6–7 billion a year

Hungary has already reached defence expenditure of around 2% of GDP. Antal’s study asks what the order of magnitude would be if, purely as an illustrative exercise, the full move to 5% were treated as three additional percentage points of GDP in new expenditure.

On Hungary’s 2025 GDP base, that would correspond to roughly EUR 6.5 billion per year; on the study’s 2026 modelling base, about EUR 6.8 billion. This should not be interpreted as the expected net fiscal cost of the NATO pledge. Up to 1.5% of GDP may include broader resilience, infrastructure, cyber and security spending, some of which could already exist elsewhere in the public budget.

Even so, the order of magnitude illustrates the policy challenge. A permanent multi-billion-euro annual increase can materially affect fiscal and debt dynamics, particularly in an economy with limited fiscal space. According to the Hungarian Central Statistical Office, public debt stood at 74.6% of GDP at the end of 2025 (KSH, 2026).

The scenarios show how wide the economic gap can become

The study therefore uses two illustrative cases within a five-year gradual spending path. The low case assumes 10% domestic value added and represents import-dependent procurement. The higher case assumes 40% and represents substantial industrial deepening and greater domestic value capture. The 40% figure is not an estimate of Hungary’s current defence-industrial structure, but an illustrative deep-localisation case.

Illustrative case Domestic value added First-year GDP effect Cumulative additional output 2026–2030 Import-intensive 10% +0.18 pp EUR 6.8bn Deep localisation 40% +0.57 pp EUR 20.9bn

The associated impact multipliers are 0.30 and 0.95. These pairings are modelling choices informed by the international literature rather than an empirically estimated causal relationship between domestic value added and the multiplier. Under the five-year ramp-up, the first-year GDP effect is approximately 0.18 percentage points in the low case and 0.57 percentage points in the higher-DVA case; cumulative additional output over 2026–2030 is approximately EUR 6.8 billion and EUR 20.9 billion, respectively. These are mechanical scenario outputs, not forecasts.

Higher domestic value added must be built, not assumed

A sustained domestic value-added share around 40% across a broader procurement portfolio would require deeper qualified Tier 1–3 SME supplier networks, greater local engineering and systems-integration capability, stronger defence-related R&D and intellectual-property creation, expanded MRO and lifecycle capacity, higher-value processing and component manufacturing, and integration into export markets. These capabilities should not be assumed to arise automatically from higher procurement volumes or local-content clauses; they would have to be built progressively alongside the spending ramp-up.

This does not mean that every military system or component should be produced in Hungary. The relevant question is where genuinely competitive domestic capability can be developed and sustained. Artificially maintaining uneconomic local production can be as costly as forgoing strategically valuable capabilities altogether. International evidence also suggests that defence industries tend to pay above-average wages and operate with relatively high R&D intensity, creating the possibility of longer-term technology spillovers (AIA, 2026; ISED Canada/CADSI, 2026).

The composition of spending matters as much as its size

Europe’s debate over the next few years is likely to focus less exclusively on what percentage of GDP each country spends on defence. A more consequential distinction will be which countries can translate larger defence budgets into competitive industrial capacity, technology, supplier networks and export capability.

For Hungary, the 5% NATO commitment is therefore also a question of industrial capacity and competitiveness. If higher spending largely turns into an import bill, the fiscal burden remains while domestic economic feedback is limited. If procurement is linked to competitive domestic production, services, technology and know-how, the same security expenditure can create substantially more economic value at home.

The question is therefore not only how much Hungary spends on defence, but how much value ultimately stays in the Hungarian economy.

World.title: “Where did public money disappear?”: Investigation into alleged abuses at Hungary’s central bank to begin this week
World.content:
The parliamentary committee investigating alleged abuses related to the operations of the Hungarian National Bank (MNB) will hold its first meeting at 1 PM on Wednesday, the TISZA parliamentary group told MTI on Sunday evening.

Attila Csőszi, chairman of the investigative committee, said in a video posted on Facebook that hundreds of billions of forints in public money had been transferred to foundations established by the Hungarian National Bank. He said the investigation would, among other things, seek to establish what happened to those funds.

According to the politician, the committee will examine “who was responsible and where the public money disappeared”, who benefited the most from it and what it was spent on. The committee began its work at the initiative of the TISZA parliamentary group.

As an example, Csőszi cited the case of Kecskemét, where the Neumann János University and Tudásváros received HUF 144 billion. However, he claimed that a significant portion of the money – HUF 127.5 billion – was “gambled away on the stock market”.







He also referred to a property in Balatonakarattya, saying that HUF 20 billion had been spent on its renovation before it was subsequently put up for sale for HUF 9 billion. Regarding the MNB’s headquarters, Csőszi raised the issue of its construction costs, saying the original budget of HUF 55 billion eventually rose to HUF 105 billion.

The chairman of the investigative committee said its aim was to establish who was responsible for what happened. He added that the ultimate goal was to ensure that similar cases could not occur in the future.

World.title: Sunshine, storms and then scorching heat: Hungary braces for a sweltering end to August
World.content:
The final week of August will begin with moderately warm, pleasant summer weather, with daytime temperatures around 30°C and refreshing mornings. However, the heatwave will return in the second half of the week. Showers and thunderstorms may occur in several parts of Hungary on Tuesday, but most of the week is expected to be sunny and dry, according to a forecast from HungaroMet Zrt. sent to MTI on Sunday.

The beginning of the week

On Monday, cloudier areas will gradually clear and become more broken, followed by plenty of sunshine alongside high and developing cumulus clouds. The northern parts of the country may remain cloudier at times, with a chance of light rain or showers. Northerly winds may occasionally produce stronger gusts. Daytime temperatures will generally range from 26 to 32°C.

On Tuesday, cloud cover will increase significantly from the south-west and west. Showers and thunderstorms may occur in several parts of Transdanubia, with rain potentially spreading further east from the evening onwards. Southerly and south-easterly winds will occasionally strengthen in Transdanubia, while easterly and north-easterly winds will pick up elsewhere. Temperatures will rise from 9–19°C in the early morning to 26–33°C in the afternoon.

Wednesday and Thursday

By Wednesday morning, patches of fog and low cloud may form in western and south-western Hungary. Once these clear, sunny weather is expected across the country, with only a few cumulus and high clouds. A few showers may still occur in the morning, but no further rainfall is expected later in the day. Winds will generally remain moderate. Morning temperatures will range from 11 to 21°C, while afternoon highs will reach 27–32°C.

Thursday will be mostly clear and sunny, with only a few high and cumulus clouds and no rainfall expected. Winds will turn south-easterly and southerly and strengthen. Overnight lows will range from 9 to 19°C, while afternoon temperatures will reach 29–34°C.

Your story. Your perspective. Our readers. Write for Daily News Hungary!

The weekend

Friday is expected to be sunny with only a few clouds. No rain is expected during the day, although showers and thunderstorms may develop overnight in northern and north-western areas. South-westerly and southerly winds will strengthen across much of the country. Temperatures will range from 14–22°C in the morning to a scorching 32–38°C in the afternoon.

On Saturday, cloud cover will temporarily increase significantly, with scattered showers and thunderstorms likely. Winds will turn north-westerly and may become strong across large parts of the country. Early morning temperatures will range from 18 to 24°C, while afternoon highs will generally reach 28–34°C.

Sunday is expected to be mostly sunny, with no significant rainfall. North-westerly winds may bring occasional stronger gusts. Temperatures will range from 11–19°C in the morning to 25–30°C in the afternoon, according to HungaroMet (met.hu).

World.title: Former House Speaker Kövér accused of refusing handshake from Tisza deputy speaker at memorial ceremony
World.content:
A dispute has erupted over an alleged handshake snub involving former parliamentary speaker László Kövér and Krisztián Kőszegi, a Tisza Party MP and deputy speaker, at a memorial ceremony in Báta on Sunday.

Kőszegi said Kövér refused to shake his hand during the event commemorating the 500th anniversary of the national assembly held in Báta before the Battle of Mohács. He shared a photograph appearing to show himself extending his hand while Kövér keeps his hands in his lap.

The photograph does not establish whether Kövér ultimately refused the handshake or whether the two politicians shook hands at another point during the ceremony.

‘We would expect more dignity from a former speaker’

Kőszegi criticised the alleged gesture, saying: “We would expect more dignity from a former speaker.” He argued that the history of the Battle of Mohács should serve as a reminder of the consequences of division replacing cooperation in a country.

The Tisza politician said Kövér’s “deliberate turning away” only deepened the social divisions he believes Fidesz had deliberately created over the past 16 years. Kövér served as Speaker of the Hungarian Parliament from 2010 until 2026, when Fidesz lost power following the parliamentary election.

Current Speaker: ‘It is simply inhumane’

Ágnes Forsthoffer, the current Speaker of Parliament, also reacted to the incident in a Facebook post, describing the photograph as “shocking”. “There is no way to sugar-coat it, this is simply inhumane to me. Humiliating,” Forsthoffer wrote.

She said a handshake should not be treated as an ideological issue, but as a basic human gesture. “A handshake is not about party affiliation, but about seeing the person in the other person first,” she wrote.

Forsthoffer also claimed that Kövér left the parliamentary office without meeting her. According to her account, he did not consider it important to say a few words of appreciation to the office staff he had worked with for 16 years.

She said Kövér came to Parliament to say goodbye to the staff while she was still undergoing her preparation for the role of Speaker, and that she had been advised to leave the building during his visit. Forsthoffer thanked Kőszegi for representing Parliament at the memorial ceremony and added: “Thank you for extending your hand on my behalf as well.”

Your story. Your perspective. Our readers. Write for Daily News Hungary!

Fidesz does not deny the alleged snub

Fidesz communications director Bertalan Havasi was asked by Telex whether Kövér had indeed refused Kőszegi’s handshake and, if so, why. Havasi did not confirm the incident, but neither did he deny it. “I don’t know, I wasn’t there, and for that reason I wouldn’t disturb our party’s national council chairman on Sunday evening,” he said.

However, he went on to argue that, if the incident had happened, Kőszegi was a representative of the Tisza Party, which Fidesz accuses of undermining the democratic rule of law.

Havasi referred to Fidesz’s July “Declaration of Resistance”, in which the party declared its total opposition to what it described as Tisza’s “anti-democratic system”. He said Fidesz members and all Hungarians had the right to freely express their opposition to the Tisza Party and its representatives.

The exchange highlights the increasingly bitter political divide between Fidesz and Tisza, which has been in government since winning the April 2026 parliamentary election.

World.title: Hungary’s Kossuth Radio to relaunch on Monday with new ‘everyone’s radio’ slogan
World.content:
Hungary’s Kossuth Radio is set to relaunch on Monday with a completely revamped programme structure, new presenters and a new slogan promising that the public broadcaster will once again be “everyone’s”.

The renewed station will officially return on 24 August, with the Rákóczi March marking the start of its new public-service programming at 4.30 AM. The station’s new slogan will be “Kossuth Radio – everyone’s again”, according to a statement from Hungary’s public media operator, MTVA.

The broadcaster said the station had spent the past month and a half broadcasting radio plays and “timeless, emblematic” interviews around the clock while its new programming was being prepared. Channel director György Kerényi said the station would preserve what was worth keeping while saying goodbye to programmes and formats that had become tired.

News and current affairs to be revamped

News programmes and several key time slots will undergo major changes. The station says its new approach will focus on reliable reporting, credible stories and knowledgeable guests, promising that its “news will be true, our stories will be authentic and our guests will be knowledgeable.”

Several new programmes will also be available as podcasts, while the station says some of its content will even be broadcast through traditional Sokol radios. Zsolt Bogár and Péter Magyari will serve as the station’s two deputy editors-in-chief.

Magyari, who previously worked for Válasz Online, will launch Nyílt titok (Open Secret) on Saturday mornings. The programme will examine controversial cases from Hungary’s past 16 years – and, according to the station, the past 36 years – with investigative reporters Róbert Báthory and Áron Kovács.

Magyari will also host Világrend (World Order), a foreign affairs analysis programme due to launch on 29 August.

The morning news and information programme Felkelő, the Krónikák news bulletins and daily current affairs programmes will be presented by Rita Benyó, Erika Hatvani Tóth, Tímea Tatár and Nóra Teszári.

György Farkas, László Illisz, István Dániel Király and Gábor Kiss will work as editors, while Dávid Dercsényi, Mátyás Fórizs, Anna Kovács, Roland Papp and Ildikó Sipos will work on the news programmes. Pálma Fazekas will head the news department.

If you missed it: Hungary’s revamped public broadcaster launches new flagship news bulletin with a surprising shift

New programmes focus on different perspectives

The revamped station will also introduce programmes covering current affairs from different perspectives. Necces, an afternoon live programme hosted by Csilla Orosz and Zsófia Sashegyi, will examine public affairs through a female perspective.

Sunday mornings will feature two new programmes focusing on Hungarians living beyond the country’s borders and religious affairs.

Anyanyelve még mindig magyar (Hungarian Is Still Their Mother Tongue) will air from 7 AM and will be hosted by Vince Rácz, a journalist at Pátria Radio, the Slovak public broadcaster’s Hungarian-language service in Bratislava.

Hetedik nap (Seventh Day) will focus on religious and church-related issues and will be hosted by journalist Dóra Laborczi. The station also plans to significantly expand its cultural programming and radio plays.

Anita Bödő will head the revamped cultural department, while new daily programmes will include Doktor Kossuth, focusing on health, and A Föld marad (The Earth Remains), dedicated to sustainability and environmental issues.

Your story. Your perspective. Our readers. Write for Daily News Hungary!

Kossuth Radio seeks a new identity

The relaunch comes after years in which Kossuth Radio and Hungary’s wider public media system were heavily criticised by opposition figures and independent media for serving as a vehicle for the former Fidesz government’s political messaging.

Former Prime Minister Viktor Orbán was a regular guest on the station’s Friday morning Jó reggelt, Magyarország! programme, where his appearances were frequently described as interviews despite rarely involving challenging follow-up questions.

The public media system itself underwent a turbulent transition earlier this summer. On 7 July, Hungary’s public media broadcasts were temporarily interrupted as an interim management team took over, with the M1 television channel displaying an apology message for an extended period.

World.title: Rare ‘water devil’ filmed on the Danube in Hungary – video
World.content:
A remarkable weather phenomenon was captured on video near Ráckeve after a swirling dust devil moved from the riverbank over the Danube and briefly transformed into a spectacular ‘water devil’.

The unusual scene was filmed by Péter Tóth, a member of the Pilis Park Forest team, who had originally gone to the Danube to document the river’s exceptionally low water level. Instead, he ended up recording a rare and striking atmospheric phenomenon.

Dust devil turns into water vortex

Tóth was working in the Ráckeve area when he noticed a small swirling column of air and dust on the riverbank. At first, he was unsure whether the phenomenon was worth filming. But when he realised that the rotating vortex was moving directly towards the Danube, he reached for his phone.

As the vortex reached the water, it began lifting droplets from the river, creating a spectacular swirling column above the surface. Tóth later described the sound of the falling water droplets as resembling a fountain operating in the middle of the river.

Although the phenomenon itself was relatively small and disappeared within a short time, it left behind a clearly visible disturbance on the Danube. According to Tóth, the vortex created waves similar to those produced by a small boat passing through the water.

What is a water devil?

The term “water devil” is commonly used to describe a short-lived rotating column of air over a body of water. However, such phenomena should not automatically be confused with a tornado or a classic waterspout.

Small vortices can form close to the surface when local heating, rising air and particular wind conditions combine. A dust devil developing over land can also move over water, as appears to have happened near Ráckeve.

Humidity, air movement, surface temperatures and local wind conditions can all influence the development of these vortices. Their appearance can be spectacular despite their typically short lifespan.

Can a water devil be dangerous?

According to Kemma, a small, short-lived water vortex is generally much weaker than a conventional tornado, but it can still pose a risk to people nearby. For small boats and kayaks in particular, sudden rotating winds, waves and disturbed water can create dangerous conditions.

The precise meteorological classification of the phenomenon filmed near Ráckeve cannot be established from the footage alone. What is clear, however, is that the vortex was strong enough to lift water from the Danube and create noticeable waves that remained visible even after the swirling column disappeared.

The extraordinary footage also provided an unexpected glimpse of nature at work during a period when the Danube has been making headlines for a very different reason: its exceptionally low water level.

World.title: Motorcyclist saves choking boy on Hungarian road after dozens of cars drive past
World.content:
A young motorcyclist has been praised for saving a choking child on Hungary’s Route 4 after reportedly being the only person to stop and help as around 30 cars passed the distressed family.

The incident happened on Friday on the stretch of Route 4 between Nyíregyháza and Kisvárda, according to the National Ambulance Service. The boy had been travelling in the back seat of his family’s car when he suddenly choked on food and began struggling to breathe.

His mother pulled over and got out of the vehicle with her son, but said she completely froze in the stressful situation. Then a motorcyclist stopped.

Motorcyclist immediately stepped in

The motorcyclist took the choking child and began providing first aid. He continued until the obstruction was cleared and the boy was able to breathe again. The whole incident happened so quickly that the family did not even manage to ask the motorcyclist his name before he left.

The National Ambulance Service subsequently shared the family’s account and praised the unknown passer-by for stepping in when help was urgently needed. The service said it was proud of members of the public who have the courage to act and provide assistance in an emergency.

The motorcyclist was later identified as Attila Horváth, who came forward in a Facebook video and confirmed that he was the person who had helped the boy.

“I’m not a hero”

Horváth said he had asked the boy’s mother to remove the appeal looking for him because he did not want the incident to become a sensation. According to the motorcyclist, helping someone in danger should be an everyday and natural thing to do.

He said he regularly travels between 20,000 and 40,000 kilometres a year and often encounters broken-down cars or people lying on the roadside while other motorists simply continue driving.

“This time, around 30 cars went past us, and nobody stopped to help,” he said.

Horváth also pointed out that basic first aid, including the Heimlich manoeuvre, is taught as part of obtaining a driving licence. He urged people not to automatically assume that someone lying by the roadside is drunk. The person could have suffered a head injury, a stroke or a heart attack, and the intervention of a passer-by could save their life.

“This doesn’t make anyone a hero. I’m not a hero either,”

Horváth said, arguing that paramedics, firefighters and police officers who risk their own lives to save others are the real heroes. Simply being in the right place at the right time and offering assistance, he said, should not be treated as extraordinary.

“If one person listens, we’ve succeeded”

Horváth asked people not to simply like his video, but to share it so that its message about helping others reaches as many people as possible. “If just one person takes this to heart and we save another life, then we’ve ended the day successfully,” he said.

The National Ambulance Service also said it wanted to find the motorcyclist after hearing the family’s story. What began as a search for an unknown passer-by has now ended with the family learning the identity of the person who intervened when their young son was unable to breathe. The incident is also a reminder that in an emergency, stopping to help can make the difference between life and death.
