World.title: German Tourists Cause Fire Inside Poreč Apartment Ending With €400,000 in Damage
World.content:
August the 23rd, 2026 – German tourists have caused enormous damage after causing a fire inside a Poreč apartment. As if that wasn’t enough, he allegedly stuck his middle finger up at the owner after the act.

German tourists caused a fire in a Poreč apartment inside a family home two weeks ago, according to a police investigation. The fire destroyed almost the entire apartment, and owner Markica Kikić estimates the damage at around €400,000. Kikić has now revealed new details of the entire incident. Index reports that he claimed that some of the guests obstructed the firefighting efforts during the blaze and is also deeply dissatisfied with the police response. “The guests simply got in the way, obstructed and interfered with putting out the fire. In the meantime the police arrived and somehow managed to move them aside,” Kikić said.

“he was getting in my face and even stuck his middle finger up at me”

He claims that one of the guests still did not calm down even after the police arrived. “One of those people was sticking his middle finger under my nose and getting right in my face. The police were removing me from him instead of throwing him out. He wasn’t registered and had no right to be on my private property. The police removed me and gave them priority,” he alleged.

Kikić also claimed there were major shortcomings in the police’s handling of the whole situation. “Believe me, there were major failings on the part of the police. They gave them documents so they could fill in their own names, surnames and the rest themselves. They didn’t take them in. The police didn’t even take a statement from them. They signed and left,” he claimed. He considers the situation was serious enough to require a stricter police response.

“This is a criminal offence of endangering life and property. In such a case, as far as I as a layman know the law, the person has to be taken in and detained,” Kikić said.

he was coming back from the beach when he noticed the flames

As a reminder of previous reports on this bizarre incident, Kikić recounted that on returning from the beach he found the apartment in flames and was particularly shocked by the behaviour of the guests whom the police link to the outbreak of the fire. “They continued with their meal, toasting, raising glasses and bottles. They even got in our way while we were frantically buying hoses so we could try to put out the fire,” he said. He stated that this year’s tourist season is over for him and that he does not know whether he will manage to renovate the apartment even by next year. “For at least the next two years, I’m financially ruined,” he said.

The owner also described the sheer scale of the damage done by the fire inside the apartment. “The entire kitchen was handmade, from the highest-quality materials. All the furniture was high-quality, luxurious, paid for a lot of money. All of this is destroyed. This is a real catastrophe,” he said, adding that the apartment had been completely furnished and renovated. “An absolutely astronomical amount of money was invested in this. Everything was made of expensive materials, there were designer paintings inside with signatures,” he said.

the police say the fire started in the kitchen

The police investigation established that the fire broke out in the kitchen while a 44-year-old German citizen was preparing food.

“Due to the transfer of heat from the stove to the pan and then to the wooden structure, the fire spread to the rest of the apartment,” the police stated. Police suspect the 44-year-old woman of the criminal offence of endangering life and property by a generally dangerous act. The competent state attorney’s office will decide on further steps. The German family has in the meantime left Poreč, while the owner has been left to deal with the consequences of the fire.

Lawyer Zvonimir Matić earlier explained that the owner must first make a proper assessment of the damage, after which he can demand compensation from the German citizen in question. “The most important thing for them now is to make a quality assessment of the damage. After that they will submit a claim to the German citizen to compensate for the damage. If she does not do so, the owner will be able to file a lawsuit with the competent court in Poreč. It is important that the law is on their side,” Matić said.

“booking.com demanded that i pay for their alternative accommodation!”

Kikić had also hoped for help from the platform through which the apartment was booked, but claims Booking.com’s response further surprised him. “An hour later I received an email from the platform informing me that they had moved the guests to other accommodation, even to the most luxurious hotel, and that I had to pay for their accommodation,” he alleged. Booking.com earlier stated that they were checking the circumstances of the case and that the guest had been placed on the blocked users list while the check is ongoing.

Kikić claims that problems with the guests began the day after their arrival, when they started bringing additional people into the apartment. “When I tried to warn him, he simply arrogantly got in my face and said that he had booked the apartment and that they could do whatever they wanted in it,” he recounted. The owner estimates the damage to stand at around €400,000 in total.

World.title: Župa Dubrovačka – An Oasis Between Dubrovnik and Konavle
World.content:
August the 23rd, 2026 – Župa dubrovačka, or the Parish of Dubrovnik, is an area located between Dubrovnik and Konavle, known for its beaches, peace and distinctly less hustle and bustle.

In the extreme south of Dalmatia lies an area that is often overshadowed by its famous, world-renowned neighbour. Yet no matter how powerful the shadow of Dubrovnik may be, this region stubbornly continues to tell its own (much more relaxed) story. Putni kofer writes that that story is made up of a series of “chapters” written by the local, very old villages.

ONE OF THE MOST BEAUTIFUL PARTS OF THE DUBROVNIK RIVIERA

First, let’s get better acquainted with a few basic facts. Župa dubrovačka is located between Dubrovnik and Konavle, with the border towards the latter marked by Duboka Ljuta – a place where, according to legend, fairies used to sing noisily at night to scare away newcomers and keep all the beauty just for themselves. It spans an area of around 2,300 hectares and has about six thousand inhabitants. It’s separated from the very centre of Dubrovnik by just six kilometres and sits in a firm embrace of rolling hills on one side and the sea on the other. Župa dubrovačka is called one of the most beautiful parts of the Dubrovnik Riviera.

Its history is long and dates back to around 6000–4000 BC. One of the pieces of evidence from that time – a stone tongue-shaped chisel – is still kept in the Dubrovnik Museum. Illyrians once lived here, Greeks passed through the area, and later the Romans eventually ruled it. In the 7th century, however, Župa dubrovačka came under Dubrovnik’s control. Its natural beauty had long caught the eye of the Dubrovnik nobility, who built their summer residences there.

KUPARI – THE OLDEST TOURIST RESORT

Over time, Župa dubrovačka also grew in tourism terms, attracting visitors slowly but surely. Tourism began to develop there after the First World War and experienced a boom in the 1960s and 1970s, when a series of hotels were built in the area.

In this “tourism” sense, Kupari must be mentioned. This place is cited as the oldest tourist resort in Župa dubrovačka, and the first hotel was built there in 1920. The place got its name from the Kuparica tile factory, which operated as early as the 13th century. It is also known for one of the most famous beaches near Dubrovnik, as well as for a hotel complex that stood abandoned for a long time and has now been demolished. A new hotel is supposed to rise in its place. The only thing in the complex that was not demolished is the first hotel in the history of Župa – Hotel Grand – which is protected. It is due to be restored.

SREBRENO aND MLINI

East of Kupari lies Srebreno. This ancient fishing village, which was popular among Dubrovnik nobles who built villas there, is mentioned as early as the 13th century and is today the administrative centre of the municipality. It is also considered one of the best-known bathing spots in the area, along with Soline. That settlement got its name from the salt pans. One of the most recognisable places in Župa dubrovačka, however, is pretty little Mlini. The name was not given without reason. There used to be a series of mills in the village (mlin in Croatian), of which only one has been preserved to this day. Mlini is now widely regarded as one of the best-known tourist destinations in this compact area. It’s often referred to as one of the most beautiful settlements in Župa dubrovačka.

PLAT IS KNOWN FOR ITS BEAUTIFUL COVES

Bracodbk

Plat, another place in Župa dubrovačka, lies further south, towards Konavle. It is known for its beautiful coves and beaches, and its name Plat (formerly called Belenum) is first mentioned in 1400. It is home to several interesting little churches, for example the Church of St John, which stands on the hill above the village and where so-called mammoth spruces once grew. The thickest of them had a trunk circumference of more than two metres.

The Church of Our Lady of the Assumption was guarded by huge cypresses about 21 metres tall. The giant cypresses and spruces are gone, but near the latter church there are stećci (medieval tombstones), including one that is said to be the most beautiful in the Dubrovnik area. Finally, it is certainly worth stepping a little away from the coast itself and exploring the hinterland of Župa in general, the old villages, vineyards and olive groves, and the ancient stone houses.

World.title: Split Port: Passengers Wait in 40 Degree Heat With No Shelter From Sun
World.content:
August the 23rd, 2026 – Split Port is rapidly turning into a proverbial pizza oven as passengers have to wait in 40 degree heat with no shelter from the sun whatsoever.

At Split Port, passengers must wait to board in temperatures above 35 degrees in the shade, while on the scorching asphalt and with high humidity the perceived heat regularly exceeds 40 degrees. Lukrecija Zderic reports for Index that all of this takes place without a canopy under which people could take any form of shelter. With all the belongings they’re carrying on their journey, they must stand on the burning asphalt, exposed to the insufferable strength of the summer sun, with almost no shade available.

Parents with children, the elderly, and those waiting for the ferry try to find at least a scrap of shade under the smaller palm trees. Ferries come and go, the queues move, and passengers wait in the sun with no place to hide from the heat.

The problem becomes even greater when the catamaran or ferry is delayed and passengers don’t know exactly when it will arrive. This is precisely what happened to one of our readers, who wished to remain anonymous. With her family she had to wait in the port, in the sun and without adequate shelter, and she told Index how disappointing the whole situation was.

“It was a working day and we were supposed to travel by catamaran to Korčula. Unfortunately it was late, but that wasn’t the only problem. The biggest problem is that in Split’s port you almost have nowhere to shelter from the sun. The berths for the catamarans are far from the main, and practically the only, canopy in the port,” our interlocutor said.

“There’s often no space in the cafe or bar, and if you don’t know exactly when the catamaran will arrive or which berth it will dock at, which happens frequently, you can’t even move away to look for a shady spot. It was a heatwave, it was extremely hot, and with children it was a truly terrible experience,” the reader told us.

“if i hadn’t found shade, i’d have become unwell in the sun”

So we went to Split’s port to check whether the catamarans were late and how passengers spend their time waiting for them in the sun. Because the fact is that at the berths there is nowhere to shelter from the heat. During our arrival and the following three hours in the port, a large number of catamarans arrived and departed, and almost all of them arrived on time. The biggest delay we recorded was around ten minutes, which can hardly be called a serious delay, and it did not bother the passengers either. But what many would apparently gladly change is a simple thing – that instead of waiting on the scorching sun, they could wait for the ferry in the shade.

“It’s extremely hot, but it doesn’t bother me that much because I’m by the sea. It’s a bit inconvenient standing in the sun waiting for the ferry to Dubrovnik, so I try to find any little scrap of shade. This is more of a shadow, but it will do,” a tourist travelling to Dubrovnik told us.

“I saw that today it’s 35 degrees, and it’s the same in London, but I have to admit it’s much nicer here. Maybe because we’re on holiday, but if I hadn’t found a little shade, I would have gone crazy in the sun,” a tourist from England told us. Catamarans in Split’s City Port don’t all dock in one place; they use different berths along the operational quay. Some of them are located outside the main building of the maritime-passenger terminal. At the same time, works are underway in Split’s port on Sv. Duje Pier, where a new international maritime-passenger terminal is being built.

infrastructure upgrades – but nothing to deal with the issue of ensuring shade

Once completed, the project should take over part of the international traffic and free up Sv Duje Pier for domestic scheduled traffic, i.e. better connections between Split and the islands. But while the port infrastructure is being changed and expanded, the question remains whether the problem of protecting passengers who wait for catamarans in the open will also be solved, especially during the summer months and heatwaves.

While waiting for their catamaran, passengers try in various, and some quite inventive, ways to protect themselves from the sun. Umbrellas, caps and hats become the main defence against the scorching rays, while some hide in long sleeves and others seek refuge in the rare scraps of shade. The benches under the palm trees thus become sought-after spots, and passengers settle into every available bit of shade, however small.

“It’s very hot, we’re not used to this. We’ve put on long sleeves and are protecting ourselves with an umbrella. We hope our catamaran to Dubrovnik will arrive soon because it’s really hard to breathe here,” Japanese passengers told us. There were, however, also those who did not allow the heat to spoil their holiday mood.

“We’re from Germany and we’re only briefly in Split, and now we’re going to Hvar. We don’t have any special way of protecting ourselves from the sun; we simply try to find a little shade, although that’s not exactly easy here. We don’t want to complain – we’ve come on holiday, we’re by the sea and we’re going to one of the most beautiful islands. We won’t let a few minutes in the sun spoil our mood,” a married couple from Germany told us.

During the summer, Split Port is one of the busiest places in the city every day, yet there’s no respite from the intense heat. Back in 2024 alone, more than five million passengers passed through it on ferries and catamarans, of which more than a million on catamarans. This is a huge number of people who pass through the port every day during the season, and some of them wait for their catamarans precisely in the open, exposed to the sun and temperatures that during heatwaves exceed 35 degrees.

World.title: Gallery: President Alar Karis to mark Ukraine's Independence Day in Kyiv
World.content:
President Alar Karis and Sirje Karis arrived in Kyiv on Monday morning to take part in events marking the 35th anniversary of Ukraine's Independence Day.

The pair traveled to the Ukrainian capital by train and were met by Estonia's new Ambassador to Ukraine Tiina Intelmann and Deputy Foreign Minister of Ukraine Mariana Betsa, who was previously the Ukrainian ambassador in Tallinn.

"Independence means that no one else decides your future. The Ukrainian people prove this every day by standing bravely and united against Russian aggression. We are in Ukraine on Ukraine's Independence Day to pay tribute to the Ukrainians' will for freedom. The Ukrainian people must be able to shape their future freely and without fear," President Karis said in a statement.

Dear Ukrainians, on your Independence Day, Estonia stands with you. Your courage and unity prove that no one else gets to write your future. You deserve a just and lasting peace—and the freedom to choose your own path. Stay strong! Слава Україні! pic.twitter.com/PFN7v5BRxl — Alar Karis (@AlarKaris) August 24, 2026

Sirje Karis will take part in the sixth Summit of First Ladies and Gentlemen, led by Ukrainian First Lady Olena Zelenska, which focuses on maintaining stability in uncertain times.

Photos released by Karis' office show he also met with President of Finland Alexander Stubb and President of the European Council António Costa.

Prime Minister Kristen Michal (Reform) is also in Kyiv for the meeting of Nordic and Baltic ministers and to participate in Independence Day events. Both officials will meet with President Volodymyr Zelenskyy.

"For 35 years, Ukrainians have built their country and shaped their future. Today, you are defending your independence with extraordinary courage. Your strength inspires Europe and makes us all safer. Estonia will stand with Ukraine for as long as it takes to achieve a just and lasting peace," Michal wrote on social media site X.

Happy Independence Day, Ukraine!



For 35 years, Ukrainians have built their country and shaped their future. Today, you are defending your independence with extraordinary courage. Your strength inspires Europe and makes us all safer.



Estonia will stand with Ukraine for as… pic.twitter.com/e2hfTvXz0F — Kristen Michal (@KristenMichalPM) August 24, 2026

Ukrainian flag raised at MFA

On Monday morning, the blue and yellow Ukrainian flag was raised at the Ministry of Foreign Affairs in the middle of Tallinn.

Minister of Foreign Affairs Margus Tsahkna (Eesti 200) also stressed the importance of Ukraine being able to determine its own future at the ceremony.

"Ukraine has come a long way over the past 35 years, and its direction is now irreversible – towards the EU and NATO," he said. "Independence is not a date on the calendar; it is the choice every Ukrainian makes every day to defend their decisions, their borders and their future."

35 years ago today, Ukraine proclaimed its independence. As has become tradition, a ceremonial flag‑raising was held in front of the Estonian MFA.



Independence is not a date on the calendar, it is a daily choice Ukrainians make: to defend their sovereignty, their borders, and… pic.twitter.com/5BTajjt7Ex — Margus Tsahkna (@Tsahkna) August 24, 2026

He said Ukraine's fight against Russia stands as an example for the rest of Europe and that the "international community must continue to isolate Russia in every sphere."

"Every concession or attempt to find common ground only strengthens Moscow's war machine," the minister added.

Following the flag-raising ceremony, Tsahkna spoke by telephone with Ukrainian Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha and discussed military and economic support for Ukraine, developments on Ukraine's path towards EU membership, and preparations for the Ukraine Recovery Conference to be held in Tallinn in January.

This article was updated to add comments from Margus Tsahkna and Kristen Michal.

World.title: Saaremaa unveils renovated 200‑year‑old Laimjala manor
World.content:
Saaremaa Municipality has preserved a key piece of local heritage by completing a €3.4 million renovation of the over 200-year-old Laimjala manor house, which now brings a local district center, library, school, and kindergarten together under one roof.

Hidden 230-year-old wall paintings uncovered during construction surprised experts and forced major changes to the original design.

"This is a painting from the time the manor was built, meaning from the first layer, and it is such a valuable thing because it is more than 230 years old," said Liis Koppel, Saaremaa adviser at the National Heritage Board.

Because of the artwork, planners altered the room layout in the central section, moving the proposed shower facilities to an outbuilding.

"Because of the painting, we can use the lift to go from the basement to the first floor. But from there to the second floor, we had to give up the lift," said Saaremaa Municipality construction engineer Mehis Kallas.

Of the former 160 manor complexes in Saaremaa, only about 10 percent survive, and just one-third of those remain in good condition. Heritage experts consider every successful restoration a major conservation milestone.

The facility houses the district center and library alongside a new manor kindergarten and school. Four children will study there starting next year, though the school can accommodate up to 30 pupils.

Despite the opening, Saaremaa Municipality announced plans to close the Laimjala branch of Orissaare High School in the coming years due to demographic shifts.

"These are demographic numbers that unfortunately show us a sad fate. And the question on the table is where we will end up. Anything can be written on paper, but whether it is final, we do not yet know, and time will tell. We are talking about steps that are three, five, and 10 years ahead," said Saaremaa Deputy Mayor Moonika Parksepp.

World.title: Ratings: SDE up, Center down as presidential race influences voters
World.content:
Support for the opposition Social Democrats (SDE) rose four percentage points to 18 percent in August, according to a recent survey.

The research, conducted by pollsters Emor on a monthly basis, found the current presidential election process may have influenced the August ratings, which saw SDE close the gap on another opposition party, Center.

Isamaa firmly topped the party ratings table with 26 percent, the opposition party's best result since January even as it has been the most-supported party for many months now.

Center polled at 19 percent in August according to Emor. The party's rating has been falling over the past two months, and it is only just ahead of SDE. In June, support for Center was 22 percent, just two percentage points behind Isamaa.

SDE's rating rose from 14 percent in July to 18 percent in August, and its popularity improved primarily among younger demographics (up to age 35), Emor reported.

Center lost support specifically among Estonian-speaking respondents, from 13 percent in this demographic in June to 8 percent in August (in July the figure was 12 percent).

Emor research expert Aivar Voog found the decline in support for Center and rise for SDE to possibly result from the ongoing presidential election process; SDE were the first party to clearly throw their support behind Ülle Madise, not only the only candidate registered to run at the time of writing with 74 MPs signing off on her, but also the most popular candidate with the public.

Center is the only party to have come out in support of Tallinn University of Technology (TalTech) Rector Tiit Land, the only recent challenger to Madise and significantly less popular with the public.

"In addition, the Center Party has been overshadowed by [Isamaa] in its communications in Tallinn. At the same time, in the case of the Social Democrats, it can be highlighted that their high support has been unstable. It lasts for two or three months and then falls back again. Unlike Isamaa, whose support is stable," Voog noted.

The coalition Reform Party and the opposition EKRE were fourth and fifth in the August survey, almost even-stevens with 13 and 12 percent support respectively. In July, both parties rated at 14 percent.

Support for the non-parliamentary Parempoolsed stood at 7 percent for the second consecutive month, lower than the 9 percent recorded in May and June but still higher than the 5 percent required to win seats at a direct election.

The other coalition party, Eesti 200, rated at 3 percent in August (up from 2 percent in July), still below the electoral threshold. The party recently saw a high-profile member, Kalev Stoicescu, leave. The pro-Kremlin Koos/Vmeste party polled at 2 percent; the Greens (Eesti Rohelised), 1 percent. Support for ERK, which broke away from EKRE a couple of years ago, and the EÜVP, fell below 1 percent in August.

Additionally, 27 percent were unable to name a preference, a higher figure than in July (25 percent) and June (23 percent). The above ratings do not incorporate undecided responses.

When respondents without a preference are factored in, Isamaa saw 18.4 percent support in August, Center 13.4 percent, SDE 13.1 percent, the Reform Party 9.1 percent, EKRE 8.3 percent, Parempoolsed 5.4 percent, Eesti 200 1.9 percent and the Greens 1.1 percent.

Among native Estonian-speaking respondents, Isamaa ranked first in August with 30 percent support, followed by the SDE with 21 percent, Reform with 14 percent and EKRE with 13 percent. Parempoolsed and Center each saw 8 percent support with this demographic. Eesti 200 polled at 3 percent and the Greens at 2 percent.

Among respondents of other ethnic backgrounds, primarily meaning Russian-speaking voters, the Center Party retained a clear lead in August, with 67 percent support (63 percent in July).

The Koos party polled at 9 percent with this population sector, higher than several mainstream parties: SDE at 6 percent, Isamaa and the Reform Party at 5 percent each, and EKRE at 4 percent.

Among voters in Tallinn, the Center Party remained most popular with 31 percent support. The capital is one of its traditional strongholds. SDE, whose support among Tallinn residents rose in August, saw that trend continue and is now in second place with 24 percent (17 percent in July). Reform was third in Tallinn with 12 percent.

Isamaa's support among Tallinn voters saw a sharp decline over the month, with 10 percent supporting the party in August (compared with 17 percent in July).

Center and Isamaa are in office together in Tallinn.

EKRE polled at 8 percent support in the capital, just ahead of Parempoolsed at 7 percent.

Center also remained the most popular choice among respondents in its other main stronghold, Ida-Viru County, where it polled at 58 percent in August. Isamaa ranked first in all other regions of Estonia in August.

By age, SDE was the most popular choice among 18- to 24-year-olds (44 percent) and 25- to 34-year-olds (34 percent).

Isamaa ranked first among 35- to 49-year-olds, 50- to 64-year-olds and 65- to 74-year-olds.

In the 75+ age group, Center and Reform shared first place with 24 percent each.

The presidential elections at the Riigikogu take place September 2-3. The next direct elections in Estonia are to the Riigikogu itself, in March 2027.

World.title: Study finds Estonia must rent at least 300 prison places to make deal viable
World.content:
Before beginning negotiations with Sweden on the prison‑rental agreement, the Ministry of Justice commissioned an analysis from PricewaterhouseCoopers (PwC) to assess under what conditions renting out Estonia's prison places would be economically reasonable, and it turned out that this begins from 300 places.

"Our goal was to get an assessment from an independent expert on what Estonia should base its pricing on during negotiations and what our position could be," said Tiina Unuks, head of prison work organization at the Prison Service.

The analysis showed that the pricing of prison places should depend on volume. "There is a clear threshold below which there would not be a sufficient risk margin for providing the service, or the deal would be unprofitable for Estonia," Unuks noted.

Renting out prison places is reasonable for Estonia only if at least 300 places are rented out. This must also be fixed in the international agreement. Regardless of how many prisoners Sweden actually sends to Estonia, payment for 300 places must be guaranteed.

Over time it will become clear how many prisoners Sweden actually sends. "They will pay for 300 places anyway, and each additional prisoner beyond that costs 8,500 euros per month," Unuks explained.

According to her, the analysis showed very clearly that Estonia must index prices and that the contract volume cannot remain the same year after year. "The current prison‑rental agreement also includes indexing of 3.5 percent per year, which we agreed on with the Swedes," Unuks said.

It has also been agreed that Sweden will always pay half a year in advance, meaning half of the total amount. If the contract volume is 30.6 million euros, then 15.3 million must be paid six months in advance.

Number of Estonian prisoners has decreased

While in 2000 there were about 4,700 prisoners in Estonia's prisons, at the end of 2022 there were about 2,100 in prisons and detention centers. In recent years the trend has been downward.

As a result, Estonia has an increasing number of vacant prison places. At the end of last year, there were 1,443 such places. Because of this, Estonia has been looking for ways to optimize the management and associated costs of its prisons, one of which is renting out vacant places to another country.

Sweden pays Estonia 30.6 million euros per year for the prison service, but this amount also covers the costs Estonia incurs from operating the rental prison, including costs of other state agencies.

Costs considered included medical services, IT, internal security, the court system and other state institutions. Therefore, the cost of housing Swedish prisoners does not fall on Estonian taxpayers.

For 300 prison places, the estimated annual operating cost base is 26.77 million euros. However, this difference cannot automatically be considered Estonia's revenue, because risks and possible additional costs associated with the service must also be taken into account.

According to the analysis, the economically reasonable number of rented places is at least 300. Such a volume allows more efficient use of existing prison infrastructure and reduces the risk that with a smaller rental volume the fixed costs of the prison would remain too high.

The impact of the agreement is assessed across the entire Estonian prison system, not only through the budget of Tartu Prison. Estonian prisoners remain in Estonian prisons, and resources are still needed for their placement and enforcement of sentences. At the same time, the workload of other prisons has increased, which means additional labor and other costs.

Analysis provided cost base and break‑even point

The analysis was a negotiation tool for Estonia. It helped calculate costs, revenue potential, volume effects and risks, and shape Estonia's negotiation position.

The analysis was carried out by PricewaterhouseCoopers Advisors (PwC), and the Ministry of Justice and the Ministry of Digital Affairs commissioned it before deciding to begin official contract negotiations with Sweden.

PwC's analysis is based on data and forecasts known as of 2024. Its calculations do not reflect today's actual costs or the final financial terms of the agreement, and they cannot be considered indicators of the actual financial outcome of the contract signed between Estonia and Sweden.

After the analysis was completed, financial terms and amounts were refined during contract preparation and negotiations. These adjustments still remain within the agreed volume and principles of the contract.

World.title: Prime minister in Kyiv: Russia shouldn't count on us tiring of Ukraine support
World.content:
Ukraine must receive everything it needs to defend itself, Prime Minister Kristen Michal (Reform) said as he arrived in Kyiv for an NB8 summit with President Volodymyr Zelenskyy.

Michal is in the Ukrainian capital on Sunday and will co-chair a summit of Nordic-Baltic (NB8) and Ukrainian leaders with Zelenskyy, and will take part in events marking Ukraine's National Flag Day.

Estonia holds the NB8 presidency this year, and Michal's visit comes at a time of intensified attacks by Russia on Kyiv and Ukraine and stalled diplomatic efforts.

The visit also closely follows the 35th anniversary of the restoration of Estonian independence. "This year marks 35 years since Estonia restored its independence and Ukraine declared its independence. Both our countries secured the right to decide their own future. Today, Ukraine is defending that right on the battlefield while standing up for the freedom and security of all Europe," Michal said.

The Nordic and Baltic countries have stood with Ukraine since the first day of Russia's full-scale war of aggression, now in its fifth year. "Ukraine must receive everything it needs to defend itself and resist Russian aggression," the prime minister went on, via a press release.

He noted that "everything Ukraine needs" primarily means more air defense, more ammunition and greater investment in Ukraine's defense industry. "At the same time, we must increase pressure on Russia, strengthen sanctions and close the loopholes Russia uses to evade them," Michal added.

Prime Minister Kristen Michal is in Kyiv Sunday for national flag day and to co-chair the NB8-Ukraine meeting, along with President Volodymyr Zelenskyy. Source: Government Office

"We are helping Ukraine prepare for winter and protect and restore critical energy infrastructure, which remains under threat because of Russia's brutality," the head of government went on.

While in Kyiv, Michal will meet his Ukrainian counterpart, Prime Minister Serhii Koretskyi, to discuss bilateral relations and preparations for the Ukraine Recovery Conference to be held in Tallinn in January next year.

Michal's visit also coincides with Ukraine's National Flag Day, which is marked annually on August 23.

The NB8 format brings together the Nordic countries — Denmark, Finland, Iceland, Norway and Sweden — and the Baltic states — Estonia, Latvia and Lithuania — for regular dialogue on security and regional issues. Following the summit, a joint press conference is expected to outline outcomes and new commitments, as Estonia's NB8 presidency has placed regional security and support for Ukraine at the top of the agenda.

Estonia has been one of Ukraine's strongest supporters since the full-scale invasion began in February 2022, providing military aid, humanitarian assistance and political backing, while consistently calling for increased international pressure on Russia. The Reconstruction Conference in Tallinn next January will bring together international partners to coordinate Ukraine's long-term recovery, and Michal's visit continues a pattern of high-level engagement between the two countries.

Michal's visit is scheduled to last one day, with the prime minister returning to Estonia later Sunday.

The summit comes as diplomatic efforts to end the war remain stalled, with Russia insisting any deal must reflect "realities on the ground" — a reference to its control of around one-fifth of Ukrainian territory. On the battlefield, fighting has intensified, while Russia continues its long-range strikes on Ukrainian cities . Ukraine has expanded its own deep strikes inside Russia.

President of Ukraine Volodymyr Zelenskyy (photo taken during Zelenskyy's visit to Tallinn on June 9, 2026). Source: Siim Lõvi / ERR

NB8, Ukrainian leaders: Ukraine's EU negotiation clusters must open in September and October

The NB8 leaders and Ukraine adopted a joint declaration at the summit, reaffirming their unwavering support for Ukraine's independence, sovereignty and territorial integrity, and pledging to continue supporting Ukraine until a just and lasting peace is achieved.

The declaration supports the immediate opening of all remaining clusters in Ukraine's EU accession negotiations as early as September and October.

"The Nordic and Baltic countries have supported Ukraine from the first day of Russia's war, and our support will not waver. We know Russia's pattern of behavior well – concessions only encourage further aggression," Michal said.

Michal noted Ukraine needs more air defense and ammunition. "Russia is not seeking peace but continues to attack Ukraine and its people. Therefore, now is not the time to reduce pressure. Sanctions are working and Russia's war economy is under growing pressure."

All the leaders also stressed that no Russian attempt to annex Ukrainian territory would be recognized as lawful, and that any peace agreement must be based on international law and must not reward aggression. Strong and credible security guarantees are a prerequisite for a just and lasting peace.

The NB8 countries also pledged to continue providing political, military, financial, humanitarian and economic assistance, and to deepen defense industry cooperation, including in drones, air defense, electronic warfare and ammunition.

Ahead of the upcoming winter, the NB8 will continue supporting the protection, repair and restoration of Ukraine's energy infrastructure. "Russia has previously tried to use winter as a weapon. We must help Ukraine prepare for this," Michal added.

The leaders also called for stronger sanctions, further restrictions on Russian energy revenues, and continued work to use frozen Russian assets for the benefit of Ukraine.

"Ukraine's place is in the European Union and NATO. Estonia will continue working to ensure that Ukraine becomes a member of both," Michal concluded.

The declaration also highlighted the Ukraine Recovery Conference to be held in Tallinn in 2027, aiming to mobilize international political and financial support for Ukraine's reconstruction.

Editor's note: This piece was updated to include the declaration from the NB8 and Ukrainian leaders.

World.title: Tallinn Fringe Festival at 10: How do you Fringe?
World.content:
Tallinn's Fringe Festival marks its 10th anniversary this year, and writer Todd Williams explains how to make the most of the month-long event taking place around the Estonian capital until September 18, and why there's something for everyone.

I was recently talking to Dan Renwick, owner and operator of Heldeke! theater-bar here in Tallinn, and he asked me an interesting question.

"How do you Fringe?" It's a good one, and, coming from the man behind the beating heart of the international celebration of all things creative, one that I've taken quite a bit of time answering.

The Tallinn Fringe Festival begins last week, and whether you're into stand-up comedy, burlesque cabaret, experimental theatre, or just stumbling into a wine tasting that turns into a concert, it's got something for you. So I guess my ultimate answer to "how do you fringe?" would be "it depends on who you are, or, perhaps, where you are."

When people arrive at a Fringe Festival, sometimes they don't know that they're even in it. They may even wander into Heldeke!, order a drink, and find themselves face-to-face with a burlesque performer mid-routine, wondering if this is just a Tuesday in Tallinn or something they should be buying a ticket for. (It's both.)

Tallinn Fringe 2025 Source: Anton Serdjukov

That's the thing about Fringe that took me a full year of living in this city to understand: Tallinn doesn't announce itself. It's a city that reveals itself in layers, with cobblestones that turn an ankle if you're not paying attention, a medieval wall that gives way to a Soviet-era block that gives way to a converted power station full of art. Fringe just turns the volume up on something that was already happening. For one month, the city stops pretending it's subtle.

Dan's answer to his own question, when I turned it back on him, was simple: "you show up." No ticket required for much of the calendar. No dress code, unless you count "willingness to be surprised." Heldeke! itself, tucked into Kalamaja, Tallinn's shabby-chic answer to Williamsburg or Shoreditch, depending on your reference points, is ground zero for this philosophy. It's not a venue so much as an artistic dream with a bar: cabaret one night, a wine tasting that turns feral by the second glass the next, a magician performing card tricks for children on a Sunday afternoon before the room resets itself for something considerably less family-friendly by nightfall.

Case in point, on opening night, the venue hosted Love is a Lube, a genre-blurring set from Lebo Sibul, d'Argento, and Cvm Unity that splits the difference between cabaret, music, and spoken word, the kind of show that resists a clean elevator pitch, which is precisely the point. Ask three people what they saw and you'll get three different shows. That's not a bug in the Fringe model. That's the whole model.

Some of TFF's local talent at a launch event in Tallinn's Raekoja plats. Source: Anton Serdjukov / Tallinn Fringe Festival

The same night, a few doors down in the same building, Ana Falcon ran "Please the People: Comedy Challenge Show", free, English-language, and built entirely around audience whim. You show up not knowing what the show is going to be, and neither, really, does Ana. That's a genuine tightrope act, performed nightly, for free, by someone who clearly doesn't need the safety net. It's the kind of thing that could only exist in a festival built on the honor system, with no gatekeepers and no curators, just an artist and a venue owner shaking hands and agreeing to see what happens.

But here's the part that surprised me most once I actually looked into how this festival works: no one person runs it on a show-to-show level. There's no central booking office, no artistic director handing down a program from on high. Performers contact venues, and if a venue says yes, the show is in. That's it. That's the entire admissions process for one of the more ambitious arts festivals in the world. It sounds like chaos. It is, a little. But it's also the most honest description of how creative cities actually function, not through committees, but through people saying yes to each other.

So if you're the type who wants a plan, Fringe will accommodate you. The full program, all 31 days of it, is sitting on fringe.ee, filterable by genre, language, and how much you're willing to spend (a lot of it, gloriously, costs nothing). Circus, dance, spoken word, burlesque, stand-up in multiple languages, an open-air magic show for kids, a Kafka adaptation, something called "AUTOTUNED: The Orchestra of Cars" that I have chosen not to investigate too closely before seeing it live. There is, genuinely, something for whoever you are.

Some of TFF's local talent at a launch event in Tallinn's Raekoja plats. Source: Anton Serdjukov / Tallinn Fringe Festival

But if you're the type who'd rather just go get a drink and see what happens, Fringe will accommodate that too, arguably better. Walk around town on a Friday night, follow the noise, and odds are decent you'll end up watching something you didn't plan on watching, in a room you didn't know existed, next to people who also just followed the noise. That's the closest thing this festival has to a mission statement.

Which brings me back to Dan's question, the one I've been chewing on since he asked it. How do you Fringe?

You don't, really, not as a verb you perform. You let it happen to you. You let a whole city hand you its stage for a month and you decide, moment to moment, whether you're a performer, an audience member, or just someone who wandered in for a beer and left with a story. Most nights in Tallinn, that line is thinner than you'd think.

The Tallinn Fringe Festival runs August 18 through September 18. Find the shows that interest you the most. Let the rest find you.

World.title: Poll: 43% support Ülle Madise as next president
World.content:
Forty-three percent of respondents support frontrunner Chancellor of Justice Ülle Madise becoming Estonia's next president, while 36 percent do not, according to a Norstat poll commissioned by the Ühiskonnauuringute Instituut.

The results of the survey showed that 43 percent of respondents chose "yes" and "rather yes" when asked if they supported Madise's election, while 36 percent answered "no" and "rather no." Twenty-one percent of respondents did not give an answer.

Madise is most popular with Reform voters (83 percent), followed by opposition party SDE (69 percent), non-parliamentary party Parempoolsed (69 percent), and Isamaa (57 percent).

The majority of respondents from opposition party EKRE (79 percent) do not support Madise's election, and half of Center (50 percent).

In the poll, respondents were also given a list of names and asked who they would like to see as the next president.

Respondents' preferences were as follows:

Chancellor of Justice Ülle Madise 29 percent, EKRE's Mart Helme 12 percent, TalTech Rector Tiit Land 9 percent, diplomat Hannes Hanso 5 percent, entrepreneur Indrek Neivelt 3 percent, diplomat Jüri Luik 2 percent, Gen. (Ret).Riho Ühtegi 2 percent, diplomat Jonatan Vseviov 2 percent, Deputy Director-General of the European Commission's Directorate-General for the Internal Market and Industry Maive Rute 0.6 percent, CEO of Estonia Pianos Indrek Laul 0.3 percent, diplomat Matti Maasikas 0.2 percent.

Fifteen percent would like to see some other candidate, while 20 percent had no preference.

Citizens support direct presidential elections

Respondents were also asked whether the president should be directly elected by the people. Seventy percent of respondents said "yes" or "rather yes," 22 percent said "rather no" or "no," and eight percent said, "don't know."

Direct presidential elections are most popular among voters of EKRE (97 percent), Center (88 percent), Isamaa (74 percent) and Parempoolsed (54 percent).

It was below 50 percent for respondents who support Reform and SDE.

The survey also showed that 66 percent of those polled think the president should initiate new legislation to change the voting procedure to direct elections.

The Norstat poll was conducted online from August 19 to 20 among Estonian citizens aged 18 and older and included 1,002 respondents.

The first round of the presidential election will take place on September 2.

World.title: 74 MPs to nominate justice chancellor as presidential candidate
World.content:
Seventy-four members of the Riigikogu will nominate Chancellor of Justice Ülle Madise for president on Monday as the nomination period draws to a close.

Estonia's president is elected by the Riigikogu, and a candidate must be put forward by MPs. At least 68 votes of a potential 101 are needed to elect the next head of state.

MPs from the Eesti 200, Isamaa, Reform and the Social Democratic Party (SDE) factions will submit 74 signatures in support of Chancellor of Justice Ülle Madise on Monday at 11 a.m.

Among members of the parties supporting Madise, SDE's Züleyxa Izmailova and Isamaa's Priit Sibul, Andres Metsoja and Helir-Valdor Seeder did not sign the nomination.

MPs from EKRE and Center did not support Madise's nomination.

The Riigikogu will meet to elect the president on September 2

Members of the Riigikogu who signed the nomination of Madise are listed below:

World.title: Ukraine backers gather as war escalates, air defence runs low
World.content:
Kyiv – Ukraine hosts a meeting of its key European backers on Monday to press for critical air-defence supplies and more pressure on Moscow, with Russian attacks killing more civilians than at any time since the first months of the invasion.

The meeting of the Coalition of the Willing will be jointly chaired by the leaders of Britain, France and Germany.

UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham will be in Kyiv for his first international trip since taking office, and several other leaders are expected to join remotely.

EU Council President Antonio Costa is also due in Kyiv for the talks, which come amid the latest, deadly escalation of the war.

Russia has been pounding Kyiv with ballistic missiles in recent weeks, ripping open apartment blocks and killing dozens of citizens in the capital.

The escalating Russian strikes have pushed civilian deaths to their highest levels since the first months of Russia’s 2022 invasion.

After almost every attack — which sees tens of thousands hunker in the Kyiv metro system and many more in basements and other shelters across the city — Zelensky has issued public pleas for more air-defence support.

Ahead of the meeting, Ukraine has forged ahead with its campaign against Russia’s logistics sites, hitting multiple warehouses belonging to e-commerce giant Ozon.

Ozon reported fires early Monday at its warehouses in Krasnodar and Makhachkala, both in southern Russia, adding that sites in Adygeysk and Nevinnomyssk were evacuated due to threats of drone attack.

Russian authorities also said debris from a Ukrainian drone attack killed two children and wounded nine others.

– UK, French support –

Ukraine celebrates independence day on Monday, which also marks exactly four-and-a-half years since Russia invaded on February 24, 2022.

“Russia should be in no doubt of our resolve,” Burnham said in a statement before his arrival in Kyiv.

“We will not back down until there is a just and lasting peace.”

Diplomacy on ending the conflict — Europe’s largest since World War II — is effectively frozen.

Russia is demanding hardline territorial and political concessions that Kyiv has rejected as a capitulation that would only enable another Russian attack.

Burnham is set to announce that the British government is authorising defence firm MBDA to release classified information needed to help Ukraine and France set up local production of the long-range SCALP missile.

And on Saturday, French President Emmanuel Macron pledged Paris would deliver new interceptor missiles.

“It is crucial to provide Ukraine with all the necessary means to defend its skies and thwart this aggression,” Macron wrote on X.

The ballistic missiles Russia has been firing in their dozens are incredibly fast and travel with a high-arching trajectory, making them difficult to stop.

Kyiv’s homegrown weapons cannot shoot them down, meaning Ukraine is reliant on advanced systems — chiefly, US Patriot interceptors — to protect its skies.

But due to shortfalls globally since the US launched its war on Iran, Ukraine has been left exposed.

– Ukraine’s missiles shortfall –

Ahead of the meeting, Zelensky revealed the extent of the deficit, releasing usually closely guarded numbers.

He said deliveries of crucial Patriot interceptors had halved since 2023.

“Over the entire of 2023, Ukraine received 675 missiles, and over all of 2025 — 364, even though Russian missile strikes have increased,” Zelensky said.

“For 2026, as currently projected, it is 264,” he added, saying Ukraine was seeking a package of at least 300 for the upcoming winter.

The United States faces its own shortfall of the missiles during its war on Iran and has resisted releasing large numbers to Ukraine.

Zelensky said Russia could produce around 100 ballistic missiles a month.

Ukraine, meanwhile, has accelerated its own campaign of long-range strikes on Russian energy and logistics sites — including oil refineries and retail warehouses.

The Coalition of the Willing is a Franco-British initiative to deliver support to Ukraine and ramp up pressure on Russia.

Originally designed as a group of countries that would be willing to deploy peacekeeping troops to Ukraine in the event a ceasefire was reached, it has become a parallel forum for marshalling support to Ukraine as uncertainty persists over US commitments under Donald Trump.

World.title: New Zealand moves to ban social media for under-16s
World.content:
Wellington – New Zealand’s government will introduce legislation on Monday banning under 16s from using social media, joining a number of countries seeking to keep youngsters off sites such as Instagram and TikTok.

New Zealand has been investigating a social media ban for over a year, after neighbouring Australia implemented its world-first legislation in December.

Under the Online Safety Bill, firms like Meta could be fined up to 10 percent of their global revenue if they fail to comply.

“We simply cannot accept the harm being done to a generation of New Zealand children,” Prime Minister Christopher Luxon said.

In announcing the Online Safety Bill, Luxon said “one in three children aged between 13 and 17 are now spending at least five hours on social media a day”.

“Social media is exposing them to harmful content, addictive technology and pressures they are not equipped to deal with, and it’s affecting their family life, mental health, sleep, and education,” he said.

Luxon specifically called out platforms Instagram, TikTok, Snapchat and Facebook, saying they would be required to take “reasonable steps to check users are over the age of 16”.

They would have to use “existing account information, facial age estimation, digital ID services and formal ID” to verify age.

Platforms would also be required to assess the risks they pose as well as report on how those dangers are being reduced, and penalties would be introduced for companies that fail to comply.

Education Minister Erica Stanford said the Bill “places legal obligations on platforms”.

“No penalties are proposed for children, their parents or caregivers,” Stanford said.

It’s unclear whether the bill will pass, as both National Party’s coalition partners — the libertarian ACT party and NZ First — have said they oppose it.

In a statement, the populist NZ First said they could not support the law given the “colossal failure” of the legislation in Australia, while ACT said they believed the law “won’t work”, and teenagers would easily get around the ban.

Australia last year banned under 16s from the likes of Facebook, Instagram and TikTok, in a crackdown designed to protect children from online bullying and “predatory algorithms”.

A team of Australia-based researchers in a peer-reviewed study published in June found little evidence to suggest teenagers have turned away from social media as a consequence, however.

World.title: UEFA’s Ceferin tells Infantino to go, but ‘not interested’ in replacing him
World.content:
London – UEFA chief Aleksander Ceferin says he is “not interested” in replacing Gianni Infantino but warned the under-fire FIFA president must quit or face a leadership challenge.

Infantino has come under increasing pressure to step down as head of world football’s governing body over his now-abandoned plan to secure private investment in FIFA tournaments, including the World Cup.

UEFA, which oversees European football, has threatened a boycott of FIFA competitions with several continental and national federations also withdrawing their support for Infantino.

But Ceferin ruled himself out of a bid to take Infantino’s place, the 58-year-old Slovenian on Monday telling The Rest is Politics podcast: “I’m not interested because of two reasons.

“One reason is that I love UEFA and I love working here, and I think that at a certain point… it’s time to also enjoy life a bit.

“And the second point is, my credibility is much, much higher if I’m not interested in the position.”

Ceferin has been vocal in his criticism since Infantino revealed his controversial plans to seek private investment in a company to run FIFA tournaments.

He now believes Infantino’s previously impregnable position is under threat, with Ceferin forecasting the Swiss will have to stand down or face a leadership challenge if he seeks re-election at the next FIFA Congress, in Morocco in March.

Infantino, a former UEFA secretary general, had the broad backing of European nations when he succeeded Sepp Blatter as FIFA president in 2016.

But Ceferin, who revealed he has not spoken to Infantino since the start of the controversy, insisted the current situation was very different.

“There are two options,” he said.

“One option is that he (Infantino) realises that he doesn’t have the support, and that’s not only a political support of the ones who vote, but the political support of the football community, the political support of fans, the political support of the players, former players, coaches.

“And the second option, that he goes to the elections in March, but in that case I think he will have a candidate against him. I don’t know yet who.”

CONCACAF president Victor Montagliani and AFC boss Sheikh Salman bin Ebrahim al-Khalifa are considered two of the most likely challengers for Infantino’s position.

– Infantino ‘support’ –

Infantino was in the Dominican Republic over the weekend for meetings with local and regional football officials, despite Montagliani reportedly asking him to stay away from a youth tournament there.

In video remarks released by FIFA on Sunday, the 56-year-old Infantino appeared to reference the furore surrounding him.

“It’s important to engage, to have a dialogue, to express views and opinions,” he said.

“A lot has been happening the last few weeks and it’s important that you hear, you listen, and you’re able to also express what your feelings are.

“So I think overall positive, very, very happy with all the support I get here.”

World.title: Oil falls as Trump pledges economic war on Iran
World.content:
Hong Kong – Oil prices fell on Monday as investors braced for details of a US plan to isolate the Iranian economy that President Donald Trump billed as the “most crushing” financial operation ever against Tehran.

Asian stocks were mostly down in early trading, with South Korea’s tech-rich Kospi falling 1.4 percent after Samsung Electronics said it spent a massive $80 billion to buy back its own shares following weeks of turbulent trading.

The chip giant’s shares, along with those of rival SK hynix, peaked in June on optimism for the artificial intelligence boom, but have since fallen amid investor jitters and a broader tech rout.

In an important week for AI, investors are also looking towards an earnings report from Nvidia, the world’s most valuable company and a bellwether for the sector.

The recurring question for the US chipmaker is whether the AI boom will continue to accelerate as the technology takes over more corners of the broader economy.

“The spending machine is still running, but the bill is getting heavier,” said Stephen Innes of SPI Asset Management.

“Nvidia must now show that the most expensive investment boom in modern market history can still pay its bills.”

Chinese tech giant Alibaba is keeping focus on the sector after announcing on Sunday that it plans to issue $10.2 billion in new shares in Hong Kong to fund its global AI ambitions.

The firm, known for its open-source “Qwen” AI models, has been ploughing tens of billions of dollars into the technology, with shareholders eager to see how it will monetise the huge investments.

Tokyo, Shanghai, Taipei and Wellington were down on Monday. Sydney, Jakarta and Bangkok posted gains, while Manila and Kuala Lumpur were flat.

Hong Kong fell more than two percent despite fast-fashion giant Shein announcing its market debut will take place in the Chinese financial hub on September 1.

The long-awaited listing would value the group — known for its vast selection of products at stunningly low prices — at close to $27 billion.

Eyes are also on US Treasury boss Scott Bessent, who said he would give more details in a news conference on Monday on a fresh push to pile economic pressure on Iran.

The United States warned allies and China on Thursday to join Trump’s new campaign, which comes as the unpopular war in the Middle East drags toward the six-month mark.

US Vice President JD Vance admitted the plan was a “delicate dance” because Iran will “try to apply economic pressure to us”.

Asked whether the United States would pressure China, Bessent told CNBC that “many conversations are best to have in private”, but called on Beijing “to get with the programme”.

Both main crude contracts were down 2.3 percent, with the Brent benchmark sitting at $92 a barrel.

Traders will also be watching this week’s annual gathering of central bankers, economists and finance chiefs in Jackson Hole in the United States, hoping for some clarification on US monetary policy.

The meeting comes after the Treasury bought its own bonds last week in an effort to push down borrowing costs after the 30-year yield surged to levels last seen in 2007, just before the global financial crisis.

Yields have risen on inflation fears and as the United States reported that its federal debt had topped $40 trillion.

World.title: Iraq’s IDC relocates drilling rig from Zubair oil field to East Baghdad field
World.content:
Baghdad (IraqiNews.com) – The Iraqi Drilling Company (IDC) is relocating the IDC-51 drilling rig from the Zubair oil field in the southern province of Basra to the East Baghdad South field.

Under the supervision of the state-owned Midland Oil Company (MOC), the step is part of a deal with EBS Petroleum, an Iraqi-registered subsidiary of Chinese state-owned firm ZhenHua Oil, to drill 17 horizontal wells to increase production capacity in Iraq’s central region.

The move entails disassembling the rig at Zubair, shipping components, reassembling, and conducting safety tests at East Baghdad South.

This project builds on the IDC’s past development phases in the same field, which featured distinct campaigns of 27 and 18 horizontal wells.

The East Baghdad South field is the extremely productive southern section of the larger, super-giant East Baghdad oilfield complex.

The oilfield is one of Iraq’s most unusual energy resources, measuring around 60 kilometers in length and 12 kilometers in its width. It is located just under the capital’s densely populated suburbs.

Appraisal drilling increased the proved reserves of the East Baghdad field to 15 billion barrels, including an enormous reservoir of medium and light oil.

World.title: Iraq’s PMF repels ISIS attack in Salah al-Din province
World.content:
Baghdad (IraqiNews.com) – Iraq’s Popular Mobilization Forces (PMF) successfully foiled on Sunday an attack by ISIS terrorists on a military position in the Tuz Khurmatu region in the eastern province of Salah al-Din.

The raid targeted an isolated outpost belonging to the Commando Regiment of the PMF’s 63rd Brigade.

ISIS militants launched an armed attack from a mountain, resulting in an intense battle, with loud gunfire and explosions reported by civilians.

The Popular Mobilization Forces (PMF) represent a coalition of Shia paramilitary groups that have been officially incorporated into Iraq’s national security forces. This coalition consists of various militias that have ties with Iran.

PMF fighters engaged the attackers immediately, compelling them to retreat into the challenging terrain without accomplishing any tactical objectives. No casualties have been reported among PMF personnel.

Iraqi Army and PMF soldiers started a coordinated, large-scale search operation in a nearby mountainous area to track down fleeing terrorists and identify their locations.

This failed attack highlights the ongoing threat of secret factions belonging to the ISIS group in isolated places.

Analysts see that these small-scale, opportunistic ambushes are intended to test local defense networks as Baghdad moves to autonomous state security ahead of the scheduled withdrawal of international coalition forces.

World.title: Iraq to repatriate 6,000 foreign prisoners held in prisons
World.content:
Baghdad (IraqiNews.com) – The Iraqi Ministry of Justice has launched legal and diplomatic efforts to repatriate about 6,000 foreign inmates to their home countries.

The Iraqi National Security Council has authorized an official direction for this large-scale initiative.

The initiative involves over 6,000 detained and sentenced individuals from 61 foreign countries.

Syrian nationals make up the biggest group. Other notable nationalities are Moroccans, Americans, Canadians, Russians, Tunisians, and Turks.

The transfer process completely excludes convicts serving death sentences in Iraq.

Under the signed court accords, transferred individuals are expected to serve their remaining imprisonments in their home countries.

The great bulk of these foreign inmates are linked to the terrorist organization ISIS and were transferred to Iraqi custody earlier in 2026.

To prevent major jail breakouts, the US Central Command (CENTCOM) arranged the removal of thousands of terrorists from vulnerable northeastern Syrian detention sites.

Baghdad received the prisoners with the clear intention that they would not stay indefinitely and is now actively pressuring other countries to take responsibility for its residents.

World.title: Baghdad hosts Iraqi-Libyan Joint Committee meetings after 25-year hiatus
World.content:
Baghdad (IraqiNews.com) – Libya’s Acting Foreign Minister Taher al-Baour is in Baghdad heading a high-level delegation to co-chair the Iraqi-Libyan Joint Committee meetings, which have resumed after a 25-year break.

Al-Baour met with Iraqi Foreign Minister Fuad Hussein to discuss strategies to enhance political, diplomatic, and regional ties between Baghdad and Tripoli.

Their discussions focused on aligning mutual political positions on regional problems and increasing combined consular and diplomatic presence.

Following their meeting, al-Baour and Hussein held a joint press conference. Al-Baour emphasized Libya’s immediate need to partner with Iraq to repair and staff key public facilities, particularly in education and healthcare.

The Libyan delegation is finalizing several memoranda of understanding covering a wide range of economic and development areas.

Al-Baour’s team includes officials from several government bodies affiliated with the Tripoli-based Government of National Unity (GNU).

According to the Iraqi Foreign Ministry, this diplomatic drive follows Iraq’s offer to resume coordination and signify a return to normalized, regular diplomatic ties between the two countries.

The delegation’s trip to Baghdad builds directly upon virtual expert meetings organized by the Libyan Ministry of Foreign Affairs to conclude trade agreements with Iraqi officials before signatures are authorized.

NEW DELHI: The government on Monday said discussions about arrangements for a leaderâs public appearance are a ânormal practice,â clarifying the context of US Ambassador to India Sergio Gorâs remarks regarding the bilateral meeting between Prime Minister Narendra Modi and US President Donald Trump in June.âDiscussions regarding arrangements for public appearances of leaders are normal practice ahead of any VVIP visit, and in this regard, the Indian side had communicated its standard practice for such visits,â government sources told ANI.The clarification followed statements by Gor at the Economic Times World Leaders Forum on Saturday, where he stated that India had âspecifically requestedâ the US administration not to take questions from the media following the bilateral interaction between PM Modi and President Trump on the sidelines of the G7 summit in France.According to Gor, although Trump initially agreed to the request, he subsequently opened the floor to reporters, turning the session into a 45-minute press conference with PM Modi sitting alongside him.Recalling the sequence of events, Gor described his âbrief conversationâ with Trump before the bilateral meeting with PM Modi.âWe were behind the scenes, behind the stage, and at one point it was just the president and I, and he asked me, he goes, âWhat the Indians are going to raise?â We went over some topics,â Gor recounted.âAnd he (Trump) said, âDo they have any asks?â And the MEA had one ask. He said, and it was, âLetâs bring in the media, but letâs not do a full press conference,ââ the ambassador added.He noted that he directly conveyed the Indian sideâs preference to Trump.âI told the president, I said, the Indians prefer no questions. He said, 'Sure, no problem',â Gor recalled.The interaction subsequently began with media personnel and technical crews present in the room. Gor noted that about 50 cameras were set up as PM Modi and Trump sat across from each other to deliver their opening statements.âSo the meeting starts, the press comes in, there must have been 50 cameras, the president is sitting here, the prime minister is sitting there, they both speak for a few minutes,â he recalled.However, immediately after the opening statements, Trump turned to the assembled reporters and asked, âAny questions?ââAnd that opened everything up,â the ambassador recalled, describing the interaction as turning into âa 45-minute press conferenceâ where âeverything was on the table."The bilateral meeting on June 17 came days after three Indian mariners were killed in an attack by the US Navy on a commercial vessel in the Strait of Hormuz.The safety and protection of Indian seafarers navigating the region were among the key issues raised by PM Modi during the exchange.The June visit proved significant as New Delhi and Washington worked towards finalising a bilateral trade agreement amid continuing tensions in West Asia that affected maritime shipping and global energy supplies.Trump also observed during the interaction that the two nations were âvery closeâ to concluding the trade deal.
