World.title: PM backs GST deal, leaves future taxpayers on the hook for billions
World.content:
PoliticsFederalGST PM backs GST deal, leaves future taxpayers on the hook for billions Shane Wright August 24, 2026 — 6:03pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Anthony Albanese has promised to keep a special deal to protect Western Australia’s share of the GST for as long as he is prime minister, reminding every other state that it was his government bankrolling an agreement that was on track to cost taxpayers $60 billion. Speaking in Perth, Albanese effectively made redundant a report into the deal by the Productivity Commission, which earlier this month declared the GST allocation system a “mistake” that will weigh on the federal budget into the next decade. Prime Minister Anthony Albanese has effectively killed speculation of a change to the GST deal that bankrolls the West Australian budget of Premier Roger Cook. Alex Ellinghausen “There will be no change to WA’s GST arrangements whilst I’m prime minister. That is my view. That has consistently been my view,” he told a press conference. “There will be no change.” The deal, put in place by then-treasurer Scott Morrison after the collapse in WA’s share of GST, was expected to cost around $2.3 billion. Instead, it had blown out to $23 billion by 2024 and is on track to cost $60 billion by the end of the decade.





A final report is due by year’s end, but Albanese’s declaration made redundant whatever the commission ultimately recommends. He said there should be no surprise that the institution would deliver an “economic rationalist” worldview on the deal. He pushed back at criticism from every other state and territory about the deal, noting that ultimately it was being paid by the federal government. Prime Minister Anthony Albanese in Perth yesterday. Matt Jelonek “[The] important thing that sometimes isn’t understood from some of the critique of WA getting its fair share of the GST is that those additional payments have not come from states and territories; they’ve come from the Commonwealth,” Albanese said. “I’m comfortable with that, and what I say to premiers and chief ministers, though, is that you need to bear that in mind when you are discussing federal-state financial relations.”



NSW Treasurer Daniel Mookhey, who described the Productivity Commission’s report as “superb”, said he would continue to fight for a change to WA GST arrangement. He acknowledged that the prime minister had pledged to stick with the deal, but the evidence for change was overwhelming. NSW Treasurer Daniel Mookhey has found to continue the fight to change the WA GST deal. James Brickwood “Right now, eight out of nine states and territories, Labor, Liberal, all say the current system rewards some Australians more than others, and I think that ultimately we’re going to have to continue to make our case,” he told News24. “This struggle for a fairer system will go on.



“What the Productivity Commission found was that this system is costing the Commonwealth a lot more. That it even found that in a scenario in which NSW faces a disaster, West Australia automatically gets a funding increase.” Related Article Opinion

GST The GST carve-up is cooked, but we need to stop piling onto WA Millie Muroi Economics Writer Queensland Treasurer David Janetzki said while WA’s resources sector was being recognised, his state’s contribution to the national economy was being penalised under the GST deal. “Jim Chalmers and Anthony Albanese must show that they back Queensland and that they get Queensland,” he said. “They must listen to the advice of the federal Productivity Commission and stop over-penalising other states that develop resources in the national interest.”



Victorian Treasurer Colin Brooks said that since the GST carve-up was introduced, his state had received $31 billion less than if it was allocated on a per capita basis. “The Productivity Commission’s interim findings just this month back up exactly what Victoria has been saying for years, and we’re glad to see it recognised,” he said. Related Article GST A $60b GST fiasco: State vs state argument erupts between WA and ‘east coast whingers’ “The current system isn’t working. It leaves other states like Victoria exposed and goes against the core purpose of fair distribution.” Premier Roger Cook said all West Australians were relieved and pleased to hear Albanese’s commitment on the agreement, while suggesting other states were envious of WA’s economy.



“There is a lot of noise coming from the east coast, and we understand that on the east coast people look to Western Australia, they see that our economy is going forward, that jobs are being created and opportunities for people who live in this state abound,” he said. Nationals leader Matt Canavan said the prime minister’s words could not be trusted, arguing he needed to make a more permanent commitment to the GST deal. “We need a tattoo on the PM saying he will not change the WA GST deal,” he said. World.title: What to stream this week: A gripping DC superhero story, plus five more picks
World.content:
What to stream this week (clockwise from top left): Kangaroo Island; Stalked; You’re Killing Me; Nowhere; Lanterns; and It’s Always Sunny in Philadelphia.

Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

This week’s picks include a new spin on the Green Lantern franchise, Brooke Shield’s light-hearted detective drama, a new season for the longest-running sitcom in US history and a provocative director’s surreal masterpiece. Lanterns ★★★ (HBO Max) Superheroes and mortals alike return to the same question in HBO Max’s gritty, psychological take on DC’s Green Lantern franchise: “Are you afraid?” The three words become a mantra for John Stewart (Aaron Pierre, Rebel Ridge; The Morning Show), a Lantern-in-training assigned to follow around Earth’s long-standing Lantern, Hal Jordan (Kyle Chandler, Friday Night Lights). Together, they investigate a strange shooting in Nevada with suspected intergalactic links. Without mental resolve, these intergalactic law officers can’t use their weapons – a magical emerald green ring that lets them fly and create objects, force fields and more out of sheer mind power. But fear itself is the powering force of Lanterns, a show that examines how it is used to justify acts of love, war and hatred across interpersonal relationships and intergalactic colonialism alike. Kyle Chandler as Green Lantern Hal Jordan in Lanterns. Warner Bros Created by Chris Mundy (Ozark) and produced by Damon Lindelof (Watchmen; The Leftovers) and DC writer Tom King, Lanterns is a detective drama first and a superhero show second, though there’s a solid amount of cheesy jokes and quips. Don’t worry: that dark, moody edge isn’t an excuse for terrible lighting or filters. Lanterns offers crisp visuals. At first, John and Hal couldn’t seem more opposite. While Hal’s decades of power and fame has left him arrogant and smarmy, John is comparatively robotic, a stoic ex-military man emotionally cauterised by a traumatic childhood. In Lanterns’ opening scene, he barely reacts when his father draws a close-range rifle in their backyard for a William Tell trick, shooting an apple atop his head.



Editor's pick Streaming He’s TV Mr Nice Guy, but Nathan Fillion’s ‘unlikeable’ superhero could be his greatest hit Both men are fearless, but through flashbacks across the seven of eight episodes offered for review, it’s revealed that their mental fortitude is not equal. As in the comics, John is a black man, one told as a boy that Hal and other white men are “privileged enough to not know fear”. That tension – of resentment at Hal’s ability to be a fool in public, such as getting arrested on purpose for the purposes of their investigation – is one of Lanterns’ most intriguing, understated qualities. Aaron Pierre and Kyle Chandler in Lanterns. With a weekly release schedule, it’s easy to imagine casual audiences might drop off, as early episodes find John cold and Hal a touch too irritating. At least the other characters – including Kelly Macdonald as a sheriff, and Nathan Fillion reprising his role from Superman as an abrasive Lantern – agree on that last point, too. As someone not particularly drawn to a trauma-led take on a lesser-known superhero, I found Lanterns gripping enough. It’s a balanced blend of cheesy one-liners, engaging action and emotional depth, with lots to love for fans of DC or superhero stories more broadly. You’re Killing Me ★★ (Stan) Putting aside the incessant, overdone jokes about Gen Z and that one of the characters is a true-crime podcaster, there’s a quaint 2000s feel to You’re Killing Me, a light-hearted detective drama with no pretense of prestige.



Brooke Shields with Andrea Walker, who plays a cocky true-crime podcaster in You’re Killing Me. Brooke Shields stars as crime novelist Allison, whose agent tells her to ditch the “menopausal murder mysteries” to find a new audience. Amalia Williamson (Sullivan’s Crossing) is Andrea, the headstrong, tech-adept 20-something podcaster who Alison reluctantly teams up with to write a bestseller. Naturally, that involves solving the murder mystery of the week, all while Allison makes fun of Andrea’s elaborate coffee order and Andrea lectures her about the “patriarchal elements” of Cinderella. Related Article ★★★★

Review Hugo Weaving’s compelling new Australian drama will leave you wanting more These beyond-tired jokes (never mind that they almost exclusively deal with Millennial, not Gen Z, tropes) ease up across the series’ six episodes. So does Shields, whose frantic, overwrought performance shoots for high-strung but gives Allison an aggressive, hostile edge, before mellowing out. It’s not a particularly pretty or well-made show, with the lighting and make-up departments breaking out into all-out war. But it’s fun enough, with intriguing investigations and overarching plots, including Allison’s flirtations with a cop (Tom Cavanagh) and a mystery around Andrea’s long-missing mother. Much like Allison’s crime novels, it’s not aiming to be anything other than an easy, unchallenging watch. In that, it’s successful. Kaitlin Olson, Rob Mac, Danny DeVito and Charlie Day in It’s Always Sunny in Philadelphia.



It’s Always Sunny in Philadelphia ★★★ (Disney+) Eighteen seasons in, It’s Always Sunny in Philadelphia is by far the longest-running sitcom in US history. Remarkable by any metric, it’s borderline incomprehensible given how the comedy trades in offence, following a group of deplorable friends who run a dive bar. The uninitiated should know it’s as if Curb Your Enthusiasm added in gross-out comedy and truly amoral characters played to perfection by Danny DeVito, Kaitlin Olsson, Charlie Day, Rob Mac and creator Glenn Howerton. Definitely not for everyone, the cult comedy keeps finding fresh ways to be filthy: Take upcoming episode title Frank Marries A Corpse as proof. Still from the HBO drama Stalked. Stalked ★★★ (HBO Max) In a chilling three-part documentary, three New Zealand women share their stories of being stalked by strangers, acquaintances and ex-partners. Rather than dedicate one episode to each woman, Stalked jumps between the stories of Jazz, Zeni and Tessa across its two-hour runtime to link their experiences, which include shrugging off early warning signs and the systemic failures of law and police to protect them. What elevates Stalked from more exploitative true-crime docs is the tenderness with which it’s made, with room for the women’s sense of humour to shine through alongside their traumas. Nowhere by Gregg Araki, starring Shannon Doherty (right).



Nowhere ★★★★★ (Brollie) Ahead of Gregg Araki releasing his first film in more than a decade this week (I Want Your Sex, starring Cooper Hoffman, Olivia Wilde and Charli xcx), why not watch the provocative director’s surreal masterpiece? Described by Araki as “90210 on acid”, Nowhere is a hyper-saturated sci-fi melodrama following a gigantic ensemble of beautiful 20-somethings (Shannon Doherty, Rose McGowan and Ryan Phillippe among them) adrift in an apocalyptic-tinged Los Angeles. Powered by an immense ’90s soundtrack (30-plus songs in its 82-minute runtime), Nowhere’s parody-indulgence of the era’s alt-nihilism is absurd, deeply evocative and undeniably cool. Rebecca Breeds plays Lou in Kangaroo Island. Kangaroo Island ★★★ (Netflix) There’s a touch of tourism ad to Kangaroo Island, a family drama that relies on the grandeur of its namesake and setting when it loses its spark. Based in Los Angeles, spiralling actor Lou (Rebecca Breeds) boards a plane back home to the island, greeted warmly by her father (Erik Thomson), less so by her sister (Adelaide Clemens). For all the cliches that follow, Breeds and Clemens add depth to Kangaroo Island, emanating the rage and fear that comes from siblings who have left deep wounds on each other. Want more TV? We’ve got you.

World.title: NRL to trial controversial kick-off rule change on Thursday night
World.content:
Breaking SportNRLNRL 2026 NRL to trial controversial kick-off rule change on Thursday night Adrian Proszenko August 24, 2026 — 6:00pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

The NRL will run the first trial of its controversial kick-off rule change on Thursday night in the match between Brisbane and Melbourne. In what could be a precursor to the permanent introduction of the rule for the 2027 season, the team that concedes a try will have the option to re-start by either kicking off or receiving the football. The NRL was keen to introduce the initiative at the start of this season, but backed down after a backlash from clubs. Clinton Gutherson prepares to kick off. Getty Images However, head office is keen to road-test the rule tweak in NRL and NRLW matches that have no finals implications, starting with Thursday night’s Broncos-Storm clash. It will add a point of interest to a match that is effectively a dead rubber in the run home to September. If implemented on a full-time basis, the rule change will be one of the biggest the game has undergone.



There has been fierce debate about the merits of the modification ever since this masthead first flagged it last November. It passed its first test, at a committee meeting of top coaches Wayne Bennett, Ivan Cleary, Craig Bellamy, Ricky Stuart and Craig Fitzgibbon in the off-season. Ultimately, it was put on hold after resistance from the clubs, who felt the game was being tampered with unnecessarily. However, all stakeholders will now get to watch how it works in practice under first-grade match conditions. The Broncos will be the first side to participate in the kick-off trial. Getty Images Some consideration was given to trialling it in the round 24 match between the Dragons and Tigers, but at that point Benji Marshall’s side still had a mathematical chance of qualifying for the play-offs. Not wanting to compromise the integrity of the competition, the NRL opted to wait until a match involving two teams totally out of the running, as is the case on Thursday night. There will be another chance to trial the change in the final-round clash between the Eels and the Dragons, while other opportunities may arise before then pending results.



Proponents of the change feel it could reduce blowout scorelines. Currently, the team that has just scored regains possession from the kick-off, making momentum difficult to stop. Giving the team that has just conceded a try the choice of either kicking or receiving the ball from the restart will add a new tactical element to the game. Bennett has been the most vocal advocate of the rule change, previously telling this masthead: “If you like the old rule, and you don’t like the new rule, stick with the old rule … If you listen to some of these guys [complaining], we’d still be playing with unlimited tackles, and players would still be wearing black boots with white laces.” Loading Panthers coach Ivan Cleary provided a counterpoint, previously stating that the change could stop epic comebacks like the one his side mounted to beat Brisbane in the 2023 grand final. The NRL has been unapologetic about tweaking the game to attract fans. In a recent interview, NRL executive chair Peter V’landys said the game wouldn’t have been able to broker a $5.3 billion broadcast deal if it didn’t introduce rule changes – like the six-again rule, captain’s challenge, the two-point field-goal and the short line drop-out – to make the product more entertaining.



Related Article Exclusive

NRL 2026 NRL to road-test controversial kick-off rule change in ‘dead rubber’ matches “All of those things are about unpredictability. You can’t predict what is going to happen in the game,” V’landys told Mark Bouris’ Straight Talk podcast. “And we got rid of the wrestle, which the fans hated. That’s why we’ve increased the [league] audience from 1.2 [million] to 2.4 [million]. We made it what the fan wants; not what the player wants, not what the coaches want, not what the club administrators or what the NRL want. “Who is your customer? It’s the fan. The record broadcast deal has been done because we worked for five years to get our game to a point where it was an entertainment product that can be sold at the highest price.”

World.title: Woman wins $24k after being fired from ex-husband’s nightclub over explicit photo
World.content:
BusinessWorkplaceUnfair dismissal Woman wins $24k after being fired from ex-husband’s nightclub over explicit photo Millie Muroi August 24, 2026 — 5:59pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

A bookkeeper who accidentally shared an explicit photo to a group chat and tampered with medical documents will receive more than $24,000 in compensation after being fired from her ex-husband’s nightclub. The woman, identified as “LL” in the Fair Work Commission’s judgment, was married to “CL”: the majority shareholder and managing director of Melbourne-based nightclub owner Platform One, until their marriage broke down in 2024 and family law proceedings began. The Fair Work Commission found the employee engaged in misconduct but was not provided with a safe work environment. Getty Images The case highlights the complexity of an employment dispute that is entwined with a deteriorating personal relationship between workers. LL had been working as a bookkeeper and business manager since 2014, but also performed some work “off the books” for the business before that date. She was employed by a trustee for the business.



In November 2025, after the marriage breakdown, LL was notified of the firm’s intention to terminate her employment because of “allegations of serious misconduct, an inability for you to return to work and perform the inherent requirements of your role”. Related Article Industrial relations Maths tutor fired after asking if girl, 14, wanted to be seen as ‘sex object’ The letter alleged that LL had increased her own salary without permission, sent an explicit photo to a work group chat and made unauthorised adjustments to her certificate of capacity. A week later, LL was dismissed. About the same time, her family lawyers contacted CL’s family lawyers, denying the allegations and alleging that CL was engaging in coercive control. At the end of 2024, LL had posted a photo exposing her upper body to a work WhatsApp group that included her ex-husband, other directors and managers. The photo was removed after a few minutes, and was accompanied by a message saying “enjoy” with a devil emoticon that LL said was a cover-up for her embarrassment and to pretend it was a joke.



LL said she was “mortified” after mistakenly posting the photo while driving, and provided evidence that she had intended to send the photo to her surgeon as part of a post-surgery check-up. A letter from her doctor confirmed that it was “part of standard post-operative care” to provide routine post-operative images for clinical review. While the commissioner said that sending a photo while driving was “concerning and extremely unsafe”, and that LL should have apologised and explained the situation rather than trying to make a joke, she accepted that LL had accidentally posted the photo. Separately, in April 2025, LL provided a certificate of capacity stating that she had no capacity for employment from April 18 to May 16, 2025 because of migraines, anxiety, poor concentration, poor sleep, apprehension and hypervigilance. LL conceded that she had made adjustments to the certificate, including adding a sentence that “migraine insets” were “more severe due to workplace bullying” and adding the company name, which the commissioner said constituted misconduct. While the commissioner found LL’s inappropriate remarks after posting the explicit photo, and her tampering with a medical certificate, counted as misconduct which “in certain circumstances could be a valid reason for dismissal”, she said that in this case, that conduct was not the real reason for LL’s dismissal.



“No one raised the photograph matter with LL until the show cause letter almost a year later,” the commissioner said, noting that the tampered certificate was also not raised until then. “The real reason for dismissal was not misconduct but rather the [company’s] reluctance to continue paying LL when she was not at work.” Related Article Exclusive

Unfair dismissal Sacked worker forced to pay for using ‘plain wrong’ AI in landmark case The commissioner said that LL’s inability to perform the inherent requirements of the job – due to disability, the relationship breakdown with CL and the nature of her duties working closely with CL – were a valid reason for dismissal, but found that she was not given a proper opportunity to respond, nor a warning before the show cause letter. Commissioner Susie Allison found LL’s salary had “more likely than not” been approved by CL and that it was “hard to believe” Platform One had not authorised and accepted the increase given they continued to pay her at the increased rate 10 months after it was discovered. Allison also said that the company had failed to provide LL with a safe work environment after she raised allegations of domestic violence and told the venue manager that she had found sexually explicit drawings in her inbox which she believed were placed there by CL.



While the firm claimed that CL was not involved in any decisions about LL’s employment after the marriage breakdown, the commissioner found that CL wielded “considerable power and influence” at the company, used his family lawyers to provide work directions to LL, including a request that she work from home, and that he had some involvement in the decision to fire LL. The company was ordered to pay LL compensation of $24,548 plus superannuation. Platform One was contacted for comment. A pedestrian has died after a car crashed into a cafe in an outer eastern Melbourne suburb. The woman, who has not been identified, was struck while she walked outside Martini and Co bar and cafe in Wantirna South on Monday afternoon. Loading Emergency services attempted to provide first aid, but she died at the scene. A second person, who was seated outside the restaurant, was assessed by paramedics but was not taken to hospital.



The 51-year-old driver of the Tesla and her passenger were taken to hospital with non-life-threatening injuries. The crash happened about 12.45pm. Brody Jones, who works at the nearby Mycar Tyre and Auto, said he and his team were on lunch in the break room when a workmate ran in to tell them what had happened. Police are investigating after a car struck a pedestrian and crashed into a café at a shopping centre in Wantirna South on Monday afternoon. Nine News They rushed out to see a car in the restaurant and people scattering away. “It was incredible, there were tons and tons of all of the emergency services,” Jones said.



“Everyone showed up relatively quickly and in massive numbers. “The [shopping centre] parking team, they were on scene almost immediately,” he said, “they weren’t trained … they had to get up and close to the scene. Police are investigating after a woman was killed when a car crashed into a cafe at a shopping centre in Wantirna South. “They were really professional and did an excellent job assisting emergency services.” Martini and Co is located in Westfield Knox. A post from the cafe on social media said it was closed until further notice.



“Please stay safe and we will keep you updated when we can reopen,” it said. World.title: Reynolds admits defeat in bid for Suncorp farewell as curtain falls on NRL career
World.content:
Updated SportNRLNRL 2026 Reynolds admits defeat in bid for Suncorp farewell as curtain falls on NRL career Christian Nicolussi Updated August 24, 2026 — 6:21pm ,first published August 23, 2026 — 4:30pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Brisbane halfback Adam Reynolds has played his last game in the NRL after the two-time premiership winner reluctantly calling time on his career with two matches of the season remaining. Reynolds completed training on Monday and was targeting a Suncorp Stadium swansong on Thursday night against the Melbourne Storm. Adam Reynolds goes down injured against Parramatta in March. Injuries have plagued his final season in the NRL. Getty Images But coach Michael Maguire and the club’s medical team were worried about Reynolds breaking down and were not prepared to entertain images of him being helped from the field on his final home appearance. The 36-year-old who played 323 games – including grand final wins in 2014 with Souths and last year with the Broncos – phoned up to 50 family and friends to tell them not to fly to Brisbane for his farewell.



“I got through training, I felt pretty good, but after talking with ‘Madge’ and the medical staff, they weren’t keen to see me go out there and finish with another potential injury, then go out like that,” Reynolds said. “They’ve worked with me behind the scenes for years, they know me better than myself. They didn’t want me being injured to be last image fans remembered me by. Adam Reynolds says he doesn’t regret playing on in 2026 and no retiring after Brisbane’s premiership win in 2025. Getty Images “I knew it was coming to an end, be it this week or next week. Once the decision was made, I thought I’d get it out there, get on with life, and keep the focus on the team because they’ve still got to go out there and perform. There are other players preparing for their last game at the club, so it’s important to celebrate them as much as myself. I just hope we get the win.” Reynolds said he did not want any fuss or presentations. “If I had my way, I don’t want any parades, and I’d prefer to go out the back door quietly,” he said.



Reynolds said Mad Monday celebrations “would now become a mad month”, before he returns next season in a coaching role, where he will work with the club’s halves and pathways. Reynolds told this masthead on Sunday he had no regrets about playing on this year, despite injury and a concussion limiting him to just 14 games. Adam Reynolds celebrates a try against the Dolphins in March. Getty Images Reynolds has been struggling with nerve pain in his left calf for most of the season, then suffered a slight strain in his right calf at training a couple of weeks ago. “The year hasn’t worked out like I had hoped for myself and the club – but there are no regrets about playing on,” he said.



“Hindsight is a wonderful thing. I’d love to go around again, to be honest, but it won’t happen with where I’m at in my career. It’s easy to say I should have finished up at the end of last year, but there was that opportunity go back to back and do something special. That doesn’t come around too often in your NRL career. Related Article NRL 2026 Record $3.3m offer not enough to end star back-rower’s PNG interest “If there is one thing we’ve learned this year, it’s knowing what is required to be at the top level week in week out, and the processes you need to get right in the pre-season and the early parts of the year.” Reynolds backed Michael Maguire to remain the long-term coach at Red Hill. “There’s always noise around ‘Madge’ – [but] he sticks to his guns, he’s got the results, and he’s a winner,” Reynolds said.



“We’ve had injuries and suspensions and inconsistent games – none of that is down to the preparation and input Madge has over the playing group. We just haven’t lived up to our potential.” Sports news, results and expert commentary.

Mark McVeigh has been appointed Essendon coach, winning the race for the top job at the Hangar ahead of club great James Hird. McVeigh, who has signed a three-year deal, beat out other candidates for the Bombers position in Jaymie Graham and Murray Davis. He was the only candidate to make a final presentation to the board. Mark McVeigh will leave his role as an assistant coach at the Swans for the Bombers’ top job. AFL Photos “We’re not looking backwards, we’re building the next great era of this football club. That’s not built on promises. It’s built on our standards, our actions and the work we put in every single day,” McVeigh said in a statement.



Related Article Updated

AFL 2026 Butters declares he’s leaving Port, but he won’t get to Collingwood. Suns spearhead also on the move “There’s genuine talent on this list, particularly in the emerging group, but talent alone doesn’t get you where you want to go. Our job is high standards, real connection, and total clarity on how we want to play and what it means to pull on the red and black. What excites me is what this group can become together. Our job as coaches is to build an environment that gives them every chance to get there. “I want us to be brave. Aggressive with the ball, relentless without it, and a defensive system our players trust. When people watch Essendon play, there should be no confusion about what we stand for. “Pre-season will be demanding. We’re establishing our standards from day one, physically, mentally, technically. There’ll be a real emphasis on competing hard and building our game model together, so every player knows exactly what’s expected of them before a ball is bounced. “I can’t wait to get started.”



Dons president Andrew Welsh said the board’s decision to appoint McVeigh was unanimous. Related Article AFL Briefing

AFL 2026 Why the AFL CEO had a public crack at Dogs star Ed Richards “We are building the next successful era for Essendon, with a view to playing finals, winning finals and competing for premierships. Mark is the best coach to take us forward to achieve that,” Welsh said. “Mark was clearly the best candidate for what this role demands. He’s developed emerging talent throughout his coaching career, and he connects with younger players in a way that matters for a list at our stage. His game plan is built for the modern game, quick ball movement, adaptable structures, and it’s suited to where this competition is heading. “He’s coached at multiple high-performing clubs and played and coached under high-performing coaches, so he knows exactly what it takes to build a winning environment. Everything he presented to us aligned with the strategy this board has already set. We weighed every candidate against what this role actually demands, and Mark was the clear standout.”



McVeigh played 232 matches at Essendon after being chosen with pick No.9 in the 1998 national draft. After retiring in 2012 he moved back to NSW where he became an assistant coach at the Giants, and served as the club’s interim coach after Leon Cameron stood down in 2022. He coached 13 matches for four wins with his former teammates James Hird and Dean Solomon in the coaches’ box alongside him. He then moved to the Sydney Swans, where he coached as an assistant under John Longmire and Dean Cox. More to come. Keep up to date with the best AFL coverage in the country.

World.title: PM backs GST deal, leaves future taxpayers on the hook for billions
World.content:
PoliticsFederalGST PM backs GST deal, leaves future taxpayers on the hook for billions Shane Wright August 24, 2026 — 6:03pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Anthony Albanese has promised to keep a special deal to protect Western Australia’s share of the GST for as long as he is prime minister, reminding every other state that it was his government bankrolling an agreement that was on track to cost taxpayers $60 billion. Speaking in Perth, Albanese effectively made redundant a report into the deal by the Productivity Commission, which earlier this month declared the GST allocation system a “mistake” that will weigh on the federal budget into the next decade. Prime Minister Anthony Albanese has effectively killed speculation of a change to the GST deal that bankrolls the West Australian budget of Premier Roger Cook. Alex Ellinghausen “There will be no change to WA’s GST arrangements whilst I’m prime minister. That is my view. That has consistently been my view,” he told a press conference. “There will be no change.” The deal, put in place by then-treasurer Scott Morrison after the collapse in WA’s share of GST, was expected to cost around $2.3 billion. Instead, it had blown out to $23 billion by 2024 and is on track to cost $60 billion by the end of the decade.





A final report is due by year’s end, but Albanese’s declaration made redundant whatever the commission ultimately recommends. He said there should be no surprise that the institution would deliver an “economic rationalist” worldview on the deal. He pushed back at criticism from every other state and territory about the deal, noting that ultimately it was being paid by the federal government. Prime Minister Anthony Albanese in Perth yesterday. Matt Jelonek “[The] important thing that sometimes isn’t understood from some of the critique of WA getting its fair share of the GST is that those additional payments have not come from states and territories; they’ve come from the Commonwealth,” Albanese said. “I’m comfortable with that, and what I say to premiers and chief ministers, though, is that you need to bear that in mind when you are discussing federal-state financial relations.”



NSW Treasurer Daniel Mookhey, who described the Productivity Commission’s report as “superb”, said he would continue to fight for a change to WA GST arrangement. He acknowledged that the prime minister had pledged to stick with the deal, but the evidence for change was overwhelming. NSW Treasurer Daniel Mookhey has found to continue the fight to change the WA GST deal. James Brickwood “Right now, eight out of nine states and territories, Labor, Liberal, all say the current system rewards some Australians more than others, and I think that ultimately we’re going to have to continue to make our case,” he told News24. “This struggle for a fairer system will go on.



“What the Productivity Commission found was that this system is costing the Commonwealth a lot more. That it even found that in a scenario in which NSW faces a disaster, West Australia automatically gets a funding increase.” Related Article Opinion

GST The GST carve-up is cooked, but we need to stop piling onto WA Millie Muroi Economics Writer Queensland Treasurer David Janetzki said while WA’s resources sector was being recognised, his state’s contribution to the national economy was being penalised under the GST deal. “Jim Chalmers and Anthony Albanese must show that they back Queensland and that they get Queensland,” he said. “They must listen to the advice of the federal Productivity Commission and stop over-penalising other states that develop resources in the national interest.”



Victorian Treasurer Colin Brooks said that since the GST carve-up was introduced, his state had received $31 billion less than if it was allocated on a per capita basis. “The Productivity Commission’s interim findings just this month back up exactly what Victoria has been saying for years, and we’re glad to see it recognised,” he said. Related Article GST A $60b GST fiasco: State vs state argument erupts between WA and ‘east coast whingers’ “The current system isn’t working. It leaves other states like Victoria exposed and goes against the core purpose of fair distribution.” Premier Roger Cook said all West Australians were relieved and pleased to hear Albanese’s commitment on the agreement, while suggesting other states were envious of WA’s economy.



“There is a lot of noise coming from the east coast, and we understand that on the east coast people look to Western Australia, they see that our economy is going forward, that jobs are being created and opportunities for people who live in this state abound,” he said. Nationals leader Matt Canavan said the prime minister’s words could not be trusted, arguing he needed to make a more permanent commitment to the GST deal. “We need a tattoo on the PM saying he will not change the WA GST deal,” he said. World.title: What to stream this week: A gripping DC superhero story, plus five more picks
World.content:
What to stream this week (clockwise from top left): Kangaroo Island; Stalked; You’re Killing Me; Nowhere; Lanterns; and It’s Always Sunny in Philadelphia.

Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

This week’s picks include a new spin on the Green Lantern franchise, Brooke Shield’s light-hearted detective drama, a new season for the longest-running sitcom in US history and a provocative director’s surreal masterpiece. Lanterns ★★★ (HBO Max) Superheroes and mortals alike return to the same question in HBO Max’s gritty, psychological take on DC’s Green Lantern franchise: “Are you afraid?” The three words become a mantra for John Stewart (Aaron Pierre, Rebel Ridge; The Morning Show), a Lantern-in-training assigned to follow around Earth’s long-standing Lantern, Hal Jordan (Kyle Chandler, Friday Night Lights). Together, they investigate a strange shooting in Nevada with suspected intergalactic links. Without mental resolve, these intergalactic law officers can’t use their weapons – a magical emerald green ring that lets them fly and create objects, force fields and more out of sheer mind power. But fear itself is the powering force of Lanterns, a show that examines how it is used to justify acts of love, war and hatred across interpersonal relationships and intergalactic colonialism alike. Kyle Chandler as Green Lantern Hal Jordan in Lanterns. Warner Bros Created by Chris Mundy (Ozark) and produced by Damon Lindelof (Watchmen; The Leftovers) and DC writer Tom King, Lanterns is a detective drama first and a superhero show second, though there’s a solid amount of cheesy jokes and quips. Don’t worry: that dark, moody edge isn’t an excuse for terrible lighting or filters. Lanterns offers crisp visuals. At first, John and Hal couldn’t seem more opposite. While Hal’s decades of power and fame has left him arrogant and smarmy, John is comparatively robotic, a stoic ex-military man emotionally cauterised by a traumatic childhood. In Lanterns’ opening scene, he barely reacts when his father draws a close-range rifle in their backyard for a William Tell trick, shooting an apple atop his head.



Editor's pick Streaming He’s TV Mr Nice Guy, but Nathan Fillion’s ‘unlikeable’ superhero could be his greatest hit Both men are fearless, but through flashbacks across the seven of eight episodes offered for review, it’s revealed that their mental fortitude is not equal. As in the comics, John is a black man, one told as a boy that Hal and other white men are “privileged enough to not know fear”. That tension – of resentment at Hal’s ability to be a fool in public, such as getting arrested on purpose for the purposes of their investigation – is one of Lanterns’ most intriguing, understated qualities. Aaron Pierre and Kyle Chandler in Lanterns. With a weekly release schedule, it’s easy to imagine casual audiences might drop off, as early episodes find John cold and Hal a touch too irritating. At least the other characters – including Kelly Macdonald as a sheriff, and Nathan Fillion reprising his role from Superman as an abrasive Lantern – agree on that last point, too. As someone not particularly drawn to a trauma-led take on a lesser-known superhero, I found Lanterns gripping enough. It’s a balanced blend of cheesy one-liners, engaging action and emotional depth, with lots to love for fans of DC or superhero stories more broadly. You’re Killing Me ★★ (Stan) Putting aside the incessant, overdone jokes about Gen Z and that one of the characters is a true-crime podcaster, there’s a quaint 2000s feel to You’re Killing Me, a light-hearted detective drama with no pretense of prestige.



Brooke Shields with Andrea Walker, who plays a cocky true-crime podcaster in You’re Killing Me. Brooke Shields stars as crime novelist Allison, whose agent tells her to ditch the “menopausal murder mysteries” to find a new audience. Amalia Williamson (Sullivan’s Crossing) is Andrea, the headstrong, tech-adept 20-something podcaster who Alison reluctantly teams up with to write a bestseller. Naturally, that involves solving the murder mystery of the week, all while Allison makes fun of Andrea’s elaborate coffee order and Andrea lectures her about the “patriarchal elements” of Cinderella. Related Article ★★★★

Review Hugo Weaving’s compelling new Australian drama will leave you wanting more These beyond-tired jokes (never mind that they almost exclusively deal with Millennial, not Gen Z, tropes) ease up across the series’ six episodes. So does Shields, whose frantic, overwrought performance shoots for high-strung but gives Allison an aggressive, hostile edge, before mellowing out. It’s not a particularly pretty or well-made show, with the lighting and make-up departments breaking out into all-out war. But it’s fun enough, with intriguing investigations and overarching plots, including Allison’s flirtations with a cop (Tom Cavanagh) and a mystery around Andrea’s long-missing mother. Much like Allison’s crime novels, it’s not aiming to be anything other than an easy, unchallenging watch. In that, it’s successful. Kaitlin Olson, Rob Mac, Danny DeVito and Charlie Day in It’s Always Sunny in Philadelphia.



It’s Always Sunny in Philadelphia ★★★ (Disney+) Eighteen seasons in, It’s Always Sunny in Philadelphia is by far the longest-running sitcom in US history. Remarkable by any metric, it’s borderline incomprehensible given how the comedy trades in offence, following a group of deplorable friends who run a dive bar. The uninitiated should know it’s as if Curb Your Enthusiasm added in gross-out comedy and truly amoral characters played to perfection by Danny DeVito, Kaitlin Olsson, Charlie Day, Rob Mac and creator Glenn Howerton. Definitely not for everyone, the cult comedy keeps finding fresh ways to be filthy: Take upcoming episode title Frank Marries A Corpse as proof. Still from the HBO drama Stalked. Stalked ★★★ (HBO Max) In a chilling three-part documentary, three New Zealand women share their stories of being stalked by strangers, acquaintances and ex-partners. Rather than dedicate one episode to each woman, Stalked jumps between the stories of Jazz, Zeni and Tessa across its two-hour runtime to link their experiences, which include shrugging off early warning signs and the systemic failures of law and police to protect them. What elevates Stalked from more exploitative true-crime docs is the tenderness with which it’s made, with room for the women’s sense of humour to shine through alongside their traumas. Nowhere by Gregg Araki, starring Shannon Doherty (right).



Nowhere ★★★★★ (Brollie) Ahead of Gregg Araki releasing his first film in more than a decade this week (I Want Your Sex, starring Cooper Hoffman, Olivia Wilde and Charli xcx), why not watch the provocative director’s surreal masterpiece? Described by Araki as “90210 on acid”, Nowhere is a hyper-saturated sci-fi melodrama following a gigantic ensemble of beautiful 20-somethings (Shannon Doherty, Rose McGowan and Ryan Phillippe among them) adrift in an apocalyptic-tinged Los Angeles. Powered by an immense ’90s soundtrack (30-plus songs in its 82-minute runtime), Nowhere’s parody-indulgence of the era’s alt-nihilism is absurd, deeply evocative and undeniably cool. Rebecca Breeds plays Lou in Kangaroo Island. Kangaroo Island ★★★ (Netflix) There’s a touch of tourism ad to Kangaroo Island, a family drama that relies on the grandeur of its namesake and setting when it loses its spark. Based in Los Angeles, spiralling actor Lou (Rebecca Breeds) boards a plane back home to the island, greeted warmly by her father (Erik Thomson), less so by her sister (Adelaide Clemens). For all the cliches that follow, Breeds and Clemens add depth to Kangaroo Island, emanating the rage and fear that comes from siblings who have left deep wounds on each other. Want more TV? We’ve got you.

World.title: NRL to trial controversial kick-off rule change on Thursday night
World.content:
Breaking SportNRLNRL 2026 NRL to trial controversial kick-off rule change on Thursday night Adrian Proszenko August 24, 2026 — 6:00pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

The NRL will run the first trial of its controversial kick-off rule change on Thursday night in the match between Brisbane and Melbourne. In what could be a precursor to the permanent introduction of the rule for the 2027 season, the team that concedes a try will have the option to re-start by either kicking off or receiving the football. The NRL was keen to introduce the initiative at the start of this season, but backed down after a backlash from clubs. Clinton Gutherson prepares to kick off. Getty Images However, head office is keen to road-test the rule tweak in NRL and NRLW matches that have no finals implications, starting with Thursday night’s Broncos-Storm clash. It will add a point of interest to a match that is effectively a dead rubber in the run home to September. If implemented on a full-time basis, the rule change will be one of the biggest the game has undergone.



There has been fierce debate about the merits of the modification ever since this masthead first flagged it last November. It passed its first test, at a committee meeting of top coaches Wayne Bennett, Ivan Cleary, Craig Bellamy, Ricky Stuart and Craig Fitzgibbon in the off-season. Ultimately, it was put on hold after resistance from the clubs, who felt the game was being tampered with unnecessarily. However, all stakeholders will now get to watch how it works in practice under first-grade match conditions. The Broncos will be the first side to participate in the kick-off trial. Getty Images Some consideration was given to trialling it in the round 24 match between the Dragons and Tigers, but at that point Benji Marshall’s side still had a mathematical chance of qualifying for the play-offs. Not wanting to compromise the integrity of the competition, the NRL opted to wait until a match involving two teams totally out of the running, as is the case on Thursday night. There will be another chance to trial the change in the final-round clash between the Eels and the Dragons, while other opportunities may arise before then pending results.



Proponents of the change feel it could reduce blowout scorelines. Currently, the team that has just scored regains possession from the kick-off, making momentum difficult to stop. Giving the team that has just conceded a try the choice of either kicking or receiving the ball from the restart will add a new tactical element to the game. Bennett has been the most vocal advocate of the rule change, previously telling this masthead: “If you like the old rule, and you don’t like the new rule, stick with the old rule … If you listen to some of these guys [complaining], we’d still be playing with unlimited tackles, and players would still be wearing black boots with white laces.” Loading Panthers coach Ivan Cleary provided a counterpoint, previously stating that the change could stop epic comebacks like the one his side mounted to beat Brisbane in the 2023 grand final. The NRL has been unapologetic about tweaking the game to attract fans. In a recent interview, NRL executive chair Peter V’landys said the game wouldn’t have been able to broker a $5.3 billion broadcast deal if it didn’t introduce rule changes – like the six-again rule, captain’s challenge, the two-point field-goal and the short line drop-out – to make the product more entertaining.



Related Article Exclusive

NRL 2026 NRL to road-test controversial kick-off rule change in ‘dead rubber’ matches “All of those things are about unpredictability. You can’t predict what is going to happen in the game,” V’landys told Mark Bouris’ Straight Talk podcast. “And we got rid of the wrestle, which the fans hated. That’s why we’ve increased the [league] audience from 1.2 [million] to 2.4 [million]. We made it what the fan wants; not what the player wants, not what the coaches want, not what the club administrators or what the NRL want. “Who is your customer? It’s the fan. The record broadcast deal has been done because we worked for five years to get our game to a point where it was an entertainment product that can be sold at the highest price.”

World.title: Woman wins $24k after being fired from ex-husband’s nightclub over explicit photo
World.content:
BusinessWorkplaceUnfair dismissal Woman wins $24k after being fired from ex-husband’s nightclub over explicit photo Millie Muroi August 24, 2026 — 5:59pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

A bookkeeper who accidentally shared an explicit photo to a group chat and tampered with medical documents will receive more than $24,000 in compensation after being fired from her ex-husband’s nightclub. The woman, identified as “LL” in the Fair Work Commission’s judgment, was married to “CL”: the majority shareholder and managing director of Melbourne-based nightclub owner Platform One, until their marriage broke down in 2024 and family law proceedings began. The Fair Work Commission found the employee engaged in misconduct but was not provided with a safe work environment. Getty Images The case highlights the complexity of an employment dispute that is entwined with a deteriorating personal relationship between workers. LL had been working as a bookkeeper and business manager since 2014, but also performed some work “off the books” for the business before that date. She was employed by a trustee for the business.



In November 2025, after the marriage breakdown, LL was notified of the firm’s intention to terminate her employment because of “allegations of serious misconduct, an inability for you to return to work and perform the inherent requirements of your role”. Related Article Industrial relations Maths tutor fired after asking if girl, 14, wanted to be seen as ‘sex object’ The letter alleged that LL had increased her own salary without permission, sent an explicit photo to a work group chat and made unauthorised adjustments to her certificate of capacity. A week later, LL was dismissed. About the same time, her family lawyers contacted CL’s family lawyers, denying the allegations and alleging that CL was engaging in coercive control. At the end of 2024, LL had posted a photo exposing her upper body to a work WhatsApp group that included her ex-husband, other directors and managers. The photo was removed after a few minutes, and was accompanied by a message saying “enjoy” with a devil emoticon that LL said was a cover-up for her embarrassment and to pretend it was a joke.



LL said she was “mortified” after mistakenly posting the photo while driving, and provided evidence that she had intended to send the photo to her surgeon as part of a post-surgery check-up. A letter from her doctor confirmed that it was “part of standard post-operative care” to provide routine post-operative images for clinical review. While the commissioner said that sending a photo while driving was “concerning and extremely unsafe”, and that LL should have apologised and explained the situation rather than trying to make a joke, she accepted that LL had accidentally posted the photo. Separately, in April 2025, LL provided a certificate of capacity stating that she had no capacity for employment from April 18 to May 16, 2025 because of migraines, anxiety, poor concentration, poor sleep, apprehension and hypervigilance. LL conceded that she had made adjustments to the certificate, including adding a sentence that “migraine insets” were “more severe due to workplace bullying” and adding the company name, which the commissioner said constituted misconduct. While the commissioner found LL’s inappropriate remarks after posting the explicit photo, and her tampering with a medical certificate, counted as misconduct which “in certain circumstances could be a valid reason for dismissal”, she said that in this case, that conduct was not the real reason for LL’s dismissal.



“No one raised the photograph matter with LL until the show cause letter almost a year later,” the commissioner said, noting that the tampered certificate was also not raised until then. “The real reason for dismissal was not misconduct but rather the [company’s] reluctance to continue paying LL when she was not at work.” Related Article Exclusive

Unfair dismissal Sacked worker forced to pay for using ‘plain wrong’ AI in landmark case The commissioner said that LL’s inability to perform the inherent requirements of the job – due to disability, the relationship breakdown with CL and the nature of her duties working closely with CL – were a valid reason for dismissal, but found that she was not given a proper opportunity to respond, nor a warning before the show cause letter. Commissioner Susie Allison found LL’s salary had “more likely than not” been approved by CL and that it was “hard to believe” Platform One had not authorised and accepted the increase given they continued to pay her at the increased rate 10 months after it was discovered. Allison also said that the company had failed to provide LL with a safe work environment after she raised allegations of domestic violence and told the venue manager that she had found sexually explicit drawings in her inbox which she believed were placed there by CL.



While the firm claimed that CL was not involved in any decisions about LL’s employment after the marriage breakdown, the commissioner found that CL wielded “considerable power and influence” at the company, used his family lawyers to provide work directions to LL, including a request that she work from home, and that he had some involvement in the decision to fire LL. The company was ordered to pay LL compensation of $24,548 plus superannuation. Platform One was contacted for comment.
